Among the first ten Fibonacci numbers, only three are even: 2, 8 and 34.

abschnitte.text: The Fibonacci sequence starts with two ones. After that, each new number is made by adding the **two previous numbers**: 1 + 1 = 2, 1 + 2 = 3, 2 + 3 = 5 and so on. So after 13 comes 21. The number 4 does not appear in the sequence, because you jump straight from 3 to 5.

Fibonacci's real name was **Leonardo of Pisa**, and he lived from about 1170 until after 1240. As a young man he travelled to North Africa and learnt about the Arabic numerals there. In his arithmetic book **Liber abaci** of 1202 he made these numerals known in Europe. In it he also set a problem about pairs of rabbits that have a new pair every month, and their number grows according to the Fibonacci sequence.

The seeds of a **sunflower** are arranged in spirals running clockwise and anticlockwise. If you count them, you often find neighbouring Fibonacci numbers such as 34 and 55. You see something similar in pine cones, pineapples and Romanesco. In this way plants achieve a very dense and even arrangement.

If you divide a Fibonacci number by the one before it, you get closer and closer to the **golden ratio** of about 1.618. For example, 55 divided by 34 is about 1.6176. If you place squares with the Fibonacci numbers as side lengths next to each other, you get a rectangle that is almost golden. If you draw quarter circles inside, a beautiful spiral appears.

The sum of the first six Fibonacci numbers, 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 8, makes 20, which is a Fibonacci number minus 1. You can also use the rule with other starting numbers: with 2 and 5 you get 2, 5, 7, 12, 19. Such sequences are called **Fibonacci-like**. The sequence even helps with converting miles into kilometres, because 5 miles are about 8 kilometres.

begriffe.erklaerung: An ordered row of numbers formed according to a rule.
A rule in which new values are calculated from the previous ones.
A special ratio of division of about 1.618.
Fibonacci's arithmetic book from the year 1202.

gewusst: Centuries before Fibonacci, Indian scholars knew these numbers from the study of poetic metres.
The name Fibonacci means roughly “son of Bonacci”.
Every third Fibonacci number is even; all the others are odd.

teile.einleitung: In mathematics a function is a rule that assigns exactly one other number to each number. For example, the function f(x) = 2x assigns every number its double. Functions are used to describe how one quantity depends on another, for example the price on the amount.
wichtigste: A function assigns exactly one y-value to each x-value.
Functions are often written as f(x) = ..., for example f(x) = 2x−8.
The graph of a function is drawn in a coordinate system.
The graph of a linear function is a straight line with a particular gradient.
The graph of a quadratic function is a parabola.
With exponential functions something grows faster and faster, for example by doubling.
The derivative tells you how steep a graph is at a point.

abschnitte.text: A **function** is like a machine: you put in a number x and get out exactly one number f(x). With f(x) = x² − 3x, x = -2 gives the value 4 + 6 = 10. The allowed input values are called the **domain**. With f(x) = √(x−4), only numbers with x ≥ 4 may be put in, because you cannot take the square root of negative numbers.

A **linear function** has the form f(x) = mx + q, and its graph is a straight line. The number m is the **gradient**: it says how much y increases when x increases by 1. The line through (1|2) and (3|8) rises by 6 while x increases by 2, so the gradient is 3. Where the graph crosses the x-axis is the **zero**; for f(x) = 2x − 8 it is x = 4.

A **quadratic function** contains x², for example f(x) = x². Its graph is a curved line, the **parabola**. A thrown ball flies roughly along a parabola. The jet of water from a fountain has this shape too.

In an **exponential function** a value multiplies at equal time intervals. A culture of 500 bacteria that doubles every 3 hours has 500 · 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 = 8000 bacteria after 12 hours. Such growth is slow at first and then becomes very fast. Interest in a savings account grows like this too.

The **inverse function** undoes a function. The inverse function of f(x) = 2x + 3 is (x−3)/2. At upper secondary level you learn about the **derivative**, which tells you how steep the graph is at every point. The derivative of x³, for example, is 3x².

Functions describe many relationships: the fare depends on the distance, the time on the speed. Fever charts, weather forecasts and share prices are graphs of functions. The Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** introduced the notation f(x) in the 18th century. Today computer programs and spreadsheets use functions all the time too.

begriffe.erklaerung: The picture of a function in a coordinate system.
How steeply a straight line rises or falls.
A point at which the function has the value 0.
The curved line of a quadratic function.
All the numbers you are allowed to put into a function.

gewusst: Leonhard Euler from Basel was one of the most important mathematicians ever and is pictured on Switzerland's former ten-franc note.
The path of a basketball thrown at the hoop is roughly a parabola.
A satnav uses functions to calculate roughly when you will arrive.

teile.einleitung: Addition is the kind of calculation in which you add numbers together. You write it with the plus sign, for example 7 + 5 = 12. You need adding all the time: when shopping, when playing and when counting points.
wichtigste: Adding means counting together.
The sign for it is the plus sign +.
The numbers you add are called addends; the result is called the sum.
The order of the addends does not matter: 7 + 5 is the same as 5 + 7.
Adding 0 does not change a number.
Larger numbers are added in steps or in columns on paper.
Addition is the opposite of subtraction.

abschnitte.text: In **addition** you put amounts together. If Tim has 12 marbles and gets 7 more, he has 12 + 7 = 19 marbles. The numbers 12 and 7 are called **addends**, and the result 19 is called the **sum**. You read the calculation as “twelve plus seven equals nineteen”.

It gets tricky when you have to go past a ten, for example with 7 + 5. One trick is to make up to the **ten** first: 7 + 3 = 10, then add 2 more, so 12. In the same way, 8 + 6: 8 + 2 = 10, plus 4 makes 14. Doubling helps too, because 9 + 9 = 18 is double 9.

With larger numbers you work out the tens and ones separately. For 34 + 5 you only add the ones: 4 + 5 = 9, so 39. For 45 + 20 you add 2 tens, which makes 65. For 27 + 14 you work out 27 + 10 = 37 and then 37 + 4 = 41. Round numbers are especially easy: 20 + 30 = 50, because 2 + 3 = 5 tens.

Very large numbers are written **in columns**, ones under ones, tens under tens. Then you work from right to left, place by place. If a place comes to more than 9, you write the **carry** as a small number in the next column. In this way you can add numbers of any length.

In addition you may swap the addends; this is the **commutative law**. You may also put brackets anywhere, for example (2 + 3) + 5 = 2 + (3 + 5). This helps with mental arithmetic, because you can add numbers that go well together first, such as working out 6 + 7 + 4 as 6 + 4 + 7 = 17. The number 0 changes nothing in addition.

You need adding when shopping, when you add up prices. In games, too, you add up points, for example with dice or when playing Jass. Anyone who wants to know how many children are in two classes adds the two numbers. The till in a shop and a calculator do nothing other than add at lightning speed.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the numbers that are added together.
The result of an addition.
A number passed on to the next place in written calculation.
The sign + for adding.

gewusst: The plus sign has been used since the 15th century and probably comes from the Latin word “et”, which means “and”.
If you add up all the numbers from 1 to 100, you get 5050.
Inside, computers reduce almost every calculation to additions.

teile.einleitung: The prisoner's dilemma is a famous thought game from game theory. It shows why two people sometimes do not cooperate, even though that would be better for both. The dilemma helps us understand conflict, competition and cooperation between people, companies and states.
wichtigste: Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher developed the game in 1950 at the RAND Corporation in the USA.
The mathematician Albert W. Tucker invented the story of the two prisoners and gave it its name.
The prisoner's dilemma is a non-zero-sum game, in which both can win or both can lose.
For each individual it pays to confess, whatever the other one does.
If both confess, they end up in the Nash equilibrium, which is worse for both than staying silent together.
In the repeated game, the strategy Tit for Tat won Robert Axelrod's tournament.
An arms race between states is regarded as a well-known real-life example.

abschnitte.text: Two suspects are questioned separately and cannot agree on anything. If both stay silent, both get only 1 year in prison for a minor offence. If both confess, both get 4 years. If only one confesses, he goes free as a **key witness**, and the other has to go to prison for 6 years.

Each prisoner thinks it through for himself: if the other stays silent, confessing is better, because then I go free. If the other confesses, confessing is also better, because then I get 4 years instead of 6. So confessing is always the better choice; this is called a **dominant strategy**. So both confess and get 8 years between them, although by staying silent they would have had only 2 years between them.

The situation in which both confess is called the **Nash equilibrium**, named after the mathematician John Nash. In this state, neither can gain anything by changing his decision alone. Even so, the result is not **Pareto-optimal**, because both could be better off at the same time if they stayed silent. This shows: if everyone looks only at their own advantage, the result can be bad for everyone.

If the same people play the game many times in a row, the situation changes. Around 1980 the political scientist Robert Axelrod had computer programs compete against each other in a tournament. The winner was the simple strategy **Tit for Tat**, submitted by the researcher Anatol Rapoport. It cooperates on the first move and after that always copies the opponent's last move.

A well-known example is the **arms race** between two states: both would save money by buying fewer weapons, but neither wants to be weaker than the other. It is similar with price wars between two shops or with protecting the environment. The pattern also appears with doping in sport or with fishing at sea. Treaties, checks and trust help to get out of the dilemma.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of mathematics that studies decisions made by several participants.
A state in which nobody does better by making a different choice alone.
Nobody can be made better off without someone else being made worse off.
Working together for a shared advantage.
A game in which one player's gain is not automatically the other's loss.

gewusst: Tit for Tat won the tournament although it did not score more points than any single opponent; it simply did fairly well against all of them.
John Nash received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1994, and his life was told in the film “A Beautiful Mind”.
Biologists use the prisoner's dilemma to explain why animals sometimes help each other.

teile.einleitung: Two shapes are similar if they look the same and differ only in size. One is then an enlarged or reduced copy of the other. We come across similarity in maps, models, photos and paper sizes.
wichtigste: Similar shapes have equal angles, and their sides are in the same ratio.
The enlargement factor is called the scale factor.
If all lengths are enlarged by the factor k, the area becomes k² times and the volume k³ times as big.
Two triangles are definitely similar if two angles match.
Maps and models are reduced, similar images of reality.
Paper sizes such as A4 have the aspect ratio 1 to √2, so that halved sheets stay similar.

abschnitte.text: In mathematics two shapes are called **similar** if all corresponding angles are equal and all sides have been enlarged or reduced by the same factor. This factor is called the **scale factor** k. A photo measuring 10 cm by 15 cm whose short side is enlarged to 20 cm has the factor 2. So the long side becomes 30 cm long. All circles are similar to each other, and so are all squares.

With triangles, very little is needed to recognise similarity. If **two angles** match, the third is equal too, because the angles always add up to 180 degrees. The Greek scholar **Thales** already used similar triangles to work out the height of a pyramid from the length of its shadow. The **intercept theorems** are based on this idea too.

If a shape is enlarged by the factor 3, its area does not become 3 times as big but 3 times 3, that is **9 times** as big. For solids the **volume** even grows with k to the power of 3. A model at a scale of 1 to 10 therefore has only a thousandth of the volume of the original. That is why a cube twice as big is not twice but eight times as heavy.

The Swiss **national maps** from swisstopo are available, for example, at a **scale** of 1 to 25,000. One centimetre on the map then equals 25,000 cm, that is 250 m. If two places are 6 cm apart, the distance as the crow flies is 1.5 km. On a 1 to 50,000 map, 1 cm² even equals 0.25 km², because you have to convert both sides. Model railways are similar reductions too; the popular H0 gauge has the scale 1 to 87.

The paper sizes of the **A series** have the aspect ratio 1 to √2. If you fold an A4 sheet in the middle, you get two A5 sheets with exactly the same shape. That is why photocopiers reduce A4 to A5 without distortion at about 71 per cent. In geometry, by the way, an **enlargement from a centre** with the factor minus 1 is the same as a point reflection.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two shapes have the same form but possibly a different size.
The number by which all lengths are multiplied when enlarging or reducing.
The ratio between a length on a map or model and the real length.
A transformation in which a shape is enlarged or reduced from a fixed point.

gewusst: Russian matryoshka dolls are nesting, almost similar figures.
An A0 sheet has an area of exactly one square metre.
A giant ten times as tall as a person would be a thousand times as heavy, but the cross-section of his bones would be only a hundred times as big.

teile.einleitung: When making up to 100, you ask how much is still missing from a number to reach exactly 100. This is an important mental arithmetic exercise in primary school. In everyday life it helps, for example, when giving change.
wichtigste: Making up to 100 means finding the number that is missing to reach 100.
From 70 to 100, 30 are missing; from 45 to 100, 55 are missing.
Numbers that add up to 100 are called number bonds to 100, for example 40 and 60.
A good trick is to make up to the next ten first.
You make the ones up to 10 and the tens up to 9.
You can check the result with the inverse calculation.

abschnitte.text: When making up, you look for the **missing number** in a calculation such as 38 + ? = 100. The answer is 62. You can also write the calculation as a subtraction: 100 − 38 = 62. Both describe the same distance between two numbers on the number line.
A tried and tested way goes via the next **ten**. With 27, you first count up to 30, which is 3. Then from 30 to 100 another 70 are missing. Together that is 73, because 27 + 73 = 100.

For many numbers there is a **rule of thumb**: make the ones up to 10 and the tens up to 9. With 81, you make the 1 up to 10, which is 9, and the 8 up to 9, which is 1. So you get 19, and indeed 81 + 19 = 100. With round tens such as 70 it is simpler: 7 tens plus 3 tens make 10 tens, so 30 are missing.

Lena pays for a chewing gum costing 65 centimes with one franc. A franc has 100 centimes, so she gets 35 centimes **change**. A book has 100 pages and Tim has already read 12, so he still has 88 to go. Making up also helps when collecting points in a game.

At school, people often use the **hundred square** with 10 by 10 dots. The dots already filled in show the number, and the empty spaces show what is missing. A counting frame with 100 beads or a number line also helps you picture it. If you know the number bonds to 10 well, you will find the ones to 100 more quickly too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Finding out how much is still missing from a number to reach a target.
A bundle of ten ones; the place to the left of the ones.
A grid of 10 by 10 dots for showing numbers up to 100.
The opposite calculation, used to check a result.

gewusst: The number missing from 99 to 100 is 1; from 1 to 100 it is 99.
For 50, the number needed to make 100 is 50 again, so the number makes itself up.
In Switzerland the franc is divided into 100 centimes, which is why making up to 100 is especially handy when paying.

teile.einleitung: A chart, or diagram, is a picture that shows numbers and data clearly. Instead of a long list, you see at a glance what is big or small and how something changes. You find charts in school books, newspapers and the weather forecast.
wichtigste: A chart shows data as a picture.
Parts of a whole are best shown with a pie chart.
Changes over time are shown with a line graph.
Column and bar charts are good for comparing amounts.
In a pie chart, 100 per cent equals a full circle of 360 degrees.
The mean and the median sum up data with a single number.
A Venn diagram uses circles to show what sets have in common and how they differ.

abschnitte.text: In a **column chart**, upright columns stand side by side: the taller the column, the bigger the value. If the bars lie horizontally, it is called a bar chart. These charts are good for comparing, for example how many bread rolls for the mid-morning snack (Znüni) were sold on each day of the week. A labelled axis and a suitable scale are important.

A **pie chart** shows how a whole is split into parts. The whole circle is 100 per cent or 360 degrees. If 25 per cent stands for the cyclists, their sector is 90 degrees, a quarter of the circle. If 12 out of 30 children like pizza best, that is 12/30 of 360 degrees, that is 144 degrees.

A **line graph** joins points with a line and so shows how something changes over time. A typical example is the temperature over a day or a year. You can see at once when it was warmest and whether the values are rising or falling. Children's growth curves are shown this way too.

Often you want to describe many values with one number. The **average** or mean is the sum of all values divided by how many there are. For 4, 7, 5, 8 and 6 rolls that makes 30 : 5 = 6 a day. The **median** is the middle value when you put all the values in order: for 3, 4, 5, 7, 9 it is the 5.

A **Venn diagram** shows sets as circles that overlap. In the shared part are things that belong to both sets. This lets you show, for example, which children have a pet, which play an instrument and which do both. It is named after the English mathematician John Venn, who made it known around 1880.

Charts can also mislead, if the axis does not start at zero. Then small differences suddenly look huge. That is why it is always worth looking closely at the labels and units. Many charts about Switzerland are published by the **Federal Statistical Office**, for example on the population or the weather.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line with a scale on which you read off the values.
A slice of the pie in a pie chart.
The sum of all values divided by how many there are.
The value in the middle when you put all the values in order.

gewusst: The Scotsman William Playfair invented the bar chart and the pie chart at the end of the 18th century.
The nurse Florence Nightingale used charts to show that many soldiers died of disease rather than of their wounds.
A climate chart shows the temperature and rainfall of a place at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Semi-written calculation is a method between mental arithmetic and written calculation. You break a calculation down into smaller, easy steps and note down the results in between. That way you can calculate even larger numbers safely and in a way you understand.
wichtigste: In semi-written calculation you split numbers into hundreds, tens and ones.
You write down the results in between, but the calculating is done in your head.
For 34 + 25 you work out 30 + 20 = 50 and 4 + 5 = 9, together 59.
When subtracting, you take away step by step, for example 85 − 30 − 2 = 53.
When multiplying, you split one factor: 6 · 14 = 6 · 10 + 6 · 4.
When dividing, you divide in suitable parts: 48 : 4 = 40 : 4 + 8 : 4 = 12.
The method is practised in Swiss primary schools before written calculation.

abschnitte.text: In **semi-written calculation** you do not write digits in columns as in written calculation. Instead you break the task into easy **steps** that you can solve in your head. You note down the results in between so that you do not forget anything. The method shows especially well how numbers are built up from **place values**.

One way is to add the tens and ones separately. For 34 + 25 you work out 30 + 20 = 50 and 4 + 5 = 9, so 59. You can also go step by step: 56 + 27 is 56 + 20 = 76 and then 76 + 7 = 83. With larger numbers such as 125 + 240, you add the hundreds, tens and ones separately and get 365.

When taking away, you first take away the tens and then the ones. So 85 − 32 becomes 85 − 30 = 55 and 55 − 2 = 53. For 73 − 45 you work out 73 − 40 = 33 and 33 − 5 = 28. You can also **count on** and ask how much is missing from 45 to 73.

When multiplying, you split one factor into tens and ones. So 6 · 14 is the same as 6 · 10 + 6 · 4, that is 60 + 24 = 84. For 3 · 23 you work out 3 · 20 = 60 and 3 · 3 = 9, together 69. When dividing, you split the number into parts that are easy to divide: 48 : 4 is 40 : 4 + 8 : 4, that is 12.

Semi-written calculation builds **number sense**, because you see why a way of calculating works. There are often several ways, and you can choose the easiest. The method is good preparation for written calculation and for mental arithmetic in everyday life. If you calculate like this, you can also estimate results better and find mistakes more easily.

begriffe.erklaerung: The value of a digit depending on its position, such as ones, tens or hundreds.
Dividing a number into smaller parts, for example 34 into 30 and 4.
The result of one step, which you note down and use further.
Roughly working out a result to check whether the exact calculation can be right.

gewusst: The trick of multiplying by splitting is called the distributive law in mathematics.
Many adults calculate in a semi-written way in everyday life without noticing, for example when adding up prices.
Sometimes it is easier to go via a round number: 99 + 46 is 100 + 46 − 1 = 145.

teile.einleitung: Rules of differentiation are calculation rules that let you find the derivative of a function quickly, without working out a limit every time. With just a few rules you can differentiate almost all the functions that come up at school. They are the basic tools of differential calculus.
wichtigste: The power rule says: the derivative of xⁿ is n · xⁿ⁻¹.
The derivative of a constant is zero.
Sums are differentiated term by term; constant factors stay as they are.
Products use the product rule, fractions the quotient rule.
Composite functions are differentiated with the chain rule.
The exponential function eˣ is its own derivative.
The derivative of ln(x) is 1/x.

abschnitte.text: The **power rule** says: with xⁿ, the exponent moves to the front as a factor and the exponent becomes one smaller. So x⁷ becomes 7x⁶. By the **constant factor rule**, constant factors simply stay as they are, and by the sum rule you differentiate each term separately. For f(x) = 3x⁴ − 2x + 5 this gives f'(x) = 12x³ − 2, because the constant 5 drops out. The power rule also works for roots and fractions: √x has the derivative 1/(2√x), and 1/x has the derivative −1/x².

If a function is a product u · v, the **product rule** applies: (u · v)' = u' · v + u · v'. So you differentiate one factor at a time and leave the other as it is. For f(x) = x · eˣ you get 1 · eˣ + x · eˣ, that is (1 + x) · eˣ. A common mistake is simply to differentiate both factors separately and multiply them. That almost always gives a wrong result.

For a fraction u/v the **quotient rule** applies: (u/v)' = (u' · v − u · v') / v². A way to remember it: “derivative of the top times the bottom, minus the top times the derivative of the bottom, all over the bottom squared.” For f(x) = x/(x + 1) you get ((x + 1) − x)/(x + 1)², that is 1/(x + 1)². The rule only works where the denominator is not zero.

When one function sits inside another, it is called a **composition**. The **chain rule** says: outer derivative times inner derivative. For f(x) = (3x + 1)² the outer derivative is 2(3x + 1) and the inner one is 3, so together 6(3x + 1). With the chain rule you can also differentiate functions such as sin(2x) or e to the power x². It is the most important rule for complicated functions.

Some derivatives are best learnt by heart. The natural **exponential function** eˣ has itself as its derivative. For other bases, for example, (2ˣ)' = 2ˣ · ln(2). The natural **logarithm** ln(x) has the derivative 1/x. For the trigonometric functions, (sin x)' = cos x and (cos x)' = −sin x.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rule for differentiating powers: xⁿ becomes n · xⁿ⁻¹.
A rule for differentiating the product of two functions.
A rule for differentiating a fraction made of two functions.
A rule for functions nested inside each other: outer times inner derivative.
A special number, about 2.718, the base of the natural exponential function.

gewusst: Apart from constant multiples, the function eˣ is the only function that stays exactly the same when you differentiate it.
If you differentiate sin(x) four times in a row, you get back to sin(x).
Many of these rules were already set out by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in the 17th century.

teile.einleitung: A subscription is a contract in which you pay regularly for something, for example for a magazine, a mobile phone, streaming or public transport. Whether a subscription is worth it can be worked out with simple maths. You compare the subscription price with the single prices.
wichtigste: With a subscription you pay a fixed amount regularly, for example per month or per year.
An annual subscription is often cheaper than twelve separate monthly subscriptions.
A subscription pays off from the number of uses at which it costs less than buying each one separately.
You find the break-even point by dividing the subscription price by the single price.
A notice period decides how long a subscription keeps running after you cancel it.
In Switzerland the Half Fare travelcard and the GA travelcard are well-known public transport subscriptions.

abschnitte.text: The German word **Abonnement** comes from French. You sign a contract and in return receive something regularly, such as a magazine every month or continuous access to music, films or the mobile network. You pay a fixed amount per month or per year. Many subscriptions renew **automatically** if you do not cancel them in time.

To compare subscriptions, it is best to work out the **annual costs**. A streaming subscription at 12.90 francs a month costs 12 times 12.90 a year, that is 154.80 francs. If a subscription costs 12 francs a month or 120 francs as an annual subscription, you save 144 minus 120, that is 24 francs, with the annual one. If a subscription is free for the first three months and costs 9.90 francs after that, you pay 9 times 9.90 in the first year, that is 89.10 francs.

A ticket to the swimming pool costs 8 francs, for example, and a **season pass** 96 francs. If you divide 96 by 8 you see: at 12 visits both cost the same, and from the 13th visit the pass pays off. This point is called the **break-even point**. A magazine costs 6 francs on its own, so twelve issues cost 72 francs; the annual subscription for 54 francs saves 18 francs, that is 25 per cent.

Mobile phone contracts often have **flat rates** and prices per minute or per gigabyte. Contract A costs, for example, 30 francs for unlimited calls, contract B 10 francs plus 0.50 francs per minute. At 40 minutes both cost 30 francs; if you phone more, contract A is cheaper. You can solve comparisons like this with a table or an **equation**.

With the **Half Fare travelcard** you travel on trains, buses and boats in Switzerland at half price. If it costs, say, 190 francs and a normal ticket costs 38 francs, you save 19 francs per journey, so after 10 journeys the travelcard has paid for itself. With the **GA travelcard** (General Abonnement) you can use almost all public transport in Switzerland as much as you like. There are special, cheaper offers for young people.

Before signing up you should read the small print: how long does the subscription run, and what **notice period** applies? With a notice period of three months, the subscription only ends three months after you cancel. Children and young people under 18 need their parents' permission for subscriptions they cannot pay for with their pocket money. It is worth checking regularly which subscriptions you really still use.

begriffe.erklaerung: A contract in which you pay regularly for a service.
The time between cancelling and the end of the contract.
The point at which the subscription and single purchases cost exactly the same.
A fixed price, no matter how much you use something.

gewusst: Lots of small subscriptions of a few francs a month can add up to several hundred francs a year.
Free trial subscriptions often turn automatically into paid subscriptions if you do not cancel in time.
Newspaper subscriptions have existed for hundreds of years, long before there was streaming.

teile.einleitung: Water is the most important substance for all life on Earth. Without water, no human, no animal and no plant could survive. Chemically, water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen with the formula H2O.
wichtigste: Water has the chemical formula H2O.
Clean water is transparent and has no smell.
At room temperature water is liquid.
At sea level water boils at 100 degrees and freezes at 0 degrees.
Most of the Earth's water is in the seas.
In Switzerland most drinking water comes from springs and groundwater.
Water that falls from the clouds is called rain.

abschnitte.text: A water molecule consists of two **hydrogen atoms** and one oxygen atom. Pure water is transparent, tasteless and has no smell. At room temperature it is liquid, below 0 degrees it turns into ice, and at sea level it boils at 100 degrees. The Celsius temperature scale was defined using exactly these two points.

Water exists in three **states of matter**: solid as ice and snow, liquid as water and gas as water vapour. Unlike most substances, water expands when it freezes. That is why ice floats on top, and frozen water can even split rocks. For this reason lakes freeze from the top down, and fish can survive underneath.

About 71 per cent of the Earth's surface is covered with water. Most of it, around 97 per cent, is salt water in the **seas**. Only a small part is fresh water, and much of that is frozen in the ice of the poles and glaciers. Water evaporates from puddles, lakes and rivers, forms clouds and falls back down as rain.

Switzerland is called the **water tower of Europe** because large rivers such as the Rhine, the Rhône and the Inn have their source here. There are around 1500 lakes; the largest lying entirely within Switzerland is Lake Neuchâtel. Most drinking water comes from **springs** and **groundwater**, a smaller part from lakes. Tap water in Switzerland is of very good quality and can be drunk without worry.

An adult's body is about 60 per cent water. We constantly lose water through sweating, breathing and going to the toilet. That is why children should drink roughly one to one and a half litres every day, ideally water or unsweetened tea. Without drinking, a person survives only a few days.

We need water for drinking, cooking, washing and in farming. In Switzerland a large share of electricity is generated with hydropower, for example in reservoirs such as the Lac des Dix. In the past, water drove mills and sawmills. Because water is so precious, waste water is cleaned in **sewage treatment plants** before it flows back into nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest particle of a substance, made of several atoms; for water it is H2O.
Water that collects in the ground between stones and sand.
Water with very little salt, as in rivers and lakes.
A facility that makes dirty waste water clean again.

gewusst: Water is densest at about 4 degrees, which is why the bottom of deep lakes is often exactly that cold.
A drop of water may already have travelled many times through clouds, rivers and living things in the water cycle.
The glaciers of the Alps store huge amounts of fresh water as ice.

teile.einleitung: A birthday calendar is a calendar in which you write down the birthdays of your family, friends or school class. Because it has no years and no days of the week, you can use it again every year. That way you never forget a birthday again.
wichtigste: A birthday calendar is arranged by the 12 months of the year.
It usually has no days of the week, so that it fits every year.
It often hangs at home in a place where you see it every day.
Many school classes have a shared birthday calendar.
With it you can put the months in order and count the days until the next celebration.
February is the shortest month and has 28 or 29 days.
Anyone born on 29 February only has a birthday on the real date every four years.

abschnitte.text: A birthday calendar shows all the days of the year, but without the year. At each date you write the names of the people whose birthday it is. Because birthdays are on the same date every year, you can use it again and again. That is why it is also called a **perpetual calendar**.

The year begins with **January** and ends with **December**. In between come February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October and November. So after March comes April. Someone whose birthday is in February celebrates earlier in the year than someone in July or October.

A birthday calendar is good for practising arithmetic. If today is 3 June and the birthday is on 10 June, there are 7 days to go. If today is Monday and the birthday is in 2 days, it falls on a **Wednesday**. And anyone who turns 7 today will be 8 on their next birthday.

In many classrooms there is a birthday calendar on the wall, often with pictures or photos of the children. That way the whole class knows when someone is celebrating and can sing a song or say happy birthday. Lisa, whose birthday is on 5 May, comes before Tim, for example, whose birthday is on 12 May. Anyone with a birthday in the **summer holidays** often celebrates at school before or after the holidays.

You can easily make your own birthday calendar. You need 12 sheets, one for each month, and write the days from 1 to 31 on them. February gets 29 boxes so that there is room for the **leap day** too. You can add new friends at any time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A way of dividing time into days, weeks, months and years.
One of the 12 parts of the year, with 28 to 31 days.
A year with 366 days, in which February has a 29th day.
A calendar without a year that you can use again every year.

gewusst: In a group of just 23 people, the probability that two share a birthday is already more than a half.
In many families in German-speaking countries, the birthday calendar traditionally hangs in the bathroom or the toilet.
People born on 29 February usually celebrate on 28 February or 1 March in the other years.

teile.einleitung: The unit price shows how much a fixed quantity of a product costs, for example one kilogram or one litre. In shops it is usually printed small on the price label. With it you can compare different pack sizes fairly and find out what is really cheaper.
wichtigste: The unit price gives the price for a fixed quantity such as 1 kg, 1 litre or 100 g.
It helps you compare packs of different sizes.
You work it out with the rule of three or a division.
In Switzerland the Price Disclosure Ordinance sets out how prices must be shown.
Large packs are often, but not always, cheaper.
If you pay attention to the unit price, you can save money when shopping.

abschnitte.text: On a price label, next to the **selling price**, there is often a smaller number, the **unit price**. It tells you how much a certain quantity costs, for example “per kg”, “per litre” or “per 100 g”. That way you can see how expensive the product itself is, no matter how big the pack. This is important because packs often contain odd quantities such as 180 g or 750 ml.

You divide the price by the quantity and scale up to the base quantity; this is the **rule of three**. If 500 g of pasta costs 2.40 francs, then 1 kg costs twice as much, that is 4.80 francs. 250 g of butter for 3.50 francs gives 14.00 francs per kilogram. A 1.5-litre bottle of mineral water for 0.90 francs costs 0.60 francs per litre.

Rice, for example, comes in a 400 g pack for 3.20 francs and in a 750 g pack for 5.70 francs. With the small pack 1 kg costs 8.00 francs, with the large pack only 7.60 francs. So here the **larger pack** is cheaper. Sometimes it is the other way round, for example with special offers on small packs, which is why it is worth looking at the unit price.

In Switzerland the **Price Disclosure Ordinance** sets out how shops must show prices. Products must be labelled with the price actually to be paid in francs. For many packaged foods and other goods sold by weight or volume, the unit price must also be given. This is meant to protect **consumers** and make price comparisons easier.

In the shop, look for the small number with “per kg” or “per l”. Compare with the same base quantity, so kilo with kilo and litre with litre. A yoghurt of 180 g for 0.90 francs costs 0.50 francs per 100 g. And a shampoo of 300 ml for 4.50 francs would cost 15.00 francs per litre; but a low unit price is only useful if you really need that quantity.

begriffe.erklaerung: The price for a fixed quantity such as 1 kg or 1 litre.
A three-step method for working from one quantity to another.
The Swiss rule on how prices must be shown in shops.
A person who buys and uses goods.

gewusst: Sometimes large packs are even more expensive per kilogram than small packs.
Spices often cost more per kilogram than meat, because you buy them only in tiny amounts.
For goods sold loose at the counter, such as cheese or meat, the price is usually shown directly per 100 g or per kg.

teile.einleitung: The arithmetic mean is what we usually call the average in everyday life. You add up all the values and divide the sum by the number of values. This is how you work out, for example, the average mark on a school report or the mean temperature of a week.
wichtigste: The arithmetic mean is the sum of all values divided by how many there are.
In everyday life it is usually just called the average or mean.
The marks 5, 4.5, 6 and 4.5 give an average of 5.
If you know the mean and the number of values, you get the sum by multiplying.
A single extremely large value can change the mean a lot.
You can also take the mean of negative numbers, such as temperatures below zero.

abschnitte.text: To find the **arithmetic mean**, you add all the values and divide by how many there are. On five days, for example, you measure 12, 15, 9, 14 and 10 degrees. The sum is 60, and 60 divided by 5 gives an **average temperature** of 12 degrees. A cyclist who rides 42 km, 35 km and 49 km manages on average 126 divided by 3, that is 42 km a day.

In Swiss schools marks go from 1 to 6, where 6 is the best and 4 or more is a pass. Lea has the marks 5, 4.5, 6 and 4.5. Together that makes 20, and divided by 4 this gives an **average mark** of 5. Sometimes tests count for different amounts; then you work out a **weighted mean**. A test with double weighting is simply counted twice.

Because the mean times the number of values gives the **sum**, you can also work backwards. If the average of 4 numbers is 8, their sum is 32. If the number 11 is added to 4 numbers with a mean of 6, the new sum is 24 + 11 = 35, and the new mean is 35 divided by 5, that is 7. If the mean of three numbers is 10 and two of them are 8 and 9, the third must be 30 minus 17, that is 13.

The arithmetic mean reacts strongly to **outliers**, single values that are extremely large or small. If nine people each earn 5000 francs and one person earns a million, the average is over 100,000 francs, although almost everyone has much less. In such cases the **median** tells you more. It is the value exactly in the middle when you put all the values in order of size.

We meet means everywhere: in the weather forecast, in sport, in traffic counts or in statistics. The calculation works the same way with **negative numbers**. The mean of minus 3, 5, 7 and minus 1 is 8 divided by 4, that is 2. The term comes from **statistics**, a branch of mathematics that collects and analyses data.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sum of all values divided by the number of values.
The middle value when you put all the values in order of size.
A value that is much larger or smaller than the others.
An average in which some values count more than others.

gewusst: The average does not even have to be one of the values; on average a family has 1.5 children, for example.
Almost everyone has more legs than the average, because a few people have fewer than two legs.
The word “arithmetic” comes from the Greek word arithmos for number.

teile.einleitung: The expected value is a number from probability theory that tells you what result you can expect on average in a random experiment. It shows, for example, whether a game of chance pays off in the long run. Insurance companies, casinos and scientists use it every day.
wichtigste: The expected value is the mean you expect over a very large number of repetitions.
You calculate it by multiplying each result by its probability and adding everything up.
When rolling a fair dice, the expected value is 3.5.
In a fair game the expected winnings are zero.
In lotteries and at the casino, the expected winnings for players are negative.
By the law of large numbers, the average of many trials gets closer to the expected value.

abschnitte.text: In a **random experiment** you do not know beforehand what will happen. The expected value tells you what happens on average if you repeat it very often. When rolling a dice, the numbers 1 to 6 are equally likely, and their average is 3.5. So the expected value does not even have to be a possible result.

You multiply each possible result by its **probability** and add everything together. A wheel of fortune pays out nothing with probability 1/2, three francs with 1/3 and twelve francs with 1/6. That gives 0 + 1 + 2, so an expected payout of 3 francs. If you roll a dice 60 times, you expect 60 times 1/6, that is 10 sixes.

A game is called **fair** if the expected winnings are zero. A ticket for 2 francs that brings 15 francs with probability 1/10 has expected winnings of minus 0.50 francs. In roulette with 37 numbers, if you bet 1 franc on red, you lose 1/37 franc on average. That is why the casino always wins in the long run.

Insurance companies use the expected value to calculate their **premiums**. If damage of 20,000 francs happens with a probability of 0.5 per cent a year, the expected damage is 100 francs a year. The premium must be at least that high so that the insurer does not lose money in the long term. The insurance is still worthwhile for customers, because it protects them from a big loss.

The idea arose in the 17th century when Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat were thinking about games of chance. The Dutchman **Christiaan Huygens** wrote one of the first treatises on it in 1657. Important calculation rules still apply today: if X has the expected value 4, then 2X + 3 has the expected value 11. With two dice, the expected values add up to 3.5 + 3.5 = 7.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number whose value depends on chance, for example the score on a dice.
How certain it is that an event happens, as a number between 0 and 1.
A game in which you neither win nor lose on average.
The rule by which the average of many trials gets closer to the expected value.

gewusst: The expected value of a single dice roll is 3.5, although you can never roll a 3.5.
For the sum of two dice, 7 is the most common result and at the same time the expected value.
In English the term is called “expected value” and in formulas it is often written E(X).

teile.einleitung: A receipt is the small strip of paper you get at the till after shopping. It shows what you have bought, how much each product costs and what the total is. With the receipt you can check whether everything is right and check your change.
wichtigste: The receipt lists all the products bought with their prices.
Right at the bottom is the total, the sum of all the prices.
The change is the amount paid minus the total.
In Switzerland people calculate in francs and centimes; 1 franc has 100 centimes.
The receipt is a proof of purchase with which you can exchange goods or make a complaint.
Many receipts are printed on thermal paper, which fades over time.

abschnitte.text: At the top of the **receipt** there are usually the name and address of the shop. Below come the products, for example bread 3 francs and milk 2 francs. If you buy several identical things, the number is often shown too, for example 3 bread rolls (Brötli) at 1 franc each. Right at the bottom is the **total**; here it would be 5 francs altogether. You can also see the date, the time and the payment method, for example cash or card.

The total is the **sum** of all the prices on the receipt. A yoghurt for 1 franc 50 and an apple for 50 centimes cost 2 francs together. Two croissants (Gipfeli) at 1 franc 50 each cost 3 francs together. When checking, it helps to add up the francs first and then the centimes. That way you quickly notice if something was entered twice at the till.

If you pay with a note bigger than the total, you get **change**. You work out the amount paid minus the total. If the shopping costs 7 francs and you pay with 10 francs, you get 3 francs back. With a total of 15 francs and a 20-franc note, it is 5 francs. With 8 francs 40 and 10 francs, you can count up from the total: 60 centimes to 9 francs and another 1 franc to 10, so 1 franc 60.

The receipt is **proof** that you have bought and paid for something. If an appliance breaks, you often need it for the **guarantee**, which in Switzerland usually lasts two years for new goods. Shops usually ask for the receipt when you exchange clothes, too. Anyone who keeps a household budget can see exactly from the receipts what the money was spent on. Many receipts in Switzerland also show how much VAT is included in the price.

Most receipts are printed on **thermal paper**. This paper turns black where the printer heats it, so it needs no ink. Over time, in sunlight or heat, the writing fades, though. Important receipts should therefore be copied or photographed. Many shops today also offer digital receipts in an app to save paper.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sum of all the prices you have to pay.
The money you get back when you have paid too much.
A paper or document that proves something happened, for example a purchase.
Value added tax, a tax included in the prices of most goods that goes to the state.
Paper that changes colour with heat and can therefore be printed without ink.

gewusst: In Switzerland thermal paper does not go in the waste paper but in the household rubbish.
A receipt often also has a receipt number so that the shop can find every purchase again.
In Switzerland a lower VAT rate applies to food than to most other goods.

teile.einleitung: The binomial formulas are three calculation rules with which you can quickly multiply out expressions such as (a + b)². They are among the most important tools of algebra. With them you can even solve difficult calculations such as 99² in your head.
wichtigste: First binomial formula: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b².
Second binomial formula: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
Third binomial formula: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
They help with multiplying out and with factorising terms.
With them you can calculate in your head, for example 99² = (100 − 1)² = 9801.
A binomial is an expression made of two terms, such as a + b.
The formulas can be shown clearly with squares and rectangles.

abschnitte.text: The **first binomial formula** is (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². The **second** is (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; it differs only in the sign of the middle term. The **third** is (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²; here the middle term disappears completely. Many people forget the middle term 2ab, so a typical mistake is (a + b)² = a² + b².

By the second formula, (x − 3)² gives x² − 6x + 9. With (3a + 2b)² you must square the whole terms: 9a² + 12ab + 4b². By the third formula, (2x + 5)(2x − 5) = 4x² − 25. And (-x − 4)² gives x² + 8x + 16, because a minus times a minus makes a plus. Also, (x + 1)² − (x − 1)² simplifies to 4x.

The formulas also work backwards; this is called **factorising**. You recognise the term x² + 10x + 25 as (x + 5)², because 25 = 5² and 10x = 2 · x · 5. In 9x² + ... + 49, the middle term must be 2 · 3x · 7 = 42x for a complete square to form. This completing is called **completing the square** and helps with solving quadratic equations.

The binomial formulas are a great trick for **mental arithmetic**. You work out 99² as (100 − 1)² = 10,000 − 200 + 1 = 9801. For 51 · 49 you write (50 + 1)(50 − 1) = 2500 − 1 = 2499. And 21² is quick too: (20 + 1)² = 400 + 40 + 1 = 441.

You can show the first formula with a square of side length a + b. It splits into a large square a², a small square b² and two equal **rectangles** ab. More than 2000 years ago, the Greek mathematician **Euclid** already described such relationships with geometric figures. The name comes from the word **binomial**, an expression with two terms.

begriffe.erklaerung: An expression made of two terms, for example a + b.
Removing brackets by multiplying every term by every other term.
Turning a sum into a product.
The middle term 2ab in the first two formulas.
Adding to a term so that a binomial formula appears.

gewusst: With the third formula you can see at once that 1000² − 999² is exactly 1999.
The binomial formulas are a special case of the binomial theorem with Pascal's triangle.
There is also a formula for (a + b)³, namely a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³.

teile.einleitung: A dozen is an old counting measure and means exactly 12 items. Eggs are still often sold by the dozen or half dozen today. The word is a leftover from a time when people liked to count in groups of twelve.
wichtigste: A dozen is 12 items.
Half a dozen is 6 items, two dozen are 24.
A gross is 12 dozen, that is 144 items.
A baker's dozen is 13 items.
The word dozen comes from the Latin “duodecim”, which means twelve.
The number 12 can be divided by 2, 3, 4 and 6, which makes it handy for sharing out.

abschnitte.text: A **dozen** is a counting quantity and means 12 items. People talk about a dozen eggs, roses or pencils. Half a dozen is 6 items, two dozen are 24. If a box for a dozen eggs has only 9 eggs in it so far, 3 are still missing.

The German word Dutzend came into German via the French “douzaine”. It goes back to the Latin **“duodecim”**, which means twelve. In the past almost every region had its own counting measures for goods. Besides the dozen there was, for example, the Mandel with 15 items and the Schock with 60 items.

Twelve dozen make a **gross**, that is 12 · 12 = 144 items. The word comes from the French “grosse douzaine”, big dozen. A **baker's dozen** is 13 items. The name is said to come from bakers in the past adding an extra item to be quite sure they did not deliver too few.

The number 12 has many divisors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. So a dozen can easily be divided into halves, thirds, quarters or sixths. The number 10, by contrast, can only be divided by 1, 2, 5 and 10. We meet 12 elsewhere too: 12 months, 12 hours on the clock face and 12 signs of the zodiac.
To convert dozens into items, you multiply by 12. 3 dozen are 36 items, and a dozen plus 3 is 15. The other way round, you divide by 12 to go from items to dozens. So 36 eggs are 3 dozen eggs.

begriffe.erklaerung: 12 items of something.
12 dozen, that is 144 items.
13 items, that is a dozen plus one more.
A number by which another number can be divided without a remainder.

gewusst: In English “dozens” also simply means “a great many”, similar to the German “dutzendweise”.
A gross of grosses, that is 12 · 144, makes 1728 items.

teile.einleitung: A timetable is a list that shows when trains, buses, trams or boats leave and arrive. If you can read one, you reach your destination on time and practise calculating with time along the way. Switzerland is famous for its dense and reliable timetable.
wichtigste: A timetable shows the departure and arrival times of means of transport.
In timetables the hours are counted from 0 to 23, so 14.00 is 2 o'clock in the afternoon.
The journey time is the difference between arrival and departure.
With a regular-interval timetable, transport runs at regular intervals, for example every half hour.
Switzerland introduced a nationwide regular-interval timetable for its railways in 1982.
The place where a bus or tram stops is called a stop.

abschnitte.text: A **timetable** sets out when a means of transport leaves from where and when it arrives. It is available as a notice at the **stop**, as a book, on screens at the station and in apps. In Switzerland times are often written with a point, for example 8.10. The hours are counted from 0 to 23, so 14.00 means 2 o'clock in the afternoon.

If the PostBus leaves at 8.10 and arrives at 8.30, the **journey time** is 20 minutes. If a train leaves at 17.50 and takes 20 minutes, it arrives at 18.10. Remember that an hour has 60 minutes, not 100. If you are at the stop at 10.05 and the bus leaves at 10.20, you wait 15 minutes.

With a **regular-interval timetable**, trains and buses run at fixed intervals, for example every half hour or every 10 minutes. If a train leaves at 9.00, the next one comes at 9.30. In 1982 Switzerland was one of the first countries to introduce a nationwide regular-interval timetable for its railways. Later came the **Rail 2000** project, so that trains meet in major stations just before the full or half hour and passengers can change easily.

For everything to work, clocks all over the country must show the same time. The famous **Swiss railway clock** with its red second hand was designed by Hans Hilfiker in 1944. The timetables of the railways, PostBus, trams and boats are coordinated with each other. That way you can reach even remote mountain villages with connections from train to bus.

First check the right **direction** and the right line. Check whether a departure applies only on working days, at weekends or on public holidays. When changing, allow enough time to make the connection. If a bus leaves every hour on the hour from 6 up to and including 9 o'clock, there are 4 departures.

begriffe.erklaerung: An overview of when means of transport leave and arrive.
A regular gap between two departures, for example 30 minutes.
Another means of transport you can change to after you arrive.
A place where buses or trams stop so that people can get on and off.

gewusst: The public transport timetable in Switzerland usually changes once a year, in December.
The second hand of the Swiss railway clock pauses briefly at every full minute before moving on.
In the past, timetables were printed in thick timetable books that came out every year.

teile.einleitung: Fractions describe parts of a whole, for example half a loaf of bread or three quarters of a pizza. When calculating with fractions, you learn how to work with such parts. This is useful for cooking, for sharing and for calculating with percentages.
wichtigste: A fraction consists of a numerator, a fraction line and a denominator.
The denominator says how many parts the whole is divided into, the numerator how many parts you have.
To add, you need a common denominator: 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6.
When multiplying, you work out numerator times numerator and denominator times denominator.
To divide by a fraction, you multiply by the reciprocal.
When simplifying, you divide the numerator and denominator by the same number.
An improper fraction can be written as a mixed number: 17/5 = 3 2/5.

abschnitte.text: A **fraction** such as 3/4 consists of the **numerator** at the top, the fraction line and the **denominator** at the bottom. If you divide a pizza into 4 equal pieces and take 3 of them, you have 3/4 of the pizza. The fraction line really means “divided by”. That is why 3/4 is the same as 3 : 4 = 0.75.

When **simplifying**, you divide the numerator and denominator by the same number, and the value stays the same. So 18/24 simplified by 6 becomes 3/4. When **expanding**, you multiply both by the same number; 1/2 becomes 3/6, for example. A fraction is fully simplified when the numerator and denominator have no common factor left.

You can only add fractions if they have the same denominator. So you look for a **common denominator**; for 1/2 + 1/3 it is 6. 1/2 becomes 3/6 and 1/3 becomes 2/6, and together that makes 5/6. Subtracting works in the same way.

When multiplying, you work out numerator times numerator and denominator times denominator: 3/4 · 2/5 = 6/20 = 3/10. When dividing, you multiply by the **reciprocal**, the fraction turned upside down. So 2/3 : 4/9 becomes 2/3 · 9/4 = 18/12 = 3/2. A fraction of a number is also a multiplication: 2/5 of 35 children is 14 children.

If the numerator is smaller than the denominator, it is a proper fraction, and it is less than 1. If the numerator is bigger, it is an **improper fraction**, such as 17/5. You can write it as a **mixed number**: 17/5 is 3 wholes and 2/5, so 3 2/5. To compare fractions, you give them the same denominator or convert them into decimals.

You meet fractions when baking, if a recipe asks for half a litre of milk. With the clock, people talk about quarters of an hour and half hours. In music there are quarter and eighth notes. Percentages are fractions with the denominator 100 too: 25 per cent is 1/4.

begriffe.erklaerung: The top number of a fraction; it counts the parts.
The bottom number; it says into how many parts the whole is divided.
The fraction turned upside down; for 2/3 it is 3/2.
A whole number together with a fraction, such as 3 2/5.

gewusst: More than 3500 years ago the ancient Egyptians were already calculating with fractions, mainly with unit fractions such as 1/2 or 1/3.
The horizontal fraction line was introduced by Arab mathematicians.
A quarter is more than a fifth, although 5 is bigger than 4.

teile.einleitung: Egyptian fractions are sums of different unit fractions, that is fractions with the numerator 1. The ancient Egyptians wrote almost all fractions in this way, for example 3/4 as 1/2 + 1/4. This way of calculating is more than 3500 years old and still keeps mathematicians busy today.
wichtigste: A unit fraction always has the numerator 1, for example 1/2, 1/3 or 1/7.
The ancient Egyptians wrote fractions as a sum of different unit fractions.
So 3/4 is written as 1/2 + 1/4 and 5/6 as 1/2 + 1/3.
As an exception, the fraction 2/3 had its own sign among the Egyptians.
The famous Rhind Papyrus contains many calculation problems with unit fractions.
Every positive fraction can be written as a sum of different unit fractions.

abschnitte.text: A **unit fraction** is a fraction with the numerator 1, such as 1/2, 1/5 or 1/10. The Egyptians used almost only such fractions. They wrote other fractions as a sum of different unit fractions. So 3/4 becomes 1/2 + 1/4, and 2/5 becomes 1/3 + 1/15. Each unit fraction was only allowed to appear once.

The **Rhind Papyrus** is a scroll more than five metres long dating from around 1550 BC. A scribe called **Ahmes** copied it from an even older text. It contains around 80 calculation problems, for example about sharing out bread or working out areas and pyramids. At the beginning there is a table that breaks down 2/n into unit fractions for many odd numbers n. Today the papyrus is in the British Museum in London.

In **hieroglyphs**, a unit fraction was written by placing a sign shaped like a mouth above the number. As an exception, there was a sign of its own for 2/3, and one for 1/2 too. According to a well-known interpretation, scribes showed fractions of a grain measure with parts of the **Eye of Horus**. The parts stand for 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 and 1/64.

Imagine 5 loaves of bread are to be shared fairly among 6 people. With Egyptian fractions each person gets 1/2 + 1/3 of a loaf. So you cut three loaves into halves and two loaves into thirds, and everyone gets one half and one third. This makes it possible to **share fairly** without cutting complicated pieces.

Around 1202, the Italian mathematician **Leonardo Fibonacci** showed a method for breaking any fraction down into unit fractions. You always take the largest unit fraction that still fits; this is called the **greedy method**. The sum 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8, for example, makes 7/8, and with more and more halved terms you get closer and closer to 1. There are still unsolved puzzles in number theory about Egyptian fractions today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fraction with the numerator 1, for example 1/4.
The number above the fraction line; it says how many parts you have.
The number below the fraction line; it says how many parts the whole is divided into.
The writing material of the ancient Egyptians, made from the pith of the papyrus plant.

gewusst: A fraction can be written as a sum of unit fractions in infinitely many different ways.
The parts of the Eye of Horus add up to only 63/64, not quite 1.
The Rhind Papyrus is named after the Scotsman Alexander Henry Rhind, who bought it in the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: Euler's number e is one of the most important constants in mathematics and is about 2.71828. It appears in compound interest, in the growth of bacteria and in the decay of radioactive substances. It is named after the Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler.
wichtigste: Euler's number e is about 2.718281828.
It is named after Leonhard Euler, who was born in Basel in 1707.
e is an irrational number; its decimal places never end and never repeat.
Charles Hermite proved in 1873 that e is even transcendental.
The function e^x is its own derivative.
The sum 1/0! + 1/1! + 1/2! + 1/3! and so on gives exactly e.
Euler's identity e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 is regarded as one of the most beautiful equations in mathematics.

abschnitte.text: Euler's number is a **constant**, that is a fixed number like the circle number π. Its value begins with 2.71828. It is **irrational**, so it cannot be written as a fraction. It can be calculated as an infinite sum: 1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/24 and so on, where the denominators are factorials.

In the 17th century, the Basel mathematician **Jakob Bernoulli** came across this number while calculating with interest. If 1 franc earns 100 per cent interest for one year, you have 2 francs at the end. If the interest is added monthly, it is about 2.61 francs. The more often interest is added, the closer you get to e, about 2.72 francs, but never more.

**Leonhard Euler** was born in Basel in 1707 and is regarded as one of the most important mathematicians of all time. He worked in St Petersburg and Berlin and died in 1783. He introduced the letter e for this number and studied many of its properties. His portrait appeared on the former Swiss 10-franc note.

The function f(x) = e^x has a unique property: it is its own **derivative**. This means that its gradient at every point is equal to its value. That is why it describes natural growth and decay especially well. The area under the graph of 1/x between 1 and e is also exactly 1, and the natural logarithm is based on this.

A chain hanging freely forms a curve called a **catenary**, which is described with exponential functions. If you put many letters into envelopes purely at random, there is a probability of about 1/e, roughly 37 per cent, that not a single one ends up in the right envelope. Euler's identity e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 links the five most important numbers in mathematics. The Frenchman Charles Hermite proved in 1873 that e is **transcendental**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed number that never changes, such as e or π.
A number that cannot be written as a fraction and whose decimal places never repeat.
Describes a number that is not a solution of any equation with whole-number coefficients.
The product of all numbers from 1 to n, written n!, for example 4! = 24.
The logarithm to the base e, shortened to ln.

gewusst: Euler published so much that publishing his collected works took more than a hundred years.
In old age Euler lost his sight almost completely but carried on working by dictating.
Computers have now calculated trillions of decimal places of e.

teile.einleitung: Core facts are especially simple multiplications that you know by heart and can use to solve harder calculations. In the times tables these are mainly the facts times 1, times 2, times 5 and times 10. If you know them well, you can cleverly work out all the other times table facts from them.
wichtigste: Core facts are easy calculations used as a support for harder ones.
In the times tables, the core facts are usually times 1, 2, 5 and 10.
From a core fact you find the neighbouring fact by adding or taking away one more lot.
Times 5 is always half of times 10.
Times 4 is double times 2.
With core facts you have less to learn by heart and understand calculating better.

abschnitte.text: A **core fact** is a simple calculation that you know quickly and surely. In the times tables these are usually the facts with 1, 2, 5 and 10. Times 1 is the number itself, times 2 is **doubling**, and times 10 adds a zero. Times 5 is half of times 10, so it is easy to find too.

From a core fact you can get to the **neighbouring fact** with one small step. If you know 5 · 6 = 30, then 6 · 6 is simply 30 + 6 = 36. From 5 · 7 = 35 it follows that 6 · 7 = 35 + 7 = 42. The other way round, 4 · 9 is worked out as 45 minus 9, that is 36.

The times 10 fact often helps too. From 10 · 7 = 70 you find 9 · 7 by taking away 7 once: 70 minus 7 = 63. For 8 · 6 you take 6 away twice from 10 · 6 = 60 and get 48. And 5 · 8 is **half** of 10 · 8 = 80, that is 40.

Many facts can be solved by **doubling**. For 4 · 7 the best help is the core fact 2 · 7 = 14, because double that is 28. In addition, you may swap the numbers when multiplying; this is called the **swapped fact**. So if you know 3 · 8 = 24, you also know straight away that 8 · 3 = 24.

In Switzerland children usually learn their times tables in the 2nd and 3rd year of primary school. Instead of learning all 100 facts one by one, they practise strategies with core facts. With the **multiplication cross** or with dot grids you can see how a calculation can be split into two easier ones. Over time, the children know all the facts automatically.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the multiplications with numbers from 1 to 10.
A simple multiplication from which other facts are worked out.
A fact that differs from the known one by only one lot.
The same calculation with the numbers swapped round, such as 3 · 8 and 8 · 3.

gewusst: If you know the core facts and the swapped facts, there are only a few facts in the whole times tables that you really have to learn from scratch.
Square numbers such as 3 · 3 or 7 · 7 are sometimes used as core facts too.
In the nine times table, the digit sum of the result always makes 9, for example with 63, because 6 + 3 = 9.

teile.einleitung: Emmy Noether was a German mathematician and one of the most important women mathematicians of all time. She shaped modern abstract algebra and found a theorem that is fundamental to physics. She had to fight many obstacles because she was a woman and Jewish.
wichtigste: Emmy Noether was born in Erlangen in 1882 and died in the USA in 1935.
From 1915 she worked at the University of Göttingen with David Hilbert.
As a woman she was at first not allowed to complete the habilitation, so for a long time she taught without a proper post.
Noether's theorem links symmetries with conservation laws.
She is regarded as one of the most important founders of abstract algebra.
In 1933 she had to leave Germany because she was persecuted as a Jew.
In the USA she taught at Bryn Mawr College; after her death Albert Einstein paid tribute to her.

abschnitte.text: Emmy Noether was born in 1882 in **Erlangen** in Bavaria. Her father Max Noether was a professor of mathematics at the university there. At that time women in Germany were at first only allowed to attend university as guest students. Noether studied mathematics anyway and gained a doctorate in Erlangen in 1907.

In 1915 the famous mathematicians **David Hilbert** and Felix Klein brought her to the University of **Göttingen**. There, as a woman, she was at first not allowed to complete the habilitation, the examination needed for a career as a professor. For a time her lectures were therefore announced under Hilbert's name. Only in 1919 did she receive permission, and even after that she never got a full professorship.

In 1918 Noether proved a theorem that is now called **Noether's theorem**. It says that for every symmetry of a physical system there is a quantity that is conserved. If the laws of nature are the same today as tomorrow, the conservation of energy follows. This link between **symmetries and conservation laws** is a foundation of modern physics.

Noether was interested in the general structures behind calculations. She studied structures such as **rings** and ideals without thinking of particular numbers. In this way she became one of the most important founders of **abstract algebra**. A group of students formed around her who were called the “Noether boys”.

In 1933 the National Socialists came to power in Germany. Noether was persecuted as a Jew and lost her permission to teach. She emigrated to the USA and taught at **Bryn Mawr College**, a college for women in Pennsylvania, and also gave lectures in Princeton. She died in 1935 after an operation. Afterwards Albert Einstein wrote in a letter to the “New York Times” that she had been the most significant mathematical genius among women since higher education for women began.

Many terms in mathematics bear her name, for example Noetherian rings. Schools, prizes and support programmes for women researchers are named after her. The German Research Foundation, for example, has an Emmy Noether Programme for young researchers. A crater on the Moon and an asteroid also commemorate her.

begriffe.erklaerung: An examination at German universities that gives you permission to become a professor.
A rule that says a quantity such as energy stays the same.
A property that does not change when something is changed, for example by turning or shifting it.
A field of mathematics that studies general structures of calculation.

gewusst: Emmy Noether's full name was Amalie Emmy Noether, but she almost always used her second first name.
Because she was not allowed to complete the habilitation, David Hilbert announced her lectures under his own name for years.

teile.einleitung: A shape has line symmetry if you can fold it along a line so that both halves fit exactly on top of each other. This line is called the mirror line or line of symmetry. Line symmetry is found in mathematics, in nature, in letters and in buildings.
wichtigste: A mirror line divides a shape into two equal, mirrored halves.
A point and its image are the same distance from the line.
A rectangle that is not a square has 2 mirror lines.
An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry, a regular hexagon 6.
A circle has infinitely many mirror lines.
The wings of a butterfly look as if they were mirrored.
The square Swiss flag has line symmetry.

abschnitte.text: With **line symmetry**, one half of a shape is the mirror image of the other. If you place a mirror exactly on the **line of symmetry**, you see the missing half in the mirror. You can also test it by folding: if both halves fit exactly on top of each other, the shape is symmetrical. A shape can have no, one or several lines of symmetry.

In a **reflection** in a line, every point is mirrored in the line. A point and its **image** are the same distance from the line. In addition, the line joining them is perpendicular to the mirror line. With a set square you can reflect shapes accurately in your exercise book this way.

A rectangle that is not a square has 2 lines of symmetry, a **square** has 4. An isosceles triangle has 1 line, an equilateral triangle 3. A regular polygon has as many lines as it has corners, so a regular hexagon has 6. A **circle** even has infinitely many, because every line through the centre is a mirror line.

Many capital letters are symmetrical if you divide them vertically down the middle, for example A, H, M, T, U, V and W. Others are symmetrical about a **horizontal line**, such as B, C, D, E and K. Among the digits, 0, 3 and 8 are horizontally symmetrical. The letters H, I, O and X even have two mirror lines.

The wings of a **butterfly** look as if they were mirrored. Many leaves, flowers and animals also have roughly line symmetry. From the outside the human body is roughly symmetrical, but the two halves never match exactly. Snowflakes often have six lines of symmetry.

The square **Swiss flag** with its white cross has four lines of symmetry: one vertical, one horizontal and two diagonal. Many buildings such as churches, castles or the Federal Palace in Bern are built symmetrically, because that looks calm and balanced. Logos and road signs are often symmetrical too. With a blot painting, where you drip paint onto paper and fold it, you can make symmetrical pictures yourself.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line that divides a shape into two mirror-image halves.
A transformation in which every point is mirrored in a line.
The point that results from another point when it is reflected.
A shape whose sides and angles are all the same size.

gewusst: If you read a word like OTTO in a mirror standing upright next to it, it looks almost unchanged.
Faces put together on a computer from two identical halves often look strange, because real faces are slightly asymmetrical.
Apart from the flag of the Vatican, the Swiss flag is the only square national flag in the world.

teile.einleitung: Propositional logic is a part of logic that looks at how statements are connected with words such as “and”, “or” and “not”. It is something like the grammar of precise thinking. Without it there would be no computers, because every processor calculates with true and false.
wichtigste: A statement is a sentence that is either true or false.
Statements are connected with connectives such as “and”, “or”, “not”, “if, then” and “if and only if”.
The disjunction A ∨ B is true if at least one of its parts is true.
The implication A → B is only false if A is true and B is false.
The equivalence is true exactly when both parts have the same truth value.
A formula that is always true is called a tautology, one that is always false a contradiction.
With truth tables you can check any formula completely.

abschnitte.text: In propositional logic a **statement** is a sentence that is either true or false, but never both. “Bern is the federal city of Switzerland” is a true statement. “7 is an even number” is a false statement. Questions such as “What time is it?” or commands such as “Tidy your room!” are not statements. Statements are usually abbreviated with capital letters such as A and B.

Linking words are called **connectives**. The negation ¬A (“not A”) reverses the truth value. The conjunction A ∧ B (“A and B”) is only true if both parts are true. The **disjunction** A ∨ B is the inclusive or: it is true if at least one part is true, so also if both are true. The equivalence A ↔ B is true if both parts have the same truth value.

The **implication** A → B means “if A, then B”. It is only false if the condition A is true and the conclusion B is false. An example: “If it is raining, the road is wet.” If it is not raining, the statement is still true, whether the road is wet or not. Equivalent to A → B is the **contrapositive** ¬B → ¬A: if the road is not wet, then it is not raining.

In a **truth table** you write down all possible assignments of the variables and work out the value of the formula for each one. With two variables there are four rows, with three variables eight. Important rules are **De Morgan's laws**: ¬(A ∧ B) is equivalent to ¬A ∨ ¬B, and ¬(A ∨ B) is equivalent to ¬A ∧ ¬B. A formula such as A ∨ ¬A is always true and is called a tautology. A formula such as A ∧ ¬A is always false and is called a contradiction.

More than 2300 years ago, the Greek philosopher Aristotle was already studying correct reasoning. The Stoics, a Greek school of philosophy, already examined connections such as “if, then”. In the 19th century the Englishman **George Boole** wrote logic down as a calculation with symbols. Gottlob Frege and others built modern mathematical logic from it.

abschnitte.titel: Logic in everyday life and in computers
abschnitte.text: Computers work with two states, 1 for true and 0 for false. Electronic **logic gates** such as AND, OR and NOT turn the connectives directly into circuits. Search engines, programming languages and databases also use “and”, “or” and “not”. Anyone who knows propositional logic also finds it easier to spot mistakes in arguments.

begriffe.erklaerung: A linking word such as “and”, “or” or “not” that joins statements.
Whether a statement is true or false.
A formula that is true for every assignment.
A formula that is false for every assignment.
A table that shows for all cases whether a formula is true or false.

gewusst: In logic, any statement at all follows from a false condition, which is why “If 1 = 2, then I am the Pope” is a true implication.
The everyday “or” is often meant to exclude, but the logical or is also true when both parts are true.

teile.einleitung: An empirical formula shows the simplest number ratio in which the atoms occur in a chemical compound. So it reveals what the recipe of a substance looks like, but not necessarily how large a single molecule is. Chemists also call it the simplest formula.
wichtigste: The empirical formula gives the smallest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound.
Glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ has the empirical formula CH₂O.
Benzene C₆H₆ has the empirical formula CH, hydrogen peroxide H₂O₂ the formula HO.
It can be calculated from the mass fractions of the elements.
With the molar mass, the molecular formula can be determined from the empirical formula.
For salts such as sodium chloride only an empirical formula is given, because an ionic lattice has no individual molecules.

abschnitte.text: The **empirical formula** says how many atoms of each kind occur in relation to each other. It is simplified as far as possible, as with a fraction.
