Glucose has the **molecular formula** C₆H₁₂O₆; all the numbers can be divided by 6, so the empirical formula is CH₂O. For water H₂O the molecular formula and the empirical formula are the same, because nothing more can be simplified.

In the laboratory you first determine what percentage of the mass belongs to each element. Then you divide each fraction by the **molar mass** of the element and so obtain the amounts of substance. Finally you divide all values by the smallest one. A substance with 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen gives CH₂O in this way. A hydrocarbon with 75 % carbon and 25 % hydrogen gives CH₄.

An iron oxide contains 70 % iron and 30 % oxygen. With the molar masses 56 g/mol for iron and 16 g/mol for oxygen, you get about 1.25 to 1.875. This corresponds to the ratio 2 to 3, that is **Fe₂O₃**. This iron oxide is known as the main component of red rust and of the mineral **haematite**.

abschnitte.titel: From empirical formula to molecular formula
abschnitte.text: Different substances can have the same empirical formula, for example ethene C₂H₄ and butene C₄H₈ with CH₂. To determine the real molecule you also need the **molar mass**. One CH₂ unit weighs 14 g/mol. If the whole molecule weighs 56 g/mol, the unit is contained in it four times, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈.

Table salt consists of sodium ions and chloride ions arranged in a huge **ionic lattice**. It contains no self-contained molecules. That is why only NaCl is written, which means: for every sodium there is one chloride. It is similar with calcium chloride CaCl₂ or with metal oxides. For such substances the empirical formula is the only meaningful formula.

begriffe.erklaerung: A formula with the smallest whole-number ratio of the atoms, also called the simplest formula.
A formula that states how many atoms of each kind there really are in a molecule.
The mass of one mole of a substance, given in grams per mole.
A regular arrangement of positively and negatively charged ions in a salt crystal.

gewusst: Glucose, acetic acid C₂H₄O₂ and formaldehyde CH₂O all have the same empirical formula CH₂O.
Benzene C₆H₆ and ethyne C₂H₂ share the empirical formula CH, although they are completely different substances.
A single grain of salt contains an unimaginable number of ions, which is why a molecular formula would not even be possible.

teile.einleitung: A fraction describes a part of a whole, for example three of eight slices of pizza. It consists of a number at the top, a line and a number at the bottom. We meet fractions every day: in a quarter of an hour, in recipes or in music.
wichtigste: A fraction consists of a numerator, a fraction line and a denominator.
The denominator says into how many equal parts the whole is divided.
The numerator says how many of these parts are meant.
If the numerator is bigger than the denominator, it is called an improper fraction.
A fraction with the numerator 1 is called a unit fraction.
Improper fractions can be written as mixed numbers, for example 11/4 = 2 3/4.
Fractions can be expanded and simplified without changing their value.

abschnitte.text: If you cut a pizza into 8 equal slices and eat 3 of them, you have eaten **3/8** of the pizza. The bottom number, the **denominator**, gives the number of equal parts. The top number, the **numerator**, counts how many parts are meant. Between them is the fraction line, which is also a division sign: so 3/8 also means 3 divided by 8. A whole hour has 4 quarters of an hour, each of them 1/4 of an hour.

In a **proper fraction** the numerator is smaller than the denominator, so it is less than a whole. In an **improper fraction** such as 7/4 the numerator is bigger. You can write it as a mixed number: 11/4 is 2 wholes and 3/4, so 2 3/4. A fraction with the numerator 1, such as 1/5, is called a **unit fraction**. Fractions such as 4/4 or 6/3 give whole numbers.

When **expanding**, you multiply the numerator and denominator by the same number: 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. When **simplifying**, you divide both by the same number: 6/8 = 3/4. The value of the fraction always stays the same; only the pieces become bigger or smaller. A fraction is fully simplified when the numerator and denominator have no common factor left.

To compare fractions, you give them a **common denominator**. Then you can see that 3/4 is bigger than 2/3, because 9/12 is more than 8/12. Exactly halfway between 1/4 and 3/4 lies 1/2. To add, you also need the same denominator: 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4. When multiplying, you simply work out numerator times numerator and denominator times denominator.

The ancient **Egyptians** were already calculating with fractions more than 3500 years ago, mainly with unit fractions. Arab mathematicians spread the horizontal fraction line, and the Italian Leonardo Fibonacci made it known in Europe in the 13th century. Today fractions are everywhere: in recipes with half a litre of milk, in music with quarter and eighth notes, and in percentages, because 1/2 is 50 per cent. Every fraction can also be written as a **decimal**; 1/4, for example, is 0.25.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number above the fraction line; it counts the parts.
The number below the fraction line; it names the kind of parts.
A fraction with the numerator 1.
A number made of wholes and a fraction, such as 2 3/4.
Dividing the numerator and denominator by the same number.

gewusst: The denominator must never be zero, because you cannot divide by zero.
Some fractions give decimals that go on for ever; 1/3, for example, is 0.333 and so on.
The German word for fraction, Bruch, comes from the idea of “breaking” a whole into pieces.

teile.einleitung: Sugar is a sweet-tasting substance that plants make with the help of sunlight. The white table sugar in our kitchen is chemically called sucrose, and in Switzerland it comes from sugar beet. Sugar provides energy quickly, but too much of it harms your teeth and your health.
wichtigste: Plants make sugar in their green leaves with the help of sunlight.
In Switzerland sugar is obtained from sugar beet, for example at the sugar factory in Aarberg in the canton of Bern.
In warm countries a lot of sugar is made from sugar cane.
Table sugar is chemically called sucrose and consists of glucose and fructose.
There is granulated sugar, icing sugar, sugar cubes and many other kinds.
Sugar dissolves well in water, but not without limit.
Lots of sweets can cause tooth decay.

abschnitte.text: In their green leaves, plants carry out **photosynthesis**. Using the energy of sunlight, they build glucose from carbon dioxide from the air and water. They use this sugar as a source of energy and as building material. Some plants store large amounts of it, such as the sugar beet in its thick root or sugar cane in its stem. Fruit tastes sweet too, because it contains sugar.

Sugars belong to the **carbohydrates**. Simple sugars include **glucose** with the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and fructose. Table sugar, **sucrose**, is a double sugar made of one glucose unit and one fructose unit. Milk contains milk sugar. Starch in potatoes and bread consists of a great many glucose units linked together.

In Switzerland sugar is made from **sugar beet**, which is grown mainly on the Swiss Plateau. In autumn the beet is harvested and taken by rail or lorry to the sugar factories in Aarberg in the canton of Bern and in Frauenfeld in the canton of Thurgau. There it is washed, cut up and soaked in hot water to draw out the sugar. The sugary juice is cleaned and thickened until sugar crystals form. In warm countries such as Brazil or India, sugar is obtained mainly from **sugar cane**.

Ordinary **granulated sugar** consists of small white grains. Icing sugar is ground very finely like flour and is good for icing. Sugar cubes are pressed into small blocks, and rock candy forms large crystals. Raw cane sugar is brownish because it is less refined. When a machine spins melted sugar into fine threads, you get candyfloss, and heated sugar turns into brown **caramel**.

Sugar gives the body energy quickly, especially the brain and muscles. But bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acids that attack tooth enamel and can cause **tooth decay**. That is why brushing your teeth after sweets is important. Anyone who constantly eats a lot of sugar also risks being overweight and illnesses such as diabetes. The World Health Organization recommends eating only a little added sugar, and sugary drinks often contain a surprising amount of it.

Sugar dissolves very well in water: at room temperature around two kilograms in one litre. But if you stir in even more sugar, some of it stays at the bottom; the solution is then **saturated**. More sugar dissolves in warm water than in cold. If you let a saturated sugar solution evaporate slowly, beautiful sugar crystals grow.

begriffe.erklaerung: The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar.
The chemical name for white table sugar.
Nutrients such as sugar and starch that provide energy.
Holes in the teeth caused by acids from bacteria.
A solution in which no more of a substance can dissolve.

gewusst: That sugar beet contains sugar was discovered by the German chemist Andreas Sigismund Marggraf in the 18th century.
Sugar used to be so expensive that it was called white gold.
Sucrose rotates polarised light, and this property can be used to measure the sugar content of a solution.

teile.einleitung: Plan and elevation are drawings that show a solid from different directions. The plan is the view from above, the elevation the view from the front. Together they describe a three-dimensional object precisely on flat paper.
wichtigste: In the plan you see a solid from above.
In the front elevation you see a solid from the front.
The view from the side is called the side elevation.
An upright cylinder appears as a rectangle in the elevation and as a circle in the plan.
A sphere looks like a circle in all three views.
The Frenchman Gaspard Monge is regarded as the founder of descriptive geometry.
Architects and engineers use such views for building plans and technical drawings.

abschnitte.text: An object in space has three dimensions, but a sheet of paper has only two. To show a solid precisely anyway, you draw it from several directions. The **plan** shows it from directly above, the **front elevation** from the front and the **side elevation** from the side. You imagine parallel rays of light casting the solid onto a flat surface, like a shadow.

A cube looks like a square in all three views. An upright **cylinder** appears as a rectangle in the elevation and as a circle in the plan. A **cone** standing on its base becomes a triangle in the elevation and a circle with a centre point in the plan. An upright pyramid with a square base shows a square with both diagonals in the plan, because from above you see the edges leading to the tip.

The plan and elevation are usually drawn one above the other, the elevation at the top and the plan below. Between them is a line, the **ground line**. Points that belong together lie exactly vertically above each other and are joined by thin **projection lines**. In this way you can read off the real shape and position of a solid from two views.

The French mathematician **Gaspard Monge** lived from 1746 to 1818. He developed the method of plan and elevation into a science of its own, **descriptive geometry**. His method was at first important for building fortresses and was treated as a military secret for a long time. Monge was also a co-founder of the famous technical university, the École polytechnique in Paris.

Every building plan of a house includes a floor plan, on which you see the rooms, doors and windows from above. The views of the façades correspond to the front and side elevations. Furniture, machines and tools are also shown in this way in technical drawings. Today this is often done by **CAD programs** on the computer, but the principle is the same.

begriffe.erklaerung: The view of a solid from directly above.
The view of a solid from the front.
The view of a solid from the side.
The study of how to show solids in space precisely on a flat surface.
An image of a solid on a surface, similar to a shadow.

gewusst: From the plan and elevation alone you cannot always identify a solid clearly, which is why the side elevation is sometimes needed as well.
In Switzerland, trainee draughtspeople learn in their apprenticeship to make plans and elevations by hand and on the computer.
Flat advertisements almost always include a floor plan so that you can see how the rooms are arranged.

teile.einleitung: A geometric sequence is a row of numbers in which you always multiply by the same number to get to the next term. Examples are 3, 6, 12, 24 or 81, 27, 9, 3. Such sequences describe growth and decrease, for example in bacteria, interest or decay.
wichtigste: In a geometric sequence, the quotient of two consecutive terms is always the same.
This fixed factor is called the common ratio q.
The nth term is calculated with the formula aₙ = a₁ · qⁿ⁻¹.
If q is greater than 1 the sequence grows; if q is between 0 and 1 it decreases and stays positive.
If q is negative, the signs of the terms alternate.
Every term is the geometric mean of its two neighbours.
Compound interest and cell division are typical examples from everyday life.

abschnitte.text: In a **geometric sequence**, each term is made by multiplying the previous one by a fixed number q. This number is called the **common ratio**, because you get it as the quotient of two neighbouring terms. In 3, 6, 12, ... q = 2; in 81, 27, 9, 3 q = 1/3. In 2, minus 6, 18, minus 54 q = minus 3, and the sign jumps back and forth.

The nth term is calculated with aₙ = a₁ · qⁿ⁻¹. For the sequence 3, 6, 12 the 10th term is therefore 3 · 2⁹ = 3 · 512 = 1536. If you know a₁ = 5 and a₄ = 40, then 5 · q³ = 40, so q³ = 8 and q = 2. With a formula of its own you can also quickly work out the **sum** of the first n terms.

In a geometric sequence with positive terms, each term is the **geometric mean** of its neighbours. You multiply the two neighbours and take the square root. So the number 10 fits between 4 and 25, because 4 · 25 = 100 and the square root of 100 is 10. The sequence is then 4, 10, 25 with the common ratio 2.5.

If a bacterium divides every 20 minutes, the number doubles at every step. In 4 hours there are 12 divisions, so one bacterium becomes 2¹² = 4096 bacteria. Such growth is called **exponential growth**. It starts slowly and then becomes very fast, which can also be seen, for example, in the spread of diseases.

If you put money into a savings account, the interest is added every year and itself earns interest the next year. This is called **compound interest**. At 2 % interest the capital is multiplied by 1.02 every year. In this way 10,000 francs become about 11,041 francs after 5 years.

If the common ratio is between minus 1 and 1, the terms keep getting smaller. Then you can even add infinitely many terms and get a finite number. An example is 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ...; this **geometric series** comes to exactly 1. This also explains why the runner in Zeno's old puzzle does catch up with the tortoise after all.

begriffe.erklaerung: An ordered row of numbers that follows a rule.
The fixed factor by which you multiply to get from one term to the next.
The square root of the product of two numbers.
Growth in which a quantity is multiplied by the same factor in equal time steps.
The sum of the terms of a geometric sequence.

gewusst: According to an old legend, the inventor of chess asked for grains of rice, twice as many on each square as on the one before, which would be more than 18 quintillion grains.
If you fold a sheet of paper, its thickness doubles every time, which is why you can usually only manage about 7 folds with an ordinary sheet.
In the equal temperament tuning commonly used today, the frequencies of the semitones form a geometric sequence.

teile.einleitung: The admission price is the amount you pay to visit, for example, a zoo, a museum, a swimming pool or a cinema. There are often different prices for children, adults and families. With a little arithmetic you can find the cheapest offer.
wichtigste: The admission price is the price for entry to an event or a place.
Children usually pay less than adults, and small children often nothing at all.
You work out the total price by calculating number times single price and adding everything up.
Family tickets, season passes and group rates can save money.
The saving is the difference between the normal price and the cheaper price.
The change is the amount you get back when you pay with more money.

abschnitte.text: For many places you need an **admission ticket**. Its price is called the admission price. It pays, for example, the wages of the staff, the food for the zoo animals or the cleaning of the swimming pool. Some museums and facilities are also supported by municipalities, cantons or foundations.

There are usually several **rates**. Adults pay the full price, while children, young people, students or senior citizens often pay less. Small children often have **free admission**, for example up to the age of 6. A 4-year-old child then pays 0 francs.

If admission for a child costs 5 francs, 2 children pay 2 · 5 = 10 francs. For 4 children at 3 francs each at the swimming pool, it is 12 francs. If adults pay 10 francs and children 5 francs, 2 adults and 2 children cost 20 + 10 = 30 francs. Three cinema tickets at 15 francs cost 45 francs.

abschnitte.titel: Saving with a family ticket and a season pass
abschnitte.text: A **family ticket** is valid for parents and children together and is often cheaper. If a family's single tickets cost 28 francs and the family ticket 22 francs, it saves 28 − 22 = 6 francs. Anyone who often goes to the same place can buy an **annual pass**. In Switzerland there is also a museum pass that lets you visit many museums.

If you pay with more money than the ticket costs, you get **change**. If the zoo costs 8 francs and you hand over 10 francs, you get 2 francs back. Many tills today also accept cards or payment apps. Even so, it is worth working out beforehand roughly how much you need.

begriffe.erklaerung: A price level, for example for children or adults.
A reduced price for certain people.
The money you get back when you have handed over too much.
A card that lets you go in as often as you like for a certain time.

gewusst: Many museums in Switzerland have special offers on International Museum Day or during museum nights.
Some theme parks charge different prices depending on the day of the week or the season; this is called dynamic pricing.

teile.einleitung: An extreme value is an especially large or especially small value of a function, that is a maximum or a minimum. On the graph you see it as a high point or low point, like the peaks and valleys of a mountain landscape. With differential calculus you can calculate such points exactly.
wichtigste: Extreme values are the maxima and minima of a function.
A local maximum is the largest value in its neighbourhood; the global maximum is the largest value of all.
At a local extremum of a differentiable function, f'(x₀) = 0 always holds.
If in addition f''(x₀) < 0, there is a local maximum; if f''(x₀) > 0, a minimum.
If f''(x₀) = 0 as well, you have to look more closely, as with f(x) = x⁴, which has a low point at 0.
The low point of f(x) = x² − 6x + 5 is at (3|-4).
On an interval you must also check the values at the ends.

abschnitte.text: A **high point** is a place where the graph lies higher than in the area close by, like a mountain peak. A **low point** is the opposite, like the floor of a valley. The corresponding function value is called a local maximum or local minimum. The largest value over the whole domain is called the **global maximum**, the smallest the global minimum.

At a high or low point of a differentiable function, the tangent is horizontal. So the derivative must be zero there: f'(x₀) = 0. For f(x) = x² − 6x + 5, f'(x) = 2x − 6, so x = 3 is the candidate. Substituting gives f(3) = 9 − 18 + 5 = -4, so the low point is at (3|-4).

Not every point with f'(x) = 0 is an extreme value. That is why you check the **second derivative**. If f''(x₀) < 0, the graph curves downwards there and there is a maximum. If f''(x₀) > 0, there is a minimum. For f(x) = x³ − 3x, f'(x) = 3x² − 3 and f''(x) = 6x, so at x = -1 there is a high point with the value 2.

If f'(x₀) = 0 and also f''(x₀) = 0, the test does not help. For f(x) = x⁴ this is the case at the point 0, and yet there is a low point there, because x⁴ is never negative. For f(x) = x³, on the other hand, there is no extreme value at 0 but a **stationary point of inflection**, also called a saddle point. You then check, for example, whether the derivative changes sign.

If you only look at a function on an **interval**, you must also check the values at the ends. On the interval from -1 to 3, f(x) = x² has its largest value, 9, at the right-hand end. There are many optimisation problems in everyday life: the largest area for a given length of fence, the box with the biggest volume or the least material for a tin. For f(x) = x · e^(-x) the maximum is at x = 1.

begriffe.erklaerung: The x-value at which a function has an extreme value.
The largest function value in a small neighbourhood.
The largest function value over the whole domain.
A point with a horizontal tangent that is neither a high point nor a low point.

gewusst: Of all rectangles with the same perimeter, the square has the largest area.
Bees build hexagonal honeycombs because this shape encloses a lot of space with little wax, an optimisation problem in nature.

teile.einleitung: The factorial of a natural number n, written n!, is the product of all natural numbers from 1 to n. So 5! = 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 = 120. With the factorial you work out in how many ways things can be put in order.
wichtigste: n! is the product of all natural numbers from 1 to n.
5! gives 120, and 0! is 1 by definition.
Six people can stand in a row in 6! = 720 ways.
Factorials grow extremely fast.
Fractions such as 10!/8! are easy to simplify: the result is 10 · 9 = 90.
Christian Kramp introduced the notation with the exclamation mark in 1808.
The number 10! = 3,628,800 ends in two zeros.

abschnitte.text: The **factorial** n! is the product of all natural numbers from 1 to n. You say “n factorial”. 3! = 1 · 2 · 3 = 6, 4! = 24 and 5! = 120. It is always true that n! = n · (n−1)!, so you can work out the next factorial from the previous one. By definition 0! = 1, so that the calculation rules work there too.

In how many ways can 6 people stand in a row? There are 6 possibilities for the first place, 5 for the second and so on. Altogether there are 6 · 5 · 4 · 3 · 2 · 1 = 720. Such arrangements are called **permutations**. If some things are the same, you divide by the factorial of how many there are: from the letters of “AARAU”, with three As, 5!/3! = 20 different sequences can be made.

Factorials quickly become huge, but in fractions a lot cancels out. 10!/8! gives 10 · 9 = 90, because 1 · 2 · ... · 8 cancels. Likewise 100!/99! is simply 100. Such fractions often come up in **combinatorics**, for example when working out lottery chances with the **binomial coefficient**.

Factorials grow even faster than powers. 10! is already 3,628,800, and 20! has as many as 19 digits. The number 10! ends in two zeros, because the pair 2 · 5 appears twice in the product, namely in 2 · 5 and in 10. A shuffled pack of 52 cards can be arranged in 52! ways, a number with 68 digits.

The idea of counting arrangements is very old and was already known in India many centuries ago. The notation with the **exclamation mark** was introduced by the French mathematician **Christian Kramp** in 1808. He chose it because it was easy to print. Later Leonhard Euler even extended the factorial to numbers that are not whole, using the gamma function.

begriffe.erklaerung: The product of all natural numbers from 1 to n, written n!.
One possible arrangement of things in an order.
The field of mathematics concerned with counting possibilities.
A number that tells you how many ways there are to choose k things from n.

gewusst: If you shuffle a pack of cards well, the resulting order has very probably never occurred before in history.
The number 145 is special, because 1! + 4! + 5! = 1 + 24 + 120 = 145.

teile.einleitung: The fundamental theorem of calculus links the two big parts of analysis. It shows that differentiating and integrating are the reverse of each other. Thanks to it, you can work out areas and integrals very simply with antiderivatives.
wichtigste: The fundamental theorem shows that differentiating and integrating are the reverse of each other.
If F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral from a to b is F(b) minus F(a).
The derivative of the integral function I(x) is the function f(x) again.
It is usually assumed that f is continuous on the interval [a; b].
Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz discovered the connection independently of each other in the 17th century.
Without the fundamental theorem, integrals would have to be calculated laboriously as limits of sums.

abschnitte.text: In analysis there are two basic tasks: finding the **gradient** of a curve and calculating the **area** under a curve. The first is solved by differentiating, the second by integrating. The fundamental theorem shows that these two calculations are closely connected. They cancel each other out, rather like plus and minus or times and divided by.

You define an **integral function** I(x) as the integral of f(t) from a fixed limit a to a variable limit x. The fundamental theorem says: the derivative of this function is exactly f(x). If, for example, I(x) is the integral of t² from 0 to x, then I'(x) = x² and so I'(3) = 9. The condition is that f is **continuous**, that is it has no jumps.

The second part is the well-known rule for definite integrals. If F is an **antiderivative** of f, then the integral from a to b is F(b) minus F(a). The integral of cos(x) from 0 to π/2 is sin(π/2) minus sin(0), that is 1. The integral of eˣ from 0 to 1 gives e minus 1, because eˣ is its own antiderivative.

We want the integral of 1/√x from 1 to 4. An antiderivative is 2√x, because its derivative is 1/√x. You put in the limits: 2 · √4 minus 2 · √1 = 4 minus 2 = 2. Without the fundamental theorem you would have to approximate the area with infinitely many narrow **rectangles**.

The first ideas about the connection between area and tangent came from the Englishman **Isaac Barrow**, Isaac Newton's teacher. **Isaac Newton** and **Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz** developed calculus independently of each other in the second half of the 17th century. There was a fierce dispute between them and their followers about who had been first. A completely precise justification was only given in the 19th century by mathematicians such as Augustin-Louis Cauchy and Bernhard Riemann.

The fundamental theorem makes integrating practical, because you only need to find antiderivatives. In physics you can use it to calculate the **distance** travelled from the speed, and the other way round. Engineers, economists and statisticians also use it every day. Many consider it one of the most important theorems in the whole of mathematics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Gives the gradient of a function at every point.
Measures, roughly speaking, the area under a curve.
A function F whose derivative is the function f.
Describes a function without jumps whose graph can be drawn without lifting the pen.
The part of mathematics that deals with functions, derivatives and integrals.

gewusst: Every function has infinitely many antiderivatives; they differ only by a constant.
When you put in the limits, this constant always drops out, so it does not matter which antiderivative you use.
The integral sign and the d in dx come from Leibniz, while Newton used quite different notations.

teile.einleitung: Integral calculus is a large field of mathematics with which you can calculate areas, volumes and much more. Its basic idea is to split something into infinitely many tiny parts and add them up again. Together with differential calculus it forms analysis.
wichtigste: The integral measures, roughly speaking, the area under the graph of a function.
The integral sign ∫ is a long stretched S and originally stood for sum.
The area is approximated with rectangles, using lower sums and upper sums.
If the lower and upper limits are the same, the integral has the value 0.
If you swap the limits, the integral changes its sign.
Integrals can be split up, and factors can be taken outside.
With antiderivatives, integrals can be calculated quickly using the fundamental theorem.

abschnitte.text: If you want to find the area under a curve, you divide it into narrow vertical strips. You replace each strip with a rectangle whose area is easy to calculate. If you take the smallest function value as the height each time, you get the **lower sum**; with the largest value, the **upper sum**. If you make the strips narrower and narrower, both sums approach the same value: the **integral**.

The integral sign ∫ was introduced by **Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz** in 1675. It is a long stretched S and stands for “sum”, because an integral is a sum of infinitely many small parts. You write the lower **limit** at the bottom and the upper limit at the top, then the function and at the end dx. The dx is a reminder of the tiny width of the strips.

The integral of x² from 0 to 2 has the value 8/3, because an antiderivative is x³/3. The integral of (2x + 1) from 1 to 3 gives 10. The **mean value** of a function over an interval is the integral divided by the width of the interval. For x² on [0; 3] the integral is 9, and divided by 3 that gives the mean value 3.

If the lower and upper limits are the same, the integral is 0, because the strip has no width. If you **swap** the limits, the sign changes: if the integral from 0 to 3 is 7, then from 3 to 0 it is minus 7. You may move constant factors in front of the integral and integrate sums term by term. If the integral of f from 0 to 4 is 5, then the integral of (2f(x) + 1) is 2 · 5 + 4 = 14.

More than 2200 years ago the Greek **Archimedes** was already calculating areas and volumes with a kind of strip method. In the 17th century Isaac Newton and Leibniz developed modern calculus. The Basel mathematician Jakob Bernoulli was the first to use the word “integral” in print, in 1690. In the 19th century **Bernhard Riemann** gave the integral a precise mathematical definition.

With integrals you can calculate the areas of plots of land with curved boundaries or the volume of barrels and bottles. In physics the integral of speed over time gives the distance travelled. The work done by an engine, or the amount of water flowing through a river, is also calculated this way. In statistics, integrals help to find **probabilities**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sum of rectangle areas whose height is the smallest function value in the strip.
A sum of rectangle areas whose height is the largest function value in the strip.
The start and end of the range over which you integrate.
A function whose derivative is the given function.
Calculating with infinitely small quantities, that is differentiating and integrating.

gewusst: Leibniz is said to have chosen the integral sign because it is reminiscent of the Latin word “summa”.
With integrals you can show that a cone has exactly one third of the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height.
Calculators and computers calculate many integrals not exactly but with a great many very narrow strips.

teile.einleitung: The chain rule is a rule of differential calculus for differentiating nested functions. A nested function is formed when you put one function inside another, as in sin(x²). In short, the rule is: outer derivative times inner derivative.
wichtigste: The chain rule applies to composite functions f(x) = u(v(x)).
It says f'(x) = u'(v(x)) · v'(x).
v'(x) is called the inner derivative, u'(v(x)) the outer derivative.
For example, the derivative of (3x + 1)⁵ is 15(3x + 1)⁴.
The derivative of e^(2x) is 2e^(2x).
The chain rule is one of the most important rules of differentiation, alongside the product and quotient rules.
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz already knew the rule in the 17th century.

abschnitte.text: Many functions are built like a **chain** of two links. With f(x) = (3x + 1)⁵ you first work out 3x + 1; this is the **inner function**. Then you take the result to the power 5; this is the **outer function**. Such a thing is called a composition, written f(x) = u(v(x)). The chain rule tells you how to find the derivative of such a composition.

The chain rule says f'(x) = u'(v(x)) · v'(x). So you first differentiate the outer function and leave the inside unchanged. Then you multiply by the **inner derivative** v'(x). In Leibniz's notation it looks especially simple: dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx. You can imagine the rates of change of the individual links of the chain multiplying together.

For (3x + 1)⁵ the outer derivative is 5(3x + 1)⁴ and the inner derivative is 3, so together 15(3x + 1)⁴. For e^(2x) the inner derivative is 2, so the derivative is 2e^(2x). For sin(x²) you get 2x · cos(x²). For the square root of x² + 1 you get x divided by the square root of x² + 1. A surprise is ln(5x): the derivative is 1/(5x) times 5, so simply **1/x**.

Often you want to know the gradient at a particular point. For f(x) = (x²−1)³, the chain rule gives f'(x) = 3(x²−1)² · 2x. At the point x = 2, x²−1 = 3, so you get 3 · 9 · 4 = **108**. Another example is e^(-x²), whose derivative is -2x · e^(-x²). This function describes the well-known **bell curve** of statistics.

In physics, engineering and economics almost all important functions are composite. If, for example, the temperature changes with height and the height changes with time, the chain rule works out how fast the temperature changes with time. The chain rule is also applied millions of times when training **artificial intelligence**; there the method is called backpropagation. Without the chain rule, many movements, oscillations and growth processes could not be calculated. That is why it is part of the basic knowledge in maths lessons at grammar school (Gymnasium).

begriffe.erklaerung: A function that tells you how steep another function is at every point.
Carrying out two functions one after the other, putting one inside the other.
The derivative of the inner function v(x) that is put inside.
The derivative of the outer function, with the inside left unchanged.

gewusst: You can also apply the chain rule several times in a row, for example for sin(e^(x²)) with three links in the chain.
The notation dy/dx comes from Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and is still used today.
Artificial intelligence programs basically learn with the help of the chain rule.

teile.einleitung: Al-Khwarizmi was a Persian scholar who lived and did research in Baghdad in the 9th century. He wrote important books on mathematics, astronomy and geography. The word algorithm comes from his name, and one of his books gave algebra its name.
wichtigste: Al-Khwarizmi lived in the 9th century, from about 780 to 850.
His name refers to the region of Khwarazm in Central Asia.
He worked in Baghdad in the “House of Wisdom”.
The word “algebra” comes from the title of his book on equations.
In it he dealt especially with quadratic equations.
He made the Hindu-Arabic numerals better known in the Arab world and later in Europe.
The word “algorithm” developed from his name.

abschnitte.text: His full name is Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi. The surname means “the one from **Khwarazm**”, a region on the lower course of the river Amu Darya that today belongs to Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Little is known about his life. What is certain is that he lived from about 780 to 850 and worked as a scholar in **Baghdad**.

At that time Baghdad was the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and one of the largest cities in the world. The caliph **al-Ma'mun** supported the **House of Wisdom**, a kind of library and research centre. There scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian writings into Arabic and developed the knowledge further. Al-Khwarizmi was one of the best-known researchers there.

Around 820, al-Khwarizmi wrote a textbook on solving **equations**. Its title contains the Arabic word al-jabr, which means something like completing or restoring. This became the word **algebra**. In it he explained step by step how to solve **quadratic equations**, and he also showed the solutions with geometric figures. The book was later translated into Latin and used in Europe for centuries.

In another book he explained calculating with the **Indian numerals** and zero. This work survives only in a Latin translation that begins with the words “Dixit Algorismi”, meaning “Algorismi has said”. From this Latinised name came the word **algorithm**, today a basic term in computer science. An algorithm is a precise step-by-step set of instructions, of the kind every computer program needs.

Al-Khwarizmi was also an **astronomer**. He drew up tables that could be used to calculate the movements of the Sun, the Moon and the planets. He also wrote a work on **geography** with the coordinates of hundreds of places and cities. With it he improved the figures of the Greek scholar Ptolemy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of mathematics in which you calculate with variables such as x and solve equations.
Precise instructions made of individual steps for solving a task.
An equation in which the unknown appears squared, for example x² + 10x = 39.
A ruler and religious leader in an Islamic empire.

gewusst: Our digits 0 to 9 are called “Arabic numerals”, but they originally come from India.
A famous example from al-Khwarizmi's algebra book is the equation x² + 10x = 39 with the solution 3.
Today the word “algorithm” comes up in every discussion about search engines and social media.

teile.einleitung: Hypatia was a scholar who lived more than 1600 years ago in Alexandria in Egypt. She taught mathematics, astronomy and philosophy and is regarded as the first known woman mathematician in history. Her life and her tragic death have made her famous to this day.
wichtigste: Hypatia lived and taught in the city of Alexandria.
She is regarded as the first known woman mathematician in history.
Her father Theon of Alexandria was also a mathematician.
She wrote explanations of works by earlier mathematicians such as Diophantus.
She studied the conic sections from the work of Apollonius.
As a teacher she taught Neoplatonism and also worked in astronomy.
According to present knowledge, she died in the year 415 AD.

abschnitte.text: Hypatia was born in the 4th century AD in **Alexandria**; her exact year of birth is not known. Alexandria lay on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt and was then one of the most important cities for science. Her father **Theon of Alexandria** was a well-known mathematician and astronomer. He taught his daughter himself, and she soon surpassed him in knowledge.

Hypatia ran her own school and gave public lectures. She taught **Neoplatonism**, a philosophy that goes back to the Greek thinker Plato. Her students included young men from noble families, among them Christians and followers of the old religions. One of her students, **Synesius of Cyrene**, wrote her letters that still survive today and reveal a lot about her.

Hypatia wrote **commentaries**, that is explanations, on important works of Greek mathematics. These included the “Arithmetica” of **Diophantus**, which deals with equations and numbers. She also studied the **conic sections** of Apollonius of Perga, that is curves such as the circle, ellipse, parabola and hyperbola. Sadly, her own writings have been lost; we know of them only from the reports of others.

Besides mathematics and philosophy, Hypatia also worked in **astronomy**. Together with her father she worked on the work of the astronomer Ptolemy, which describes the movements of the stars and planets. From the letters of Synesius we know that she understood the **astrolabe**. With this instrument you could find the position of the stars and work out the time.

In the year 415 AD Hypatia was caught up in a fierce power struggle between the Roman prefect of the city and the Christian bishop of Alexandria. She was killed by an angry mob. Her death shocked people even at that time. Today Hypatia is regarded as a role model for women in **science**, and there are books, pictures and a feature film about her.

begriffe.erklaerung: An ancient port city in Egypt, famous for its great library.
A school of philosophy that builds on the teachings of Plato.
A piece of writing that explains another work.
A curve formed when a cone is cut by a plane.
An old measuring instrument for finding the position of the stars.

gewusst: An asteroid and a crater on the Moon are named after Hypatia today.
Almost everything we know about Hypatia comes from texts by other people, because no work by her has definitely survived.
The 2009 feature film “Agora” tells her story.

teile.einleitung: An irrational number is a number that cannot be written as a fraction of two whole numbers. Its decimal places go on for ever without ever repeating in a regular pattern. Famous examples are the square root of 2, the circle number π and the golden ratio.
wichtigste: Irrational numbers cannot be written as a fraction p/q of whole numbers.
Their decimal form is infinitely long and does not recur.
The square root of a natural number n is only rational if n is a square number.
Johann Heinrich Lambert from Mulhouse was the first to prove, in the 18th century, that π is irrational.
Ferdinand von Lindemann showed in 1882 that π is even transcendental.
The Pythagoreans in ancient Greece were the first to discover such ratios of quantities.
Together with the rational numbers, the irrational numbers form the real numbers.

abschnitte.text: A rational number is a fraction such as 3/4 or -7/2, and every whole number belongs to them too. As a decimal, a fraction either ends, like 0.75, or repeats regularly, like 0.333... An **irrational number** does neither. Its digits run on **for ever** without any fixed pattern ever repeating. That is why you can never write it down exactly as a decimal, only approximately.

The square root of 2 is about 1.41421 and gives the length of the diagonal in a square with side length 1. The **circle number π** is about 3.14159 and describes the ratio of the circumference to the diameter of a circle. The **golden ratio** is about 1.618 and appears in art, architecture and nature. Euler's number e, about 2.71828, is also irrational, as Leonhard Euler showed in the 18th century. The square roots of 3, 5, 6 or 7 are irrational too, because these numbers are not square numbers.

If you multiply a rational number other than 0 by an irrational number, the result is always irrational. So 3 times the square root of 2, for example, is irrational again. With the **sum** of two irrational numbers it is different: it can also be rational. If you work out the square root of 2 plus (minus the square root of 2), for example, you get 0. The product of two irrational numbers can also be rational, because the square root of 2 times the square root of 2 gives exactly 2.

The **Pythagoreans**, a school around the Greek scholar Pythagoras, at first believed that everything could be described by whole numbers and their ratios. Then they discovered lengths that have no common measure, so-called **incommensurable** quantities, such as the side and diagonal of a square. According to a legend, Hippasus of Metapontum is said to have given away this discovery. In the 18th century **Johann Heinrich Lambert**, who was born in Mulhouse, proved that π is irrational. Later mathematicians such as Georg Cantor showed that there are even far more irrational than rational numbers.

Some irrational numbers are solutions of simple equations: the square root of 2 is a solution of x² − 2 = 0. Such numbers are called **algebraic**. A **transcendental number**, on the other hand, is not a zero of any polynomial with whole-number coefficients. In 1882 **Ferdinand von Lindemann** proved that π is transcendental. This also made it clear that you cannot use compasses and a ruler to construct a square exactly the same size as a given circle: the famous squaring of the circle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that can be written as a fraction of two whole numbers.
Describes a decimal in which a sequence of digits repeats again and again, such as 0.1212...
Describes two lengths for which there is no common measure that fits both exactly.
A number that is not a solution of any equation with whole-number coefficients, such as π.
All rational and irrational numbers together, that is all points on the number line.

gewusst: There are infinitely many rational numbers, but the irrational numbers are still far more numerous.
Computers have already calculated the circle number π to trillions of decimal places, and still no pattern ever repeats.
Johann Heinrich Lambert was born in 1728 in Mulhouse, which was then allied with the Swiss Confederation.

teile.einleitung: Multiplying and dividing fractions sounds difficult, but it is often easier than adding. You do not need a common denominator. With two simple rules and the reciprocal, you always get there.
wichtigste: When multiplying, you work out numerator times numerator and denominator times denominator.
2/3 · 3/5 gives 6/15, simplified 2/5.
You get the reciprocal of a fraction by swapping the numerator and denominator.
To divide by a fraction, you multiply by its reciprocal.
“2/3 of 90 francs” means 2/3 · 90 and gives 60 francs.
Before working it out, you can often cancel crosswise.
If you divide by a fraction smaller than 1, the result gets bigger.

abschnitte.text: The rule is: **numerator times numerator, denominator times denominator**. So 2/3 · 3/5 gives 6/15, and simplified by 3 that is 2/5. A whole number is written as a fraction with the denominator 1. So 4 · 3/10 becomes 12/10, simplified 6/5. You can also write the result as the mixed number 1 1/5.

When people say “2/3 of something” in everyday life, they mean a multiplication. 2/3 of 90 francs is 90 : 3 · 2 = 60 francs. Discounts work this way too: 1/4 of 80 francs is 20 francs. If you multiply by a proper fraction, that is a fraction smaller than 1, the result is **smaller** than the starting number.

You get the **reciprocal** of a fraction by swapping the numerator and denominator. The reciprocal of 5/8 is 8/5, and the reciprocal of 5 is 1/5. A fraction times its reciprocal always gives 1. You need the reciprocal for dividing.

To divide by a fraction, you multiply by its **reciprocal**. 3/4 : 1/2 becomes 3/4 · 2/1 = 6/4 = 3/2. And 5/6 : 5 is 5/6 · 1/5 = 5/30 = 1/6. An everyday example: how many 1/4-litre glasses can you fill from a 3-litre bottle? You work out 3 : 1/4 = 3 · 4 = 12 glasses.

Before multiplying, you can **cancel crosswise** and so avoid large numbers. With 7/9 · 3/14, you cancel 7 and 14 by 7, and 3 and 9 by 3. What is left is 1/3 · 1/2 = 1/6. The result is the same as if you first worked out 21/126 and then simplified, but much quicker.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fraction in which the numerator and denominator are swapped.
A fraction whose numerator is smaller than its denominator, so it is less than 1.
Simplifying the numerator of one fraction with the denominator of the other before multiplying.

gewusst: If you divide by 1/2, the number doubles, because every whole contains two halves.
Multiplying by a fraction can make a number smaller, which surprises many children at first.

teile.einleitung: When calculating with money, you add up coins and notes, work out prices and find the change. In Switzerland people pay with francs and centimes (Rappen). If you are good at calculating with money, you always know when shopping whether you have enough.
wichtigste: In Switzerland people pay with Swiss francs, shortened to CHF or Fr.
1 franc has 100 centimes.
The most valuable Swiss coin is the 5-franc piece.
Five 20-centime pieces make 1 franc.
When paying, you work out the change.
Several identical things are worked out by multiplying.
Small amounts are often written in centimes, larger ones in francs.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are coins of 5, 10, 20 and 50 centimes and of 1, 2 and 5 francs. The **5-franc piece**, also called the Fünfliber, is the coin with the highest value. The 1- and 2-centime coins are no longer legal tender. In everyday speech the half-franc piece is not called a **Fränkli** but simply a 50-Räppler.

Besides coins there are banknotes of 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. They are issued by the **Swiss National Bank**. The current series of notes shows typical sides of Switzerland, for example its diversity and creativity. The notes have many security features so that they cannot be forged.

If you want to know how much money you have, you add up all the coins. A 2-franc coin and a 1-franc coin make 3 francs together. 50 centimes and 50 centimes make 100 centimes, that is 1 franc. If an apple costs 80 centimes and a banana 70 centimes, both together cost 150 centimes, that is 1 franc 50.

If you pay with more money than something costs, you get **change**. If an exercise book costs 3 francs and you hand over 5 francs, you get 2 francs back. A good trick is **counting on**: you count up from the price to the amount paid. Many shop assistants at the till do it this way too.

If you buy several identical things, you can multiply. A croissant (Gipfeli) costs 2 francs, so 3 croissants cost 3 · 2 = 6 francs. Calculating also helps with dividing: how many 20-centime pieces make 1 franc? There are 5, because 5 · 20 = 100 centimes.

With **pocket money** many children learn to plan how to use their money. It helps to think before shopping about how much you want to spend. If you save part of it, you can afford something bigger later. Today many people also pay by card or mobile phone, for example with Twint, but calculating is just as important.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hundredth part of a franc, called Rappen in German.
Money you get back when you have paid too much.
Money that children are allowed to manage themselves regularly.
The bank that issues money in Switzerland.

gewusst: The 5-franc piece shows an Alpine herdsman, and the edge reads “Dominus providebit”.
The 1000-franc note is one of the banknotes with the highest value in the world.
The Swiss franc was introduced in 1850.

teile.einleitung: An equation of a plane describes an infinitely large, flat plane in three-dimensional space using numbers and vectors. You can imagine such a plane as a huge, infinitely thin sheet of glass. Equations of planes belong to analytic geometry, which is usually taught at grammar school (Gymnasium).
wichtigste: A plane in space can be described with an equation or with vectors.
The coordinate form is ax + by + cz = d.
The vector (a, b, c) is a normal vector and is perpendicular to the plane.
The parametric form needs a position vector and two direction vectors.
In the Hesse normal form, the normal vector has length 1.
The xy-plane has the equation z = 0.
Equations of planes are used to calculate intersection points, distances and angles in space.

abschnitte.text: In mathematics a plane is a **flat surface** with no thickness that extends infinitely far in all directions. Exactly one plane passes through three points that do not lie on a straight line. An example is the plane through (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1) with the equation x + y + z = 1. A sheet of paper or a table top is a small piece that you can imagine as a plane.

In the **parametric form** you start at a point on the plane, given by the position vector. Then come two direction vectors that point in different directions within the plane. With two numbers, the parameters, you can reach every point on the plane. The form looks like this: x = p + s·u + t·v.

The **coordinate form** is ax + by + cz = d. The vector (a, b, c) is a **normal vector**; it is perpendicular to the plane. With this form it is easy to find where the plane meets the axes: for 2x + 3y + 6z = 12 you set y and z equal to 0 and get the point (6, 0, 0). The plane 4x − 2y + 4z = 1 is parallel to 2x − y + 2z = 5, because their normal vectors point in the same direction.

It is named after the German mathematician **Ludwig Otto Hesse**, who lived in the 19th century. Here you divide the equation so that the normal vector has exactly length 1. Then the **distance** of a point from the plane can be read off directly. So the origin is at a distance of 3 from the plane x + 2y + 2z = 9, because the normal vector has length 3 and 9 divided by 3 gives 3.

With equations of planes you can check where a line meets a plane. The line x = t·(1, 2, 3) meets the plane x + y + z = 6 at the point (1, 2, 3), because there 6t = 6. In **computer graphics** and video games, rays of light and surfaces are calculated in this way. Architects, engineers and surveyors also use this geometry.

begriffe.erklaerung: An arrow that is exactly perpendicular to a plane.
An arrow that gives a direction within the plane.
The arrow from the origin to a fixed point on the plane.
The part of mathematics that describes figures with coordinates and equations.

gewusst: The basic idea of describing points with coordinates goes back to the French philosopher René Descartes.
The same plane can be described by infinitely many different equations, if you multiply all the numbers by the same factor.
Two planes in space that are not parallel always intersect in a straight line.

teile.einleitung: A pentagon is a flat shape with five corners and five straight sides. If all its sides and angles are equal, it is called a regular pentagon. Pentagons are found in nature, on footballs and even as the shape of a famous building.
wichtigste: A pentagon has 5 corners and 5 sides.
The word pentagon comes from the Greek word for five.
The angles in a pentagon always add up to 540 degrees.
In a regular pentagon each angle is 108 degrees.
A pentagon has 5 diagonals, which together form a five-pointed star.
A classic football has 12 black pentagons.
The US Department of Defense is a five-sided building called the Pentagon.

abschnitte.text: A pentagon is a **polygon** with exactly five corners and five sides. The name comes from Greek: **pentagon**, because “pente” means five and “gonia” angle or corner. Pentagons can look very different: lopsided, stretched or even with one corner bent inwards. The best known is the **regular pentagon**, in which all sides are the same length and all angles the same size.

The interior angles of every pentagon add up to **540 degrees**. You can remember this because a pentagon can be divided into three triangles, and each triangle has 180 degrees. In a regular pentagon each angle is therefore 108 degrees. A pentagon has 5 **diagonals**, lines joining corners that are not next to each other.

If you draw all the diagonals in a regular pentagon, you get a five-pointed star, the **pentagram**. In the middle of the star there is another small pentagon. The pentagon and the pentagram contain a special ratio of lengths, the **golden ratio**. Many artists found this ratio especially beautiful.

Many flowers have five petals, for example apple blossom, wild roses or forget-me-nots. Starfish usually have five arms. If you cut an apple across the middle, you see a star with five chambers for the pips in the centre. The cross-sections of some fruits, such as the **star fruit**, are also five-sided.

A classic football is made of **12 pentagons** and 20 hexagons, which together almost form a sphere. In Washington stands the **Pentagon**, the headquarters of the American Department of Defense, which is built as a pentagon. In the USA some road signs near schools and many old fortresses have five-sided shapes. By the way, you cannot cover a surface without gaps using pentagons alone, as you can with squares or hexagons.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Greek-based word for a five-sided shape.
A straight line between two corners that are not next to each other.
A five-pointed star formed by the diagonals of a pentagon.
For a shape, this means all sides and all angles are the same size.

gewusst: If you cut an apple across the middle, you see a five-pointed star.
You cannot tile a floor without gaps using regular pentagons.
A classic football has exactly 12 pentagons.

teile.einleitung: With integrals you can calculate how big an area under a curved line is. This is much harder than with rectangles or triangles, because the edge is not straight. Integral calculus solves this old problem elegantly and precisely.
wichtigste: The definite integral measures the area between a graph and the x-axis over an interval.
Areas below the x-axis give negative values when you integrate.
That is why you split the integral at the zeros of the function and add the absolute values of the parts.
The area between two graphs is calculated with the integral of the difference of the two functions.
The limits are often found by working out where the graphs intersect.
Even some infinitely long areas have a finite size.
You can work out the integral with an antiderivative using the fundamental theorem.

abschnitte.text: You split the area under a curve into many narrow rectangles and add up their areas. The narrower the rectangles, the more closely the sum matches the real area. In the limit of infinitely many, infinitely narrow strips, you get the **definite integral**. More than 2200 years ago, the Greek scholar **Archimedes** already used a similar idea to find the area under a parabola.

First you look for an **antiderivative** F of the function f, that is a function whose derivative is f. Then you substitute the upper and lower limits and work out the difference F(b) minus F(a). An example is f(x) = x³ between x = 0 and x = 2. An antiderivative is x⁴/4, and you get 16/4 minus 0, so the area is 4.

If part of the graph lies below the x-axis, the integral gives a **negative value** there. If you simply integrated over everything, positive and negative parts could cancel each other out. For sin(x) from 0 to 2π, for example, the integral gives 0, although the area is 4. That is why you first find the **zeros**, integrate piece by piece and add the absolute values.

You get the area between two graphs by subtracting the lower function from the upper one and integrating this difference. The limits are usually the **points of intersection**, the x-values where the graphs meet. Between f(x) = x and g(x) = x², from 0 to 1, the area is 1/6. Between f(x) = 3x and g(x) = x², from 0 to 3, the area is 4.5.

Sometimes an area stretches to infinity, for example under f(x) = 1/x² from x = 1 onwards. You then calculate an **improper integral** by moving the upper limit further and further to the right. The value gets closer and closer to the number 1. So this infinitely long area is exactly as big as a square with side length 1.

Calculating areas with integrals is needed all the time in engineering, physics and economics. Engineers use it, for example, to calculate the cross-section of bridge arches or canals. In physics, the area under a speed curve equals the **distance** travelled. Computer programs also often calculate areas approximately with many small strips.

begriffe.erklaerung: A method of calculation for finding areas under curves and much more.
A function whose derivative is the given function.
A point where a graph crosses or touches the x-axis.
The start and end of the interval over which you integrate.
An integral in which one limit is infinite or the function becomes unbounded.

gewusst: The parabola f(x) = 4 minus x² encloses an area of 32/3 with the x-axis, a little over 10.67 square units.
Archimedes found that a segment of a parabola is exactly 4/3 as big as a particular inscribed triangle.
With a mechanical device called a planimeter you can measure areas on plans simply by tracing round the edge.

teile.einleitung: Water hardness tells you how much calcium and magnesium is dissolved in water. Hard water leaves white limescale in the kettle and on the shower wall. In Switzerland the water is very different in hardness depending on the region.
wichtigste: Calcium and magnesium ions make water hard.
When hard water is heated, limescale forms; chemically it is calcium carbonate, CaCO3.
In Switzerland hardness is usually measured in French degrees of hardness.
1 French degree of hardness equals 10 milligrams of calcium carbonate per litre.
Water from granite and gneiss areas is usually rather soft, water from limestone areas rather hard.
An ion exchanger softens water by swapping calcium for sodium.
In very hard water soap lathers poorly, because lime soap forms.

abschnitte.text: Rainwater contains almost no dissolved substances. As it seeps through the soil and rock, it dissolves minerals, above all **calcium** and **magnesium**. These dissolved particles are called **ions**. The more of them there are in the water, the harder it is. Water from which practically all salts have been removed is called distilled water.

How hard the water is depends on the rock. In the **Jura** and the Swiss Plateau there is a lot of limestone, so the water there is often hard. In the Alps, spring water often flows through **granite** and gneiss, which hardly dissolve, so it is rather soft there. Every municipality's water supply publishes the hardness of its water.

Switzerland and France use the **French degree of hardness**, shortened to °fH. One degree equals 10 milligrams of calcium carbonate per litre of water. Germany, on the other hand, uses German degrees of hardness. At home you can check the hardness with **test strips**, which change colour depending on the hardness.

When hard water is heated, **limescale** is deposited; chemically it is calcium carbonate with the formula CaCO3. It forms crusts in the kettle, in the coffee machine and on heating elements. These crusts are called **scale** and waste energy because they conduct heat poorly. Acids such as vinegar or citric acid dissolve limescale. In hard water, soap also forms insoluble lime soap and lathers poorly.

An **ion exchanger** is a resin that holds on to calcium ions and releases sodium ions into the water instead. Such devices are found in dishwashers, which is why you top them up with regeneration salt. Washing powders contain substances that balance out the hardness. Hard water is not harmful to our health, though; it even supplies a little calcium and magnesium.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how much calcium and magnesium is dissolved in water.
An electrically charged particle, for example a calcium ion.
A hard limescale crust that forms when hard water is heated.
A device or resin that swaps certain dissolved particles for others.

gewusst: Stalactites and stalagmites in caves form from the lime deposited by hard water.
Soft water is often better for coffee and tea, because the flavours develop better.
Limescale spots on glasses are only dried minerals and are not poisonous.

teile.einleitung: The geometry set square (Geodreieck) is a transparent plastic triangle that is in almost every school bag. It is a ruler, a protractor and a help for right angles all in one. With it you can measure lines, draw angles and draw parallel lines.
wichtigste: A geometry set square has the shape of a right-angled isosceles triangle.
It has one right angle and two acute angles of 45° each.
The zero point of the centimetre scale is in the middle of the long side.
The centre line from the zero point to the tip helps when drawing perpendiculars.
The angle scale goes from 0° to 180°.
Fine lines parallel to the long side help when drawing parallel lines.
The German name is short for “geometry triangle”.

abschnitte.text: The geometry set square is a **right-angled isosceles triangle**. The long side lies opposite the right angle, and the two short sides are the same length. So the other two angles each measure 45°. Because it is transparent, you can see exactly what is underneath when you draw.

A **centimetre scale** with millimetre marks is printed along the long side. Its zero point is not at the edge but in the middle of the long side. From there it counts to the left and to the right. That way you can mark off a line of equal length in both directions from the midpoint.

A semicircular **angle scale** from 0° to 180° is printed along the edge. There are usually two rows of numbers, so that you can measure an angle from the left or from the right. You put the zero point on the vertex of the angle and the long side along one arm. If you read off 130°, for example, it is an **obtuse angle**, because it lies between 90° and 180°.

From the zero point to the tip runs a **centre line** that is exactly perpendicular to the long side. If you lay it on a straight line, you can draw a perpendicular along the long side. The fine lines parallel to the long side help when drawing **parallel lines**: you lay one of these lines on the given straight line and draw along the long side. This gives you accurate figures such as rectangles and parallelograms.

The geometry set square is an important tool in geometry lessons at primary and secondary school. Together with a **pair of compasses** and a sharp pencil, you use it to draw triangles, quadrilaterals and figures with circles. The name “Geodreieck” was originally a brand name of the company Aristo from Hamburg. Today many manufacturers make similar triangles, and the name is in general use.

begriffe.erklaerung: An angle of exactly 90°, like the corner of a sheet of paper.
An angle smaller than 90°.
An angle between 90° and 180°.
A straight line that is the same distance from another straight line everywhere.
A straight line that forms a right angle with another.

gewusst: With a geometry set square you can also draw angles over 180°, by measuring the rest up to the full angle of 360°.
The right angle of the geometry set square lies exactly above the zero point of the centimetre scale.
With two set squares slid along each other you can draw especially long parallel lines.

teile.einleitung: Factorising means turning a sum into a product, that is splitting it into factors. So 6x + 9 becomes 3(2x + 3). It is the opposite of multiplying out and helps with solving equations and simplifying terms.
wichtigste: Factorising turns a sum into a product.
The simplest method is taking out a common factor.
Binomial formulas help with factorising terms such as x² + 4x + 4.
Quadratic terms such as x² − 5x + 6 can often be split into (x − 2)(x − 3).
By grouping you can also factorise four terms.
Factorising helps you find zeros.
Not every term can be factorised over the real numbers, for example x² + 1.

abschnitte.text: A **factor** is a number or term in a multiplication. When factorising, you write a sum as a product. With numbers you know this as **prime factorisation**, for example 12 = 2 · 2 · 3. In algebra you split up terms with variables. Factorising is the opposite of **multiplying out**.

If all the terms have a common factor, you can **take it out**. In 6x + 9, 3 is contained in both parts, so 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3). In 4a²b − 6ab² you take out 2ab and get 2ab(2a − 3b). In x³ − x you first take out x and get x(x² − 1).

The **binomial formulas** can also be used backwards. From the third formula, x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1), so x³ − x = x(x − 1)(x + 1). With 2x² + 8x + 8 you first take out 2 and then recognise x² + 4x + 4 = (x + 2)². So the result is 2(x + 2)².

For terms of the form x² + px + q, you look for two numbers whose product is q and whose sum is p. For x² − 5x + 6, -2 and -3 fit, because (-2) · (-3) = 6 and (-2) + (-3) = -5. So x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). For x² + x − 12, 4 and -3 fit, so the result is (x + 4)(x − 3).

With four terms, **grouping** sometimes helps: ax + ay + bx + by = a(x + y) + b(x + y) = (a + b)(x + y). Not every term can be factorised. x² + 1 has no zero for real numbers, because x² is never negative, so the term cannot be split into factors over the real numbers. A big advantage of factorising: a product is zero exactly when one factor is zero, so you can find solutions of equations quickly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number or term that is multiplied by another.
Writing a common factor in front of a bracket.
Three rules for multiplying out and factorising terms such as (a + b)².
A value at which a term or function equals 0.

gewusst: Splitting large numbers into their prime factors is so hard, even for computers, that much of the encryption on the internet is based on it.
Every natural number greater than 1 can be split into prime factors in exactly one way, if you ignore the order.

teile.einleitung: An abacus is an ancient calculating device in which you slide beads back and forth on rods or in grooves. With it you can count, add, subtract and even multiply. It needs neither electricity nor batteries and is still used in some countries today.
wichtigste: The abacus is a calculating device with sliding beads.
Each row or rod stands for a place value, such as ones, tens or hundreds.
A counting frame at school often has 10 rows of 10 beads each, so 100 beads.
The Japanese abacus is called the soroban, the Chinese one the suanpan.
An abacus never needs electricity or batteries.
In everyday life it has largely been replaced by the pocket calculator.

abschnitte.text: An abacus consists of a frame with rods on which **beads** sit. By sliding the beads, you show numbers and calculate with them. Each rod stands for a **place value** in the decimal system: ones, tens, hundreds and so on. This lets you show even large numbers clearly. The word comes from Latin and Greek and originally meant something like board or tablet.

In Swiss schools many children learn arithmetic with a **counting frame**. It often has 10 rows of 10 beads each, 100 in total. Often five beads at a time are a different colour, so you can recognise amounts more quickly. If you slide 3 beads and then another 4 beads to the side, you see at once that together they make 7. This makes **adding** and subtracting easy to picture.

In Mesopotamia, in ancient Greece and among the Romans, people already calculated with pebbles on counting boards. The Latin word **calculus** means pebble, and our word calculate comes from it. The Romans also used small metal hand abacuses with grooves. In the Middle Ages, merchants in Europe calculated on **counting tables** with lines, until written arithmetic with Hindu-Arabic numerals took over.

The Chinese abacus is called the **suanpan** and has two beads at the top and five at the bottom of each rod. The Japanese **soroban** is slimmer and has one bead at the top and four at the bottom. An upper bead counts five, a lower bead one. In Japan and other Asian countries children still learn with it today, and there are even competitions. Skilled calculators just imagine the abacus in their heads and calculate lightning fast.

In everyday life the **pocket calculator** has mostly replaced the abacus since the 1970s. Still, the abacus has advantages: it never needs electricity, hardly ever breaks and helps you understand numbers and place values. There are also special abacuses for blind people that are easy to feel. In some shops in Asia you can still see one at the till today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A calculating device with sliding beads or pebbles.
The value of a digit depending on its position in the number, for example ones or tens.
A Japanese abacus with one upper and four lower beads on each rod.
A number system in which ten units are always grouped into the next place.

gewusst: Skilled abacus users can sometimes calculate faster than someone with a calculator.
Our word “calculate” comes from the Romans' counting pebbles.
The abacus is one of the oldest calculating devices and many hundreds of years older than any calculating machine.

teile.einleitung: Hydrogen is the lightest and simplest of all chemical elements. In space it is the most common substance of all, because stars like our Sun are made mostly of it. On Earth it is found mainly in water, which is also where its German name, meaning “water substance”, comes from.
wichtigste: Hydrogen is the lightest chemical element.
Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe.
Its symbol is H; a hydrogen molecule has the formula H2.
When hydrogen burns with oxygen, water is formed.
Electrolysis uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
In the laboratory hydrogen is detected with the squeaky pop test.
Hydrogen is seen as a possible clean fuel of the future.

abschnitte.text: A hydrogen atom consists of just one **proton** in its nucleus and one electron. That is why it stands right at the front of the periodic table with atomic number 1. Under normal conditions hydrogen is a colourless gas with no smell. Two atoms join to form a **molecule** with the formula H2.

Hydrogen is the most common element in the **universe**. Stars such as the Sun are made mostly of hydrogen. Deep inside them, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium; this is called **nuclear fusion**. It releases so much energy that the Sun shines and warms us.

Hydrogen is much lighter than air, so it rises. In the past it was used to fill **airships** such as the Zeppelins. In 1937 the airship Hindenburg caught fire in the USA and burned up; after that, balloons were usually filled with harmless helium. Hydrogen catches fire very easily.

A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen is called **oxyhydrogen**. If you light it, it burns with a loud bang and water is formed. The **squeaky pop test** is based on this: you hold a test tube of the gas to a flame. A squeaky or barking pop shows that hydrogen is present.

In **electrolysis**, an electric current is passed through water. This splits the water into hydrogen and oxygen. Twice as much hydrogen forms at the negative pole as oxygen at the positive pole. If the electricity comes from sun, wind or hydropower, it is called **green hydrogen**.

In a **fuel cell**, hydrogen reacts with oxygen and produces electricity; the only exhaust is water. Cars, buses and lorries can run on it. In Switzerland, hydrogen lorries were on the roads from 2020. Hydrogen is also used in industry, for example to make fertiliser.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance made of only one kind of atom.
The joining of atomic nuclei, which releases a great deal of energy.
Splitting a substance using electric current.
A device that makes electricity from hydrogen and oxygen.

gewusst: The name hydrogen means “water former”, because water is produced when it burns.
Almost three quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe is hydrogen.
Hydrogen was described as a substance of its own in 1766 by the Englishman Henry Cavendish.

teile.einleitung: A water filter removes dirt and other substances from water. It can be a simple tea strainer, a layer of sand and gravel or a large plant that prepares drinking water for a whole city. But each filter only holds back certain things.
wichtigste: A filter separates solid particles from a liquid, depending on the size of its holes.
A paper filter holds back sand, but dissolved salt passes through.
Home-made filters often consist of layers of gravel, sand and cotton wool.
Activated carbon binds substances that cause smell and taste to its huge surface.
In nature, rainwater is cleaned as it seeps through gravel and sand to the groundwater.
A lake waterworks turns water from a lake into drinking water.
A simple sand filter does not make stream water safe, because tiny germs get through.

abschnitte.text: A filter works like a very fine sieve. Particles bigger than its holes get caught, smaller ones flow through with the water. A **tea strainer** holds back the tea leaves, and a paper coffee filter even holds back fine sand. But substances that are **dissolved** in water, such as salt or sugar, are so tiny that they pass through any normal filter. The clear liquid after filtering is called the **filtrate**.

You can build a simple filter in a cut-off plastic bottle. Cotton wool goes at the bottom, fine **sand** above it and coarse **gravel** on top. If you pour cloudy water in, it comes out at the bottom much clearer. You still must not drink this water, because **bacteria** and viruses are much smaller than the gaps between the grains of sand.

**Activated carbon** is a special charcoal with countless tiny pores. One gram of it has an inner surface of several hundred square metres. Smelly substances, chlorine and some pollutants stick to this surface; this is called **adsorption**. That is why activated carbon is found in many water filter jugs, aquarium filters and breathing masks.

When rain soaks into the ground, the water flows slowly through soil, **gravel** and sand. Dirt and many germs get caught on the way, and soil bacteria break down substances. This is how clean **groundwater** forms. In Switzerland most drinking water comes from groundwater and springs, a smaller part from lakes.

A **lake waterworks** pumps water from deep in a lake and cleans it in several stages. These include sand filters, activated carbon filters, and ozone or UV light, which kills germs. Zurich and other towns on Lake Zurich, Lake Geneva or Lake Constance get part of their drinking water this way. Modern plants also use **membrane filters** with pores so fine that even bacteria are held back.

begriffe.erklaerung: The liquid that has passed through a filter.
Charcoal with a great many tiny pores to which substances stick.
Water that collects in the ground between sand, gravel and rock.
A very thin layer with tiny holes that only lets small particles through.

gewusst: Swiss tap water is so clean that you can drink it safely almost everywhere.
You cannot filter out salt, but you can separate it from water by evaporation or distillation.
There are drinking straws with a built-in filter that hikers can use to drink water from streams.

teile.einleitung: Division is the kind of calculation in which you split a number into equal parts. It is also called sharing or dividing, and in Switzerland it is written with the sign :. When you share out sweets fairly, you are already doing a division.
wichtigste: Dividing means sharing fairly.
The sign is the colon :, and in other countries also ÷ or /.
10 : 2 = 5 means that 10 in two equal parts makes 5.
Division is the opposite of multiplication.
Anyone who knows their times tables can also divide.
Sometimes a division leaves a remainder.
You must never divide by zero.

abschnitte.text: In **division** an amount is split into equal parts. If 24 apples are shared fairly among 6 children, each gets 24 : 6 = 4 apples. The number being divided is called the **dividend**, and the number you divide by is called the divisor. The result is called the **quotient**.

There are two ways of understanding a division. In **sharing**, you ask how much each one gets, for example 20 : 4 = 5 sweets per child. In **grouping**, you ask how many groups there are. If 16 children form groups of four, there are 16 : 4 = 4 groups.

Division is the opposite of **multiplication**. Because 3 · 7 = 21, you also know that 21 : 3 = 7. In the same way, 2 · 4 = 8 tells you that 8 : 2 = 4. That is why it is so important to know your **times tables** well.
