Dividing by 10 is especially easy: with numbers ending in zero, you simply take one zero away. So 30 : 10 = 3 and 200 : 10 = 20. Dividing by 2 means halving: 10 : 2 = 5. If you divide a number by 1, you get the same number again.

Not every division comes out exactly. If you share 13 marbles among 4 children, each gets 3 marbles and 1 is left over. You write 13 : 4 = 3 **remainder** 1. With larger numbers you work it out on paper place by place, or you carry on calculating with decimals.

Dividing by **zero** is not allowed in mathematics. That is because there is no number that gives, for example, 5 when multiplied by 0. Zero divided by a number, on the other hand, is allowed and always gives 0. Calculators show an error message for a division by zero.

begriffe.erklaerung: The result of a division.
The number that is divided.
The number you divide by.
What is left over when a division does not come out exactly.

gewusst: The colon as a division sign goes back to the German mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.
A fraction line also means divided by, so 3/4 is 3 : 4.
A number can be divided by 3 if the sum of its digits can be divided by 3.

teile.einleitung: A letter arithmetic puzzle, also called a cryptarithm, is a number puzzle in which letters stand for digits. You have to find out which digit is hiding behind which letter. The most famous example is SEND + MORE = MONEY.
wichtigste: In a letter arithmetic puzzle, each letter stands for a digit.
The same letters mean the same digits; different letters usually mean different digits.
The first digit of a number with several digits normally must not be 0.
Henry Dudeney published the puzzle SEND + MORE = MONEY in 1924.
The solution is 9567 + 1085 = 10652, so M = 1 and O = 0.
You solve such puzzles by thinking logically about carries and place values.
A good puzzle has exactly one solution.

abschnitte.titel: What is a letter arithmetic puzzle?
abschnitte.text: In a **letter arithmetic puzzle** a calculation is encoded: instead of digits there are letters. The same letters mean the same digit, and different letters normally stand for different digits. A number must not begin with 0. The technical term **cryptarithm** comes from Greek and means roughly “hidden number”.

In 1924 the English puzzle inventor **Henry Dudeney** published the puzzle SEND + MORE = MONEY. You can read it like a request for money: “Send more money!”. The solution is 9567 + 1085 = 10652. Dudeney is regarded as one of the greatest puzzle inventors of his time.

You start with the surest reasoning. In SEND + MORE = MONEY, the result is one digit longer than the numbers being added. Two four-digit numbers make at most 19,998 together, so M must be 1. From this it follows, step by step, that O = 0. The **carries** are important, the numbers you take into the next place when adding in columns.

In A + A + A = BA, 3 · A is a two-digit number ending in A, and that only works for A = 5, because 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. In AB + B = BA you find 89 + 9 = 98. In A · A = 2A you are looking for a number between 20 and 29 that is a square number and ends in A; that is 25 = 5 · 5. In AA + B = BCC you get 99 + 1 = 100, so C = 0.

abschnitte.titel: What such puzzles are good for
abschnitte.text: Letter arithmetic puzzles train **logical thinking** and understanding of the place value system. You learn to rule out cases systematically instead of guessing wildly. For computers, such puzzles are a popular practice example, because they can be solved by trying out all the possibilities. In puzzle magazines they appear alongside sudoku and crosswords.

begriffe.erklaerung: A calculation puzzle in which letters stand for digits.
The number you take into the next place in written calculation.
The value of a digit, which depends on the position it is in.

gewusst: The puzzle SEND + MORE = MONEY has exactly one solution, although it contains eight different letters.
There are also letter arithmetic puzzles whose words form meaningful sentences on both sides, which is very hard to invent.

teile.einleitung: Area tells you how big a surface is, for example a garden, a floor or a football pitch. It is measured in square units such as square metres. For many shapes there are handy formulas with which you can work out the area quickly.
wichtigste: Area tells you how much space a surface takes up.
It is measured in square units such as cm², m² or km².
Rectangle: length times width; a garden 12 m by 7 m has 84 m².
Triangle: base times height divided by 2.
Circle: pi times radius times radius.
A square metre has 10,000 square centimetres.
A hectare has 10,000 square metres.

abschnitte.text: **Area** counts how many unit squares fit into a shape. A square with a side length of 1 cm has exactly 1 **square centimetre** (cm²). A rectangle of 3 cm by 2 cm can be covered with 6 such squares. Area is something different from the **perimeter**, which gives the length of the edge.

The most important units are mm², cm², dm², m², ares, hectares and km². Because a metre has 100 centimetres, a square metre has 100 · 100 = 10,000 cm². A **hectare** is a square of 100 m by 100 m, that is 10,000 m². Farmers in Switzerland often measure their fields in hectares, and a football pitch is about 0.7 hectares.

For a **rectangle** you work out length times width: a garden 12 m by 7 m has 84 m². In a square all sides are equal, so you work out side times side. A square with an area of 64 cm² therefore has sides 8 cm long. Its perimeter is then 4 · 8 cm = 32 cm.

A **triangle** is exactly half of a matching rectangle, so you work out base times height divided by 2. With a base of 10 cm and a height of 6 cm, that gives 30 cm². For a **trapezium** you take the average of the two parallel sides times the height. With 8 cm and 4 cm and a height of 5 cm, that is (8 + 4) : 2 · 5 = 30 cm².

For the circle you need the number **pi**, which is about 3.14. The area is pi times radius times radius. With a radius of 5 cm, that is about 3.14 · 25 = 78.5 cm². The radius is the distance from the centre to the edge.

If you put down a new floor or paint a wall, you need to know the area. Flats are described by their living area in square metres. The area of Switzerland is about 41,285 km². The ancient Egyptians already calculated areas to measure out their fields again after the Nile floods.

begriffe.erklaerung: The area of a square with a side length of 1 m.
An area of 100 m by 100 m, that is 10,000 m².
The length of the edge of a shape.
A special number, about 3.14, used for calculations with circles.

gewusst: Of all rectangles with the same perimeter, the square has the largest area.
A football pitch is often used as a comparison to make large areas easier to imagine.
The word geometry means “land measuring” in Greek.

teile.einleitung: The limit of a function describes what value the function approaches when x moves closer and closer to a particular point or towards infinity. It is the foundation of analysis, that is differential and integral calculus. With limits you can calculate gradients, speeds and areas precisely.
wichtigste: A limit is the value that a function gets as close to as you like.
It is written with the sign lim, short for the Latin word limes.
The limit of sin(x)/x as x approaches 0 is 1, even though the function is not defined at 0.
As x approaches infinity, (3x² + 1)/(x²−5) has the limit 3.
A function is continuous at a point if the limit exists there and equals the function value.
The derivative is itself a limit of gradients.
L'Hôpital's rule helps with limits of the form “0 over 0”.

abschnitte.text: You ask: what value does f(x) get closer and closer to when x approaches a point x₀? This target value is called the **limit**. The function does not necessarily have to reach the value. For sin(x)/x, x = 0 is not allowed, yet the function gets as close to 1 there as you like.

Often you want to know how a function behaves for very large x. In (3x² + 1)/(x²−5), the numbers +1 and -5 become meaningless compared with x², so the limit is 3. In (2x + 1)/(x² + 3) the denominator grows faster, and the limit is 0. e^x also tends to 0 as x approaches minus infinity; there the x-axis is an **asymptote**.

Sometimes substituting gives the expression “0 over 0”. Then **cancelling** often helps: (x³−1)/(x−1) becomes x² + x + 1, and as x approaches 1 you get 3. If that does not work, **L'Hôpital's rule** helps, which differentiates the numerator and denominator. It actually comes from the Basel mathematician Johann Bernoulli and was published in 1696 in the textbook of the Marquis de L'Hôpital.

The gradient of a curve at a point is calculated as the limit of the gradients of secants. For f(x) = x² at the point 2, you look at ((2 + h)²−4)/h. If you let h approach 0, you get 4, the **derivative** at this point. Instantaneous speeds can be calculated in this way too, for example that of a falling stone.

Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed differential calculus in the 17th century, but still worked with vague “infinitely small” quantities. Only in the 19th century did **Augustin-Louis Cauchy** and Karl Weierstrass give the limit a precise definition. The limit is also used to explain **continuity**: a function is continuous if its graph has no jump or hole at that point. With 1/x, on the other hand, the graph shoots up towards plus infinity near 0 from the right.

begriffe.erklaerung: Latin for boundary; the abbreviation lim stands for the limit in formulas.
A straight line that a graph keeps getting closer to without reaching it.
The property of a function whose graph can be drawn without jumps.
The gradient of a function at a point, calculated as a limit.

gewusst: Engineers use the fact that sin(x)/x tends to 1 for small angles: there sin(x) is almost equal to x.
For the Romans, the word limes also meant a fortified frontier wall.
Without limits there would be no exact way of calculating areas under curved lines.

teile.einleitung: A triangle is a flat shape with three corners and three straight sides. It is the simplest of all polygons and turns up everywhere, from road signs to roof gables. Because triangles are very stable, engineers like to use them when building bridges and towers.
wichtigste: A triangle has three corners, three sides and three angles.
The three interior angles of a triangle always add up to 180°.
In an equilateral triangle all sides are the same length and every angle measures 60°.
In an isosceles triangle the two equal sides are called legs.
The longest side in a right-angled triangle is called the hypotenuse.
Any two sides together must always be longer than the third side, otherwise no triangle can be built.
The Swiss road sign “Give way” has the shape of a triangle standing on its point.

abschnitte.text: A triangle is formed when you join three points that do not lie on a line with straight lines. The points are called **vertices** or corners and are usually labelled A, B and C. The lines between them are the **sides** a, b and c. In every triangle, the three interior angles add up to exactly 180 degrees.

If all three sides are the same length, it is called an **equilateral triangle**, and each angle measures 60°. If two sides are the same length, it is called an **isosceles triangle**. The two equal sides are called legs, and the third side is called the base. If all the sides are different lengths, it is a scalene triangle.

If all the angles are smaller than 90°, the triangle is **acute-angled**, for example with 50°, 60° and 70°. If it has exactly one right angle of 90°, it is called right-angled. If one angle is bigger than 90°, as with 30°, 50° and 100°, it is called **obtuse-angled**. More than one obtuse angle is impossible, because the sum would then be more than 180°.

In a right-angled triangle, the longest side lies opposite the right angle: the **hypotenuse**. The two shorter sides are called the legs. By the famous **Pythagoras' theorem**, a² + b² = c². A well-known example is the triangle with sides of 3, 4 and 5 cm, because 9 + 16 = 25.

Triangles do not bend out of shape as easily as quadrilaterals, so they are very **stable**. That is why you find them in truss bridges, electricity pylons, cranes and roof frames. In Switzerland, warning signs are triangular, and the “Give way” sign is a triangle too. If you put two identical triangles together along their long side, you get a **quadrilateral**.

You cannot make a triangle from just any three sticks. The **triangle inequality** says: any two sides together must be longer than the third. With 4 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm it works, because 4 + 5 = 9 is bigger than 7. With 2 cm, 3 cm and 8 cm, however, it does not.

begriffe.erklaerung: The longest side in a right-angled triangle; it lies opposite the right angle.
One of the two shorter sides that form the right angle.
The two sides of equal length in an isosceles triangle.
An angle inside the shape; in a triangle all three add up to 180°.

gewusst: The Great Pyramid of Khufu in Egypt has four triangular faces.
Every polygon can be divided into triangles, which is why computer graphics in games are made of millions of tiny triangles.
The musical instrument triangle gets its name from the Latin word for triangle.

teile.einleitung: Dominoes is a game with rectangular tiles that are divided into two halves with dots. You place tiles next to each other so that the numbers of dots match. You can also stand dominoes up in long rows and make them fall over.
wichtigste: A domino is divided into two halves.
A normal set with at most 6 dots per half has 28 tiles.
An empty half counts as 0 dots.
The double six tile has 12 dots altogether.
You place a tile against a half with the same number of dots.
Dominoes originally comes from China and reached Europe in the 18th century.
In the domino effect, all the tiles fall over one after another when you push the first one.

abschnitte.text: A **domino** is a flat rectangle divided by a line into two square halves. Each half has 0 to 6 dots, as on a dice. A tile with the same number of dots on both sides is called a **double**, for example the double six with 12 dots. A tile with 2 and 5 dots has 7 dots altogether.

In a normal set, every combination of two numbers between 0 and 6 appears exactly once. There are 7 doubles and 21 tiles with two different numbers. Together that makes 7 + 21 = **28 tiles**. There are also bigger sets, for example up to double nine with 55 tiles.

At the start, each player draws some tiles. Taking turns, you place a tile at an open end of the chain so that the **numbers of dots** match. So only a half with 4 dots fits against a half with 4 dots. Anyone who cannot place a tile has to draw one or miss a turn, and whoever gets rid of all their tiles first wins.

Domino games have been known in **China** for many centuries. They appeared in Europe in the 18th century, first in Italy. The name probably comes from a black and white hooded cloak called a domino. In the past the tiles were often made of bone or ivory with black ebony; today they are usually made of plastic or wood.

If you stand dominoes on end in a row and push the first one, they topple over one after another. This is called the **domino effect**. The term is also used figuratively when one event sets off a whole chain of consequences. In record attempts, millions of tiles are set up to form huge pictures.

Dominoes is good arithmetic practice, because you are constantly adding up dots. Mathematicians also study how surfaces can be covered completely with dominoes. A well-known puzzle asks whether you can cover a chessboard with two opposite corner squares removed using dominoes. The answer is no, because the two missing squares are the same colour and every tile covers one light and one dark square.

begriffe.erklaerung: A domino with the same number of dots on both halves.
A chain reaction in which one event sets off many more.
A game in which you place pieces next to each other according to rules.

gewusst: In a normal set of dominoes, each number from 0 to 6 appears on exactly eight halves.
A falling domino can knock over a slightly bigger one, so a chain can end with bigger and bigger tiles.

teile.einleitung: The half-life is the time after which only half of an amount is left. It is best known for radioactive substances, which decay over time. Researchers use it, for example, to find out how old bones, wood or mummies are.
wichtigste: After one half-life, half of a radioactive substance has decayed.
After 2 half-lives a quarter is left, after 3 an eighth.
Only after 7 half-lives is less than 1 per cent left.
Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years.
The half-life does not depend on the amount of the substance.
The amount left is calculated with N(t) = N₀ · (1/2)^(t/T).
Half-lives range from fractions of a second to billions of years.

abschnitte.text: Radioactive atoms decay randomly; you never know exactly when a single atom will decay. But with a very large number of atoms there is a fixed rule: after a certain time, half of them have decayed. This time is called the **half-life**. The principle is an example of **exponential decay**.

After each half-life the amount halves again. So after 3 half-lives, 1/2 · 1/2 · 1/2 = 1/8 is still there. **Iodine-131** has a half-life of about 8 days, so of 80 mg, 10 mg are left after 24 days. In general N(t) = N₀ · (1/2)^(t/T), and T is linked to the **decay constant** λ by T = ln(2)/λ.

The half-life is fixed for each substance and does not depend on how much you have. If you take twice as much, half of it has still decayed after the same time. Heat, pressure or chemical reactions hardly change it either. That is why it is an excellent **clock** for science.

Living things constantly take in carbon, including a small amount of **carbon-14**. After death no new carbon is added, and what is there decays with a half-life of about 5730 years. If you measure how much is still left, you can find out the age of wood, bones or remains of fabric. The American Willard Libby developed this **radiocarbon dating** method and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1960.

Half-lives are very different: iodine-131 takes about 8 days, uranium-238 on the other hand about 4.5 billion years. In medicine, substances with a short half-life are used so that they leave the body again quickly. With radioactive waste from nuclear power stations, long half-lives are a big problem, because it has to be stored safely for a very long time. That is why Switzerland, too, has been searching for decades for a suitable site for a **deep geological repository**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The property of some atoms of decaying by themselves and giving off radiation.
The change of an unstable atom into another atom.
A rare, radioactive form of carbon used for dating.
A number λ that tells you how fast a substance decays.

gewusst: Radiocarbon dating showed that the glacier mummy Ötzi lived more than 5000 years ago.
The idea of half-life is also used in medicine, for example for how quickly a medicine is broken down in the body.
Uranium-238 is so long-lived that only about half of it has decayed since the Earth was formed.

teile.einleitung: An arithmetic sequence is a row of numbers in which you always add the same amount to get to the next number. An example is 5, 8, 11, 14 and so on; here 3 is added each time. We meet such sequences in stairs, savings plans and rows of seats.
wichtigste: In an arithmetic sequence the difference d between two neighbouring terms is always the same.
The nth term is calculated with a(n) = a1 + (n minus 1) times d.
The sequence 5, 8, 11, 14 has the explicit formula a(n) = 3n + 2.
If you plot the points (n, a(n)), they lie on a straight line.
Every middle term is the average of its two neighbours.
The sum of the first n terms is n times (first plus last term) divided by 2.

abschnitte.text: A **sequence** is an ordered list of numbers; its entries are called **terms**. In an arithmetic sequence you get each new term by always adding the same number. This number is called the **common difference** d. In 6, 10, 14, 18, d = 4. If d is negative, the sequence gets smaller, for example 20, 17, 14, 11.

With an **explicit formula** you can calculate any term directly: a(n) = a1 + (n minus 1) times d. If a sequence starts with a1 = 3 and d = 4, then a20 = 3 + 19 times 4 = 79. The sequence 5, 8, 11, 14 can be written briefly as a(n) = 3n + 2. The other way round, you can ask which term of the sequence 7, 12, 17, 22 is the number 102: it is the 20th term.

Every term lies exactly halfway between its neighbours. If a5 = 10 and a7 = 22, then a6 is the average, that is 16. This is where the name comes from, because the **arithmetic mean** of two neighbours gives the term in between. If a3 = 11 and a8 = 31, there are five steps between them, and 20 divided by 5 gives d = 4. Going two steps back gives a1 = 3.

A well-known story tells of the young **Carl Friedrich Gauss**, who as a pupil was supposed to add all the numbers from 1 to 100. He made pairs: 1 + 100, 2 + 99, 3 + 98 and so on, each making 101. There are 50 such pairs, so the sum is 5050. From this comes the **sum formula**: number of terms times (first plus last term) divided by 2. So 2 + 4 + 6 up to 200 makes exactly 100 times 202 divided by 2, that is 10,100.

If you plot the points (n, a(n)) in a coordinate system, they all lie on a **straight line**. The common difference d corresponds to the gradient. In everyday life you find arithmetic sequences wherever the same amount is added regularly. Anyone who puts 5 francs into their piggy bank every week has 5, 10, 15, 20 francs. The heights of the steps of a staircase or the house numbers on one side of a street also form such sequences.

begriffe.erklaerung: An ordered list of numbers with a first, second, third term and so on.
A single number in a sequence.
The constant gap between two neighbouring terms of an arithmetic sequence.
A formula with which you can calculate any term directly from its number n.

gewusst: The sum of the first n odd numbers is always a square number, for example 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.
Gauss later became one of the most famous mathematicians of all time.
The numbers on a tape measure also form an arithmetic sequence.

teile.einleitung: A cone is a geometric solid with a round base and a tip. Its side surface, the curved surface, joins the edge of the circle to the tip. We meet cone shapes everywhere, for example in ice-cream cones, funnels or traffic cones.
wichtigste: A cone has a circular base, a curved surface and a tip.
Its volume is one third times base area times height.
A cone with radius 3 cm and height 4 cm has a volume of about 37.7 cm³.
The curved surface area is pi times radius times slant height.
A cone with radius 3 cm and slant height 5 cm has a curved surface area of about 47.1 cm².
If you cut a cone parallel to a slant line, you get a parabola.
If a cone-shaped funnel is filled to half its height, only an eighth of its volume is full.

abschnitte.text: A **cone** is a solid with a circle as its **base** and a tip, also called the apex. If you join every point on the edge of the circle to the tip with a straight line, you get the curved **surface**. If the tip is exactly above the centre of the circle, it is called a right cone. The height h is the distance from the tip to the base. The line from the edge of the circle to the tip is called the **slant height** s.

The volume of a cone is exactly a third of that of a cylinder with the same base and height. The formula is: V equals one third times pi times r² times h. With a radius of 3 cm and a height of 4 cm, that gives one third times 3.14 times 9 times 4, about 37.7 cm³. You can try this out by filling a cone-shaped cup with sand three times and pouring it into a matching cylinder. The Greek mathematician Archimedes already knew this relationship.

abschnitte.titel: Curved surface and total surface area
abschnitte.text: If you cut open the curved surface of a cone and lay it flat, you get a **sector**, a slice of a circle like a piece of cake. The curved surface area is calculated with M equals pi times r times s. With a radius of 3 cm and a slant height of 5 cm, that gives about 47.1 cm². The total surface area is the curved surface plus the base circle. You find the slant height with Pythagoras' theorem, because r, h and s form a right-angled triangle.

If you cut a cone with a flat plane, different curves appear depending on the angle: the **conic sections**. A cut parallel to the base gives a circle, a slightly sloping cut an ellipse. If the cut runs parallel to a slant line, you get a **parabola**. An even steeper cut gives a hyperbola. The Greek mathematician Apollonius of Perga described these curves in detail more than 2000 years ago.

A cone-shaped funnel with its tip pointing down is filled with water up to half its height. You might think it is half full, but that is not true. The water itself forms a small cone whose radius and height are only half as big. Because the volume depends on three lengths, it becomes ½ times ½ times ½, that is an **eighth** as big. Only when you fill the funnel to about four fifths of its height is it roughly half full.

Many things are cone-shaped, for example an **ice-cream cone**, a party hat, a funnel or the red and white traffic cones at roadworks. Volcanoes such as Mount Fuji in Japan also look almost like a cone. The tip of a sharpened coloured pencil is also a small cone. Sand or gravel that is poured out forms a cone by itself, a heap cone. Cone shapes are practical because they stand firmly and stack well.

begriffe.erklaerung: The line from the edge of the base to the tip of the cone.
The curved side surface of a cone.
A curve formed when a cone is cut by a plane.
A piece of a circle that looks like a slice of cake.

gewusst: The paths of planets and comets round the Sun are conic sections, namely ellipses, parabolas or hyperbolas.
Depending on the angle, the cone of light from a torch draws a circle, an ellipse or a parabola on the wall.

teile.einleitung: Citric acid is an acid found in lemons, limes and many other fruits. It gives them their sour taste. Today we find it in drinks, sweets and descalers, and it even plays an important role in every one of our body cells.
wichtigste: Lemons and limes contain especially large amounts of citric acid.
Pure citric acid is a white, crystalline powder.
As a food additive it has the number E 330.
Today it is mostly produced industrially using a mould.
A citric acid molecule has three carboxyl groups (COOH).
Its salts are called citrates.
The Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele first obtained it in pure form from lemon juice in the 18th century.

abschnitte.text: Citric acid is an organic acid with the molecular formula C₆H₈O₇. Its molecule carries three **carboxyl groups**, that is three COOH groups, each of which can release a hydrogen ion. Pure citric acid is a white, **crystalline** powder that dissolves very well in water. The solution tastes pleasantly sour. Its salts are called **citrates**.

Lemons and limes contain especially large amounts of citric acid, but so do oranges, currants, pineapples and tomatoes. Even milk and our bones contain small amounts. Lemon juice contains about five to six per cent of it. The sour taste of many fruits comes mainly from it.

In the past, citric acid was obtained from lemons, above all from Italy. Today it is mostly produced with the **mould** Aspergillus niger. The mould grows in large tanks in a sugary solution and gives off citric acid as it does so. This process is called **fermentation**. More than a million tonnes are produced worldwide every year.

As a food additive with the number **E 330**, citric acid makes lemonades, sweets and jams sour and helps them keep longer. In sherbet powder it reacts with bicarbonate of soda and fizzes. Because it dissolves limescale, it is found in many **descalers** for coffee machines and kettles. Unlike strong acids, it is relatively mild and is quickly broken down in nature.

In our cells, a cycle of chemical reactions runs all the time to get energy from food. It is called the **citric acid cycle** or citrate cycle, because citrate plays a central role in it. The German-British biochemist Hans Krebs worked it out in 1937, which is why it is also called the Krebs cycle. He received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it in 1953.

begriffe.erklaerung: The group of atoms COOH that makes carboxylic acids acidic.
A salt of citric acid.
Making a substance with the help of microorganisms such as fungi or bacteria.
A code for approved additives in food.

gewusst: Besides citric acid, Carl Wilhelm Scheele also discovered many other substances, including oxygen.
The citric acid in drinks usually does not come from lemons but from moulds.
Effervescent tablets fizz because citric acid forms carbon dioxide with bicarbonate of soda.

teile.einleitung: A geometric series is the sum of the terms of a geometric sequence, in which each number is made by multiplying by the same factor. The surprising thing is that an infinitely long sum sometimes has a finite value. So 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 and so on comes to exactly 2.
wichtigste: In a geometric sequence you multiply each term by the same factor q.
The geometric series is the sum of these terms.
For finitely many terms the formula is a1 · (q^n−1) / (q−1).
An infinite geometric series only has a value if the absolute value of q is less than 1.
Its value is then a1 / (1−q).
The series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 and so on comes to exactly 2.
The recurring number 0.999... is exactly equal to 1.

abschnitte.text: A **geometric sequence** is made when you start from a number a1 and keep multiplying by the same factor q. In 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 q = 2; in 3, 1, 1/3, 1/9 q = 1/3. If you add up the terms, you get a **geometric series**. It is one of the most important examples of series in mathematics.

For finitely many terms there is a handy **sum formula**: a1 · (q^n−1) / (q−1). In 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 512 there are 10 terms with q = 2, so 2 to the power 10 minus 1, which gives 1023. That way you do not have to add every number separately. The formula works for every q except 1.

If the absolute value of q is less than 1, the terms keep getting smaller and the sum approaches a fixed value. We say the series **converges**, and its value is a1 / (1−q). So 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... comes to exactly 2, and 3 + 1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + ... to exactly 4.5. The series 1 + x + x² + ... has the value 4 when x = 3/4.

Every recurring decimal can be written as a geometric series. The number 0.121212... is 12/100 + 12/10000 + ... and gives the fraction 4/33. Likewise 0.999... equals 9/10 + 9/100 + ... and is therefore exactly **1**. This surprises many people, but it is mathematically exact.

Around 2500 years ago, the Greek philosopher **Zeno of Elea** claimed that Achilles could never catch up with a tortoise, because he always first had to reach the place where it had just been. The geometric series solves this puzzle, because infinitely many ever shorter distances add up to a finite distance. It is similar with a ball that falls from a height of 2 m and each time bounces back to half its height. In theory it travels exactly 6 m altogether.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sum of the terms of a sequence of numbers.
The fixed factor by which you multiply in a geometric sequence.
To get closer and closer to a fixed value.
A decimal whose decimal places repeat for ever.

gewusst: A square that you keep halving, laying the halves side by side, shows clearly that 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... comes to exactly 1.
Geometric series help banks calculate instalments and pensions.
If q is 1 or greater, the infinite sum grows without limit.

teile.einleitung: Finger counting means calculating with the help of your own fingers. It is probably the oldest calculating aid of humankind, because you always have your fingers with you. With a few tricks you can even work out the nine times table with them.
wichtigste: With your fingers you can count, add and subtract.
Two hands have 10 fingers altogether, which is probably connected with our decimal system.
A whole hand shows 5; for 8 you need 3 more fingers of the second hand.
In the nines trick, for n · 9 you fold down the nth finger.
The fingers to the left of the folded finger are the tens, those to the right the ones.
For 4 · 9, 3 fingers stay up on the left and 6 on the right, so the result is 36.
In many cultures there were elaborate finger numbers going into the thousands.

abschnitte.text: Small children often learn to count with their fingers. For 4 + 3 you first hold up 4 fingers, then 3 more, and see 7 fingers up. If you show 10 fingers and fold down 4, 6 stay up, which matches the calculation 10 − 4 = 6. If a child holds up 9 fingers, exactly 1 finger is folded down. Fingers make numbers **visible** and something you can touch.

Most people have two hands with **10 fingers** altogether. Many experts believe that this is why we calculate in the **decimal system**. Three children with all their fingers up show 30 fingers, that is three tens. Some cultures also counted their toes and calculated with the base 20. You can find traces of this in French, where 80 is “quatre-vingts”, that is four times twenty.

Lay both hands in front of you with all ten fingers spread out. For 4 · 9, you fold down the **fourth finger**, counting from the left. To the left of it are 3 fingers, which are the tens, and to the right 6 fingers, which are the ones, so 36. For 7 · 9 you fold down the seventh finger: there are 6 on the left and 3 on the right, which makes 63. The trick works because n · 9 = n · 10 − n.

People do not count the same way everywhere. In Switzerland and Germany many people start counting with the **thumb**, in the USA often with the index finger. In parts of Asia people use the thumb to count off the finger joints of the other fingers and so reach 12 with one hand. In the Middle Ages the English monk **Bede** described a finger system with which you could show numbers into the thousands.

Calculating aids such as counting stones and the **abacus** developed from finger counting. In Korea in the 20th century the Chisanbop method was invented, with which children add large numbers quickly using their fingers. Finger counting is not a sign of weakness. It helps many people understand numbers until they can do the calculations in their heads.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number system with the base 10, as we use it today.
A counting board with sliding beads.
The places of a number that tell you how many ones and how many tens it has.

gewusst: The word “digital” comes from the Latin “digitus”, which means finger.
With the thumb and the finger joints of one hand you can count to 12, which fits the dozen.

teile.einleitung: Gödel's incompleteness theorems are among the most famous results in mathematics. In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved that there are true statements in mathematics that cannot be proved with the rules of a system. With this he showed that mathematics has fundamental limits.
wichtigste: Kurt Gödel published his incompleteness theorems in 1931.
The first theorem says: every consistent system of arithmetic contains true statements that it cannot prove.
The second theorem says: such a system cannot prove its own consistency.
Gödel's theorems disproved Hilbert's programme in its original form.
For the proof, Gödel encoded formulas and proofs as natural numbers; this is called Gödel numbering.
Gödel was born in Brünn in 1906 and later became a friend of Albert Einstein.
Alan Turing's result from 1936 that the halting problem is undecidable is closely related.

abschnitte.text: Kurt Gödel was born in 1906 in **Brünn**, which is now called Brno and lies in the Czech Republic. He studied mathematics and philosophy in Vienna and was only 25 years old when he published his famous theorems. In 1940 he moved to the USA, to the **Institute for Advanced Study** in Princeton. There he was a close friend of Albert Einstein, and the two often went on long walks together.

In the 1920s the German mathematician **David Hilbert** wanted to put the whole of mathematics on a firm foundation. His aim was a system of basic rules, the **axioms**, with which every true statement could be proved. It should also be possible to prove that this system never leads to contradictions. This plan is called **Hilbert's programme**.

Gödel showed that Hilbert's plan cannot succeed in this form. Every consistent system that is strong enough to calculate with natural numbers contains **true but unprovable statements**. To show this, Gödel built a statement that says, in effect: “This statement cannot be proved.” If it could be proved, it would be false and the system would contain a contradiction, so it must be true and unprovable.

The second incompleteness theorem goes even further. Such a system cannot prove its own **consistency** from within itself. For that you would always need an even stronger system, for which the same problem applies again. It is a bit like trying to pull yourself out of a swamp by your own hair.

For his proof Gödel had a brilliant idea. He assigned a unique natural number to every sign, every formula and every proof. This method is called **Gödel numbering**, and the numbers are called Gödel numbers. In this way statements about numbers could at the same time be statements about formulas and proofs, much as computers today store everything as numbers.

Gödel's results changed mathematics and philosophy greatly. In 1936 the Englishman **Alan Turing** used a similar idea to show that no computer program can decide for all programs whether they will stop at some point. This **halting problem** is a foundation of computer science. Gödel died in Princeton in 1978 and is regarded as one of the greatest logicians of all time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic principle that is assumed to be true without proof.
Describes a system in which you cannot prove both a statement and its opposite.
Calculating with natural numbers, that is plus, times and so on.
A complete logical explanation of why a statement is true.
The question of whether a program will stop at some point or run on for ever.

gewusst: Gödel's famous paper of 1931 appeared in a specialist journal and was only about 25 pages long.
Einstein is said to have remarked that he went to the institute mainly for the privilege of walking home with Gödel.
Gödel's theorems do not mean that mathematics is unreliable, only that no system can prove everything.

teile.einleitung: In mathematics a straight line is a perfectly straight line that goes on infinitely in both directions. It has neither a beginning nor an end, and no thickness. You can only ever draw a piece of it, best with a ruler.
wichtigste: A straight line is a straight line with no beginning and no end.
Exactly one straight line passes through two points.
A piece of a straight line between two points is called a line segment.
A line with a starting point but no end is called a ray.
Straight lines are best drawn with a ruler.
Two straight lines that never meet are called parallel.
Straight lines are usually labelled with small letters such as g or h.

abschnitte.text: A **straight line** is a line that is not bent anywhere and goes on without end in both directions. In mathematics it is imagined as infinitely thin. Because it is infinitely long, you can never draw the whole of it on paper. So you draw a piece and imagine the rest.

A **line segment** is the part of a straight line between two points, so it has a beginning and an end and a length you can measure. A **ray** starts at a point and then goes on infinitely in one direction, like the beam of a torch. The straight line itself has no beginning and no end. Line segments are written, for example, as AB, where A and B are the end points.

Through two different points you can always draw exactly one straight line. This is one of the basic rules of geometry, which the Greek mathematician **Euclid** wrote down more than 2000 years ago. That is why, when drawing, you place the ruler against two points and join them. If three points lie on the same straight line, they are called **collinear**.

Two straight lines in a plane can meet at one point or never meet. If they never meet, they are called **parallel**, like the two rails of a railway track. If they cross at a right angle, that is at 90 degrees, they are called **perpendicular** to each other. With a geometry set square you can draw parallel and perpendicular lines accurately.

In everyday life we meet many almost straight lines: the edges of tables, tight strings, road markings and rays of light. Bricklayers stretch a **guide line** so that a wall turns out nice and straight. The **number line** in maths lessons is also a straight line on which numbers are marked in order. In a coordinate system, straight lines can be described exactly with a formula.

begriffe.erklaerung: A piece of a straight line with a start point and an end point.
A line with a starting point that goes on infinitely in one direction.
Two lines that are always the same distance apart and never meet.
A straight measuring tool with a scale for drawing and measuring straight lines.
A straight line on which numbers are placed at equal distances.

gewusst: Nobody can draw a true mathematical straight line, because it is infinitely long.
More than 2000 years ago Euclid already described that exactly one straight line passes through two points.
A laser beam is so straight that it is used on building sites for lining things up.

teile.einleitung: Differential calculus is a branch of mathematics that describes how fast something changes. Its most important tool is the derivative, which gives the gradient of a curve at every point. It was developed in the 17th century by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.
wichtigste: The derivative f'(x₀) gives the gradient of the tangent at the point x₀.
The difference quotient (f(x + h)−f(x))/h measures the average gradient between two points.
If you let h go towards 0, the difference quotient becomes the derivative.
The derivative of 5x² is 10x, the derivative of sin(x) is cos(x).
At maximum and minimum points of a differentiable function, f'(x) = 0.
If f'(x) > 0 everywhere, the function is strictly increasing.
Newton and Leibniz developed differential calculus independently of each other.

abschnitte.text: Imagine you are cycling up a road that is sometimes steeper and sometimes flatter. The **derivative** tells you at every point how steep it is right there. Geometrically, f'(x₀) is the gradient of the **tangent**, the straight line that only touches the graph at the point x₀. For f(x) = x², the gradient at the point x = 3 is exactly 6.

abschnitte.titel: From the difference quotient to the derivative
abschnitte.text: Between two points on a graph you can calculate the average gradient. This is done with the **difference quotient** (f(x + h)−f(x))/h. If you let the distance h get smaller and smaller, the secant approaches the tangent. This limit is called the **differential quotient** or derivative.

There are simple rules for many functions. By the **power rule**, xⁿ has the derivative n · xⁿ⁻¹, so x² has the derivative 2x. A constant factor stays, so the derivative of 5x² is 10x. The derivative of sin(x) is cos(x), and a constant has the derivative 0. Further rules such as the product and chain rules help with composite functions.

With derivatives you can investigate the shape of a graph. Where f'(x) > 0 the function rises; where f'(x) < 0 it falls. At a maximum or minimum point the tangent is horizontal, and there f'(x) = 0. This **curve sketching** is an important part of maths lessons at grammar school (Gymnasium).

The Englishman **Isaac Newton** and the German **Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz** developed differential calculus independently of each other in the second half of the 17th century. Newton needed it for the physics of motion; Leibniz invented the practical notation dy/dx. A fierce dispute arose between the two and their followers about who had been first. Later the Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler and the Basel Bernoulli family greatly extended the method.

Speed is the derivative of the distance travelled with respect to time. In physics, engineering and economics, differential calculus describes all kinds of change. Engineers use it to calculate bridges, economists to find the best production quantity. Weather forecasts and space travel would not be possible without it either.

begriffe.erklaerung: A function that gives the gradient of the graph at every point.
A straight line that touches a graph at one point.
The average gradient between two points on a graph.
Describes a function whose values keep getting bigger to the right.

gewusst: The function f(x) = eˣ is its own derivative.
The signs dy/dx and the long stretched S for the integral come from Leibniz and are still used today.

teile.einleitung: Graph theory is a field of mathematics that studies points and the connections between them. Such networks are called graphs, and they describe, for example, railway lines, friendships in social networks or the internet. It was founded in 1736 by the Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler.
wichtigste: A graph consists of vertices and edges that connect the vertices.
Leonhard Euler founded graph theory in 1736 with the Königsberg bridge problem.
The degree of a vertex tells you how many edges end at it.
The sum of all vertex degrees is always twice the number of edges.
A tree with n vertices has exactly n−1 edges.
The four colour theorem was proved in 1976 with the help of a computer.
Satnavs use graph theory to find the shortest route.

abschnitte.text: In graph theory a **graph** is not the picture of a function but a network of points and lines. The points are called **vertices** or nodes, the connecting lines **edges**. A town map, for example, can be shown as a graph, with junctions as vertices and streets as edges. All that matters is what is connected to what, not the exact position.

In the 18th century, seven bridges crossed the river Pregel in the city of Königsberg. People wondered whether you could take a walk that crossed each bridge exactly once. **Leonhard Euler** from Basel showed in 1736 that this is impossible. Such a route only works if at most two vertices have an odd number of edges.

The number of edges at a vertex is called its **degree**. Because each edge has two ends, the sum of all the degrees is twice the number of edges, so 24 for 12 edges. In the complete graph with 6 vertices every vertex is connected to every other, which gives 15 edges. A **tree** is a graph without cycles, and with 10 vertices it always has 9 edges.

The **four colour theorem** says that any flat map can be coloured with four colours so that neighbouring countries have different colours. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken proved it in 1976, with a computer checking many cases, which was controversial at the time. A cycle that visits every vertex exactly once is called a Hamiltonian cycle. The **travelling salesman problem** looks for the shortest round trip through all cities and is extremely hard when there are many cities.

When a satnav or the SBB timetable looks for the fastest connection, it calculates with graphs. Social networks store who is friends with whom as a huge graph. Power grids, water pipes and the internet are planned this way too. A graph that can be drawn on paper without crossings is called **planar**, which is important, for example, when designing computer chips.

begriffe.erklaerung: A point in a graph, for example a city or a junction.
A connection between two vertices, for example a road.
The number of edges that end at a vertex.
A connected graph without closed cycles.
A graph that can be drawn without any edges crossing.

gewusst: You can draw the German puzzle figure “Haus vom Nikolaus” (the house of Saint Nicholas) in one go, because exactly two corners have an odd degree.
The city of Königsberg is now called Kaliningrad and belongs to Russia.
At every party, the number of guests who have shaken hands with an odd number of people is even.

teile.einleitung: All whole numbers are either even or odd. Even numbers can be divided by 2 without a remainder, odd numbers cannot. This grouping helps with calculating, with counting in twos and even with finding house numbers.
wichtigste: An even number can be divided by 2 without a remainder.
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.
Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.
Even and odd numbers always take turns.
From 1 to 10 there are 5 even and 5 odd numbers.
Even plus even always gives an even number.
In many streets the house numbers on one side are even and on the other side odd.

abschnitte.text: A number is **even** if you can divide it by 2 without a remainder. That means you can share the amount fairly into two equal groups. 14 children, for example, make exactly 7 pairs. The number 0 also counts as an even number.

With an **odd** number, exactly 1 is always left over when you divide by 2. With 21 children, 10 pairs form and one child is left on their own. Odd numbers include 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 21 or 33. After 15 comes 16, an even number, and the next odd number is 17.

You can tell whether a number is even or odd from its **last digit**. If it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8, the number is even. If it ends in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9, it is odd. This works for very large numbers too: 1,000,000 is even and 999 is odd.

On the **number line**, even and odd numbers always take turns. That is why there are exactly 5 even numbers from 1 to 10: 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. If you count in **twos** starting from 2, you only meet even numbers. The smallest even number bigger than 10 is 12.

There are fixed rules for even and odd numbers. Even plus even is even, for example 4 + 6 = 10. Odd plus odd is also even, for example 3 + 5 = 8. Even plus odd, on the other hand, always gives an odd number, and any number times 2 is even.

In many Swiss streets the houses on one side have even and on the other side **odd house numbers**. So anyone looking for number 33 knows straight away which side of the street to look on. Seats in theatres or cinemas are also sometimes divided into even and odd seats. In the game “odds or evens”, people decide something with their fingers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that can be divided by 2 without a remainder.
A number that leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 2.
A line on which the numbers are arranged in order.
What is left over when dividing.

gewusst: The only even prime number is 2.
If you add up the first odd numbers, you always get a square number: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.
A product is only odd if all its factors are odd.

teile.einleitung: In chemistry, saponification is the splitting of an ester with an alkali. The best known is the saponification of fats: this produces soap. People have been making soap this way for thousands of years.
wichtigste: Saponification is the splitting of an ester with an alkali.
Fat and sodium hydroxide solution produce glycerol and soap.
With potassium hydroxide solution you get soft soap, with sodium hydroxide solution solid plain soap.
For 1 mol of fat you need 3 mol of sodium hydroxide.
Saponification is practically irreversible, because the carboxylate ion no longer reacts with the alcohol.
The saponification value indicates how many milligrams of potassium hydroxide are needed for 1 g of fat.
A soap anion has a water-loving head and a fat-loving tail.

abschnitte.text: An **ester** consists of an acid part and an alcohol part. An **alkali** such as sodium hydroxide solution splits it back into these two parts. Ethyl ethanoate and sodium hydroxide solution thus produce sodium acetate and ethanol. With fats, **glycerol** and the salts of the fatty acids are produced, and these salts are nothing other than soap.

If an ester is split with acid, an equilibrium is established and the reaction can run backwards. In saponification, on the other hand, a negatively charged **carboxylate ion** is formed. This no longer reacts back with the alcohol. That is why saponification goes almost to completion. A fat molecule has three ester bonds, so for 1 mol of fat you need 3 mol of sodium hydroxide.

Fats or oils are heated and stirred with alkali until the mixture thickens. **Sodium hydroxide solution** produces solid **plain soap**, **potassium hydroxide solution** soft soap. By adding table salt, the soap is separated from the glycerol. Soap makers use the **saponification value** to calculate the right amount of alkali. Because alkalis are corrosive, safety goggles and gloves are needed.

A soap anion is built like a match: the charged head, the **carboxylate group**, loves water. The long tail of carbon and hydrogen loves fat. During washing, many soap particles stick their tails into the fat and surround it. This produces tiny balls, the **micelles**, which the water can rinse away.

As early as ancient Mesopotamia, people boiled soap from fat and plant ash, which contains an alkali. Later soap became famous in the Mediterranean region, for example olive oil soap from **Marseille** or Aleppo. For a long time soap was a luxury; today it is available everywhere. Modern detergents often contain artificial surfactants that work in a similar way to soap.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of an ester, especially a fat, with an alkali.
An aqueous solution of a base, for example sodium hydroxide solution. It is corrosive.
A sweetish-tasting alcohol that is bonded to fatty acids in fats.
A tiny ball of soap particles that encloses fat inside it.

gewusst: The word “saponification” is now used for the splitting of any ester with an alkali, even if no soap is produced at all.
Glycerol, the by-product of soapmaking, is now found in many creams and toothpastes.
In very hard water, soap forms insoluble lime soap with calcium, which can be seen as a grey ring in the bath.

teile.einleitung: A centrifuge is a device that spins very fast and so separates substances by their density. Heavy particles are pushed outwards, light ones stay further in. Centrifuges are found in laboratories, in dairies and even in the kitchen and the washing machine.
wichtigste: A centrifuge separates mixtures according to the density of their parts.
Because of the fast spinning, centrifugal force pushes heavy particles outwards.
The spinning speed is given in revolutions per minute.
Centrifuged blood separates into blood cells at the bottom and blood plasma at the top.
In a dairy, a centrifuge separates the cream from the milk.
The salad spinner and the spin cycle of a washing machine work on the same principle.
Opposite tubes in a laboratory centrifuge must weigh the same.

abschnitte.text: If you leave a mixture standing for a long time, heavy particles slowly sink to the bottom; this is called **sedimentation**. A centrifuge speeds this process up enormously. The fast spinning produces **centrifugal force**, which pushes everything outwards. Particles with a higher **density** are pushed outwards more strongly than lighter ones. Laboratory centrifuges reach many times the pull of gravity, some even more than a hundred thousand times.

abschnitte.titel: In the kitchen and at home
abschnitte.text: In a **salad spinner**, the water drops fly outwards through the slots while the lettuce leaves stay in the basket. During the **spin** of a washing machine, the drum turns very fast and the water is forced out of the washing. Juice centrifuges also separate juice from fruit pulp. The speed is given in **revolutions per minute**, for washing machines often 1000 to 1600.

In the laboratory, samples are put into small tubes and centrifuged. Blood separates into the heavy red **blood cells** at the bottom and the yellowish **blood plasma** at the top. This lets doctors examine the blood values. Before starting, opposite tubes must weigh the same, otherwise the centrifuge becomes dangerously unbalanced.

Fresh milk contains droplets of fat that are lighter than the rest of the milk. In a dairy, a **milk centrifuge** separates the fatty **cream** from the skimmed milk. The Swedish inventor Gustaf de Laval developed a successful cream separator in the 19th century. In the past, milk had to stand for hours until the cream floated on top and could be skimmed off.

An **ultracentrifuge** spins so fast that it can even separate proteins and viruses from each other. The Swedish chemist Theodor Svedberg developed it and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1926. There are also huge centrifuges for people. In them, pilots and astronauts train for what strong acceleration feels like when a rocket is launched.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that separates substances of different density by spinning fast.
A force that pushes everything outwards during a rotation.
The slow sinking of heavy particles in a liquid.
An uneven distribution of weight in a spinning device that makes it wobble.

gewusst: The word centrifuge comes from Latin and means roughly “fleeing from the centre”.
You can feel centrifugal force on a roundabout too, when you are pushed outwards.
Honey is spun out of the combs in a honey extractor, which is also a centrifuge.

teile.einleitung: The unit circle is a circle with radius 1 whose centre is at the origin of a coordinate system. With it you can explain sine and cosine clearly for any angle. It is the most important tool of trigonometry.
wichtigste: The unit circle has radius 1 and its centre at the origin (0 | 0).
For the angle α, the corresponding point on the unit circle is (cos α | sin α).
By Pythagoras, for every angle: sin²α + cos²α = 1.
The circumference of the unit circle is 2π, so a full circle equals 360° or 2π in radians.
One radian, that is an angle with arc length 1, is about 57.3°.
Sine and cosine repeat every 360° or 2π.
The tangent is sin α divided by cos α and is not defined at 90°.

abschnitte.text: The **unit circle** is a circle with radius 1 in a coordinate system, with its centre at the **origin**. Angles are measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. Each angle α corresponds to exactly one point on the circle. Its x-coordinate is the **cosine** of α, its y-coordinate the **sine** of α. This lets you find sine and cosine not just for acute angles in a right-angled triangle but for all angles.

The axes divide the circle into four **quadrants**. Between 0° and 90°, sine and cosine are both positive. Between 90° and 180°, the sine is positive and the cosine negative, which is why, for example, sin(120°) equals sin(60°). At 180° the point is at (-1 | 0), so cos(180°) = -1. At 270°, or 3π/2, it is right at the bottom, so sin(3π/2) = -1, and sin(225°) has the exact value -√2/2.

Instead of in degrees, angles can also be given in **radians**. Here you measure the length of the arc on the unit circle. A whole circle has the circumference 2π, so 360° equals exactly 2π and 180° exactly π. An angle with arc length 1 is called a **radian** and is about 57.3°. In higher mathematics and physics, people almost always calculate in radians.

If you let a point run round and round the unit circle and plot its height, you get the wave-shaped **sine curve**. After one full turn, that is after 2π, everything repeats; this is the **period**. Because cos(-α) = cos(α), the cosine curve is symmetrical about the y-axis. The tangent is sin α divided by cos α. At 90° the cosine is zero, so the tangent is not defined there.

Circular motion and oscillations are everywhere, for example in a Ferris wheel, a pendulum, sound waves and the alternating current from the socket. With sine and cosine you can calculate them precisely. Computer games use them too, to rotate characters. In ancient times astronomers such as **Hipparchus** already calculated tables for arcs of circles. In the 18th century the Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** shaped the modern view of sine and cosine as functions on the circle.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point (0 | 0) where the x-axis and y-axis cross.
The y-coordinate of the point on the unit circle for an angle.
The x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle for an angle.
A way of giving angles by the length of the arc of the circle.
The distance after which a curve repeats exactly.

gewusst: With Pythagoras' theorem in the unit circle you can see at once why sin²α + cos²α always comes to exactly 1.
The sine and cosine of 45° are equal, namely about 0.707.
As it turns, the gondola of a Ferris wheel has a height that follows exactly a sine curve.

teile.einleitung: Exponential growth means that a quantity always grows by the same factor in equal time intervals, for example doubling every hour. At first this seems harmless, but soon the numbers become huge. It is found in bacteria, in compound interest and in the spread of diseases.
wichtigste: In exponential growth you multiply by the same factor in equal time intervals.
In linear growth, on the other hand, the same amount is always added.
An increase of 4 per cent a year corresponds to a growth factor of 1.04.
The doubling time is the time in which a quantity doubles.
If something grows by 7 per cent a year, it doubles in about 10 years.
In a chart with a logarithmic y-axis, exponential growth appears as a straight line.
In nature nothing can grow exponentially for ever.

abschnitte.text: In **exponential growth** a quantity is multiplied by the same number in equal time intervals: the **growth factor**. In linear growth, by contrast, the same amount is always added, for example 5 francs into the money box every day. The formula is N(t) = N₀ · a^t, where N₀ is the starting value. An increase of 4 per cent a year means the factor 1.04.

A culture of 100 bacteria that doubles every hour has 3200 bacteria after 5 hours. Under good conditions some **bacteria** can even divide about every 20 minutes. A well-known puzzle tells of water lilies that double their area every day and cover the whole pond on the 30th day. The pond was only half covered on the 29th day, just one day before.

According to an old legend, the inventor of chess asked for grains of rice as a reward. There should be 1 grain on the first square, and on each further square twice as many as on the one before. On the 64th square there would then be 2⁶³ grains, about 18 quintillion altogether. That would be far more rice than is harvested in the whole world in many centuries.

Money in a savings account also grows exponentially if interest is paid on the interest too. This is called **compound interest**. If something grows by 10 per cent every year, the growth after 2 years is not 20 but 21 per cent, because 1.1 times 1.1 gives 1.21. A rule of thumb for the **doubling time** is 70 divided by the percentage, so at 7 per cent about 10 years.

In reality exponential growth never goes on for ever, because space, food or other resources run short. Then the curve flattens out and approaches an upper limit; this is called **logistic growth**. With a logarithmic y-axis, exponential growth is easy to recognise because it appears as a straight line. The opposite is exponential decay, for example in radioactive substances.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number you multiply by for each time step; for a 4 per cent increase it is 1.04.
The time in which an exponentially growing quantity doubles.
Growth in which the same amount is added at each time step.
Growth that is fast at first and then reaches an upper limit.

gewusst: If you keep folding a sheet of paper in half, its thickness doubles every time; after 42 folds it would in theory reach the Moon.
For decades the number of components on computer chips doubled roughly every two years; this is called Moore's law.
People often underestimate exponential growth because they tend to think in even steps.

teile.einleitung: The times tables include all multiplications with the numbers from 1 to 10. If you know them by heart, you calculate much faster in everyday life, for example when shopping or counting things. They are one of the most important foundations of all mathematics.
wichtigste: The basic times tables cover all products of the numbers from 1 to 10.
They are arranged in tables, for example the two, five or nine times table.
Multiplying is a shortened addition: 3 times 4 means 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
The order of the numbers does not matter: 6 times 7 is the same as 7 times 6, both make 42.
Tricky ones include 7 times 8 = 56 and 8 times 9 = 72.
All results in the five times table end in 0 or 5.
The extended times tables go up to 20 times 20.

abschnitte.text: The times tables are a collection of **multiplications** that you learn by heart. In the basic times tables, you multiply every number from 1 to 10 by every number from 1 to 10. That makes 100 calculations, from 1 times 1 = 1 to 10 times 10 = 100. The result of a multiplication is called the **product**.

The times tables are usually learnt one **table** at a time. The two times table goes 2, 4, 6, 8 and so on up to 20. The five times table consists of 5, 10, 15 up to 50, which is why 32 is not a result in the five times table. The ten times table is especially easy, because you just add a zero.

A bicycle has 2 wheels, so 8 bicycles have 8 times 2 = 16 wheels. A week has 7 days, so four weeks have 28 days. If you buy 6 packs of 6 yoghurts each, you have 36 yoghurts. This saves you a lot of adding up.

Because 6 times 7 is the same as 7 times 6, you only have to learn about half the calculations. This is called the **commutative law**. In the nine times table, the digit sum of the results always makes 9, for example 81 with 8 + 1 = 9. A well-known finger trick also helps with the nine times table. You can also work calculations out from others: 9 times 9 is 10 times 9 minus 9, that is 81.

About 4000 years ago, the ancient Babylonians were already writing multiplication tables on clay tablets. A well-known times table grid is often attributed to the Greek scholar **Pythagoras**. In the Middle Ages, many people still calculated with the **abacus**. Today children in Switzerland usually learn their times tables in the 2nd and 3rd year of school.

begriffe.erklaerung: The result of a multiplication; for 6 times 7 the product is 42.
One of the numbers that are multiplied together.
All the multiples of a number, for example the three times table 3, 6, 9, 12.
A number times itself, such as 6 times 6 = 36 or 9 times 9 = 81.

gewusst: In the times table square up to 10 times 10, the number 24 appears four times: 3 times 8, 4 times 6, 6 times 4 and 8 times 3.
The German word “Einmaleins” comes from the first calculation: one times one.
If you forget 7 times 8 = 56, you can remember the sequence of digits 5, 6, 7, 8.

teile.einleitung: The binomial coefficient “n choose k” tells you in how many ways you can choose k things from n things if the order does not matter. It helps with counting possibilities, for example in the lottery or when putting teams together. The binomial coefficients also appear in the famous Pascal's triangle.
wichtigste: “n choose k” counts the ways of choosing k elements from n elements.
The formula is n! divided by k! · (n−k)!.
“5 choose 2” has the value 10, and “n choose 0” is always 1.
“n choose k” equals “n choose n−k”, for example “12 choose 11” = 12.
In Pascal's triangle the binomial coefficients stand next to each other row by row.
A set with 5 elements has 2⁵ = 32 subsets.
The binomial coefficients are the numbers you get when multiplying out (x + y)ⁿ.

abschnitte.text: The **binomial coefficient** is written as n over k, with n at the top and k at the bottom inside large brackets. It says how many different groups with k members you can form from n people. From 8 pupils, for example, a committee of 3 people can be chosen in 56 ways. In such choices the **order** does not matter; all that counts is who is included.

The formula uses the **factorial**: n! is the product of all the numbers from 1 to n, so 5! = 120. “n choose k” = n! / (k! · (n−k)!). For “5 choose 2” this gives 120 / (2 · 6) = 10. Because choosing k people is the same as leaving out n−k people, “n choose k” = “n choose n−k”. That is why there are 15 ways to make a team of two and a team of four from 6 people, whether you choose the two or the four.

If you write the binomial coefficients in rows one below the other, you get **Pascal's triangle**. Each number is the sum of the two numbers diagonally above it, and there are always ones along the edge. It is named after the French mathematician Blaise Pascal, who described it in detail in the 17th century. But it was already known centuries earlier in China and Persia. The sum of a row is a power of two, which is why a set with 5 elements has 32 subsets.

The numbers get their name from the **binomial theorem**, which says how to multiply out (x + y)ⁿ. For (x + y)² you get the coefficients 1, 2, 1, that is x² + 2xy + y². In (x + y)⁶, the term x²y⁴ has the coefficient “6 choose 2” = 15. This lets you work out large powers too, without laboriously multiplying everything out.

In **probability theory**, binomial coefficients are essential. If you roll a dice four times, there are “4 choose 2” = 6 ways for exactly two sixes to fall. The probability of exactly two sixes is therefore 6 · (1/6)² · (5/6)², rounded 11.6 per cent. In the Swiss number lottery with 6 out of 42 numbers there are “42 choose 6” = 5,245,786 possible entries.

begriffe.erklaerung: The product of all natural numbers up to n, written n!.
A selection of things in which the order does not matter.
A triangle of numbers in which each number is the sum of the two numbers above it.
An expression made of two terms, such as x + y.
A selection of elements from a set.

gewusst: If you colour in all the odd numbers in Pascal's triangle, you get a pattern that looks like the Sierpinski triangle.
In each row of Pascal's triangle, the sum of the numbers is twice as big as in the row before.
With 10 people there are 45 different handshake pairs, because “10 choose 2” is 45.

teile.einleitung: Algebra is the part of mathematics in which you calculate with letters instead of only numbers. A letter such as x stands for a number that you do not know yet or that can be anything. This lets you write down rules that work for all numbers and solve tricky puzzles.
wichtigste: In algebra, letters called variables stand for numbers.
A mathematical expression made of numbers and variables is called a term.
The first binomial formula is (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b².
The third binomial formula helps with factorising: x² − 49 = (x + 7)(x − 7).
Powers with the same base are multiplied by adding the exponents.
Fractions with variables can be simplified and added just like number fractions.
The word algebra comes from Arabic.

abschnitte.text: In algebra you use **variables** such as x, y, a or b as placeholders for numbers. An expression like 3a² − 2ab is a **term**. If you put in numbers, you can work out its value: for a = 2 and b = -1 you get 3 · 4 − 2 · 2 · (-1) = 12 + 4 = 16. Terms let you write rules briefly and generally.

A **power** such as x³ means x · x · x. When you multiply powers with the same base, you add the exponents: 2x³ · 3x⁴ = 6x⁷. When expanding a bracket, you multiply every term by every other term. So (2x − 3)² becomes the term 4x² − 12x + 9.

Three especially important rules are called **binomial formulas**. The first is (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², the second (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b². The third is (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b². They let you do clever mental arithmetic: 101 · 99 = (100 + 1)(100 − 1) = 10,000 − 1 = 9999.

When **factorising**, you write a sum as a product. Using the third binomial formula, x² − 49 becomes (x + 7)(x − 7). This helps when simplifying algebraic fractions: (x² − 9) : (x − 3) gives x + 3, as long as x is not 3. You must never divide by zero.

Fractions with variables can also be added if you give them a common **denominator**. So 1/x + 1/y becomes (x + y)/(xy). The same rules apply as for ordinary fractions. It is important that the denominator must never become zero.

The name algebra comes from a book by the Persian scholar **al-Khwarizmi**, written in Baghdad around 825. In it he described how to solve equations. Later the Frenchman François Viète introduced letters for numbers. Today algebra is needed in physics, computer science, economics and in programming computer games.

begriffe.erklaerung: A letter that stands for a number.
A mathematical expression made of numbers, variables and operation signs.
Three rules for quickly multiplying out brackets.
Turning a sum into a product.
The small raised number that says how many times to multiply.

gewusst: The word algorithm also comes from al-Khwarizmi's name.
Writing x for an unknown number was made popular by the Frenchman René Descartes in the 17th century.
With binomial formulas you can work out 49 · 51 in your head: 2500 − 1 = 2499.

teile.einleitung: The golden ratio is a special ratio of division of about 1.618, written with the Greek letter φ (phi). If you divide a line so that the whole line is to the larger part as the larger part is to the smaller part, you have the golden ratio. It has fascinated mathematicians, artists and architects since ancient times.
wichtigste: The golden ratio φ has the exact value (1 + √5) / 2, about 1.618.
It satisfies the equation φ² = φ + 1.
A line of 10 cm is divided in the golden ratio into about 6.18 cm and 3.82 cm.
In a regular pentagon, the diagonal and the side are in the golden ratio.
Euclid called it division in extreme and mean ratio.
The architect Le Corbusier from La Chaux-de-Fonds used it for his system of measures, the Modulor.
The golden angle of about 137.5° determines the arrangement of many parts of plants.

abschnitte.text: You divide a line into two unequal parts. In the **golden ratio**, the ratio of the whole line to the larger part is exactly the same as the ratio of the larger part to the smaller part. This ratio is about 1.618 and is called **φ**. For a line of 10 cm, the larger part is about 6.18 cm long.

The exact value is (1 + √5) / 2, an **irrational number**. It satisfies the equation φ² = φ + 1, so its square is exactly 1 bigger than the number itself. Its continued fraction consists only of ones. That is why φ is regarded as the number that is hardest to approximate with fractions.

A **golden rectangle** has sides in the golden ratio. If you cut off a square on the short side, a golden rectangle is left again. In a regular pentagon, the diagonal and the side are also in the ratio φ. That is why the golden ratio appears many times in the pentagram, the five-pointed star.

In sunflowers and many other plants, each new seed or leaf follows the previous one at an angle of about 137.5°. You get this **golden angle** if you divide the full circle in the golden ratio. This creates dense spiral patterns, and the leaves shade each other as little as possible. The Fibonacci numbers, whose ratios approach φ, are also found here.

Around 300 BC **Euclid** already described division in extreme and mean ratio in his “Elements”. The name “golden section” only came into common use in the 19th century. The architect **Le Corbusier**, born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1887, developed from it the system of proportions called the Modulor. Whether famous buildings such as the Parthenon in Athens were deliberately built according to it is disputed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A comparison of two quantities by dividing, for example 10 to 5 = 2.
A Greek letter used as the sign for the golden ratio.
An angle of about 137.5° that results from dividing the circle in the golden ratio.
A system of measures by Le Corbusier based on the human body and the golden ratio.

gewusst: The reciprocal of φ is about 0.618, which is exactly φ minus 1.
Le Corbusier was pictured on the Swiss 10-franc note of the eighth series.
Many supposed examples of the golden ratio in art and the human body do not stand up to precise measurement.

teile.einleitung: The rule of three is a three-step method for calculating an unknown value from a known ratio. If you know what 3 croissants (Gipfeli) cost, you can use it to find out what 7 croissants cost. The rule of three is one of the most useful calculation tools in everyday life.
wichtigste: The rule of three has three steps: starting value, value for one unit, value you are looking for.
In the middle step you work out the value for one unit.
If 3 croissants cost 4.50 francs, one costs 1.50 francs and 7 croissants cost 10.50 francs.
In the direct proportion rule of three: the more, the more.
In the inverse proportion rule of three: the more, the less.
You need the rule of three when shopping, cooking, changing money and travelling.

abschnitte.titel: What is the rule of three?
abschnitte.text: The rule of three links two quantities that are in a fixed **ratio**, such as amount and price. You know one pair of values and are looking for a missing value. The German name, Dreisatz, refers to the three sentences or steps in which you calculate. Mathematicians call such relationships **proportional**.

Example: 3 croissants cost 4.50 francs. In the second step you divide by 3 and get the price for **one unit**, that is 1.50 francs per croissant. In the third step you multiply by 7 and get 10.50 francs. In the same way, 5 exercise books cost 9.00 francs if 8 exercise books cost 14.40 francs, because one exercise book costs 1.80 francs.

If 250 g of cheese cost 6 francs, then 1 kg, four times as much, costs 24 francs. If a tap fills 27 litres in 3 minutes, that is 9 litres per minute and 72 litres in 8 minutes. If a car needs 28 litres of petrol for 400 km, it needs 17.5 litres for 250 km. It also helps when **changing money**: if 100 euros cost 94 francs, then 250 euros cost 235 francs.

“The more, the more” is not always true. If 4 people do a job in 6 hours, 8 people need only 3 hours. Here one quantity rises while the other falls; this is called **inversely proportional**. In the middle step you then multiply first and divide afterwards.

It is best to write the values one below the other in a small **table**. Before calculating, think about whether the result must get bigger or smaller. That way you can quickly tell whether your result makes sense. Sometimes you can do without the single unit, for example going straight from 12 litres of paint for 90 m² to 20 litres for 150 m².

begriffe.erklaerung: Two quantities grow in the same ratio: twice as many goods cost twice as much.
If one quantity becomes twice as big, the other becomes half as big.
A single item or measure, for example 1 croissant, 1 kg or 1 minute.
How two quantities relate to each other, such as price per kilogram.

gewusst: The rule of three was already known in old Chinese and Indian arithmetic books.
In the Middle Ages it was also called the “Golden Rule” in Europe, because it was so valuable for merchants.
You can use the rule of three to convert many recipes from 4 to 6 people.

teile.einleitung: The Babylonians lived around 4000 years ago in what is now Iraq and wrote their numbers in cuneiform on clay tablets. Their number system was based on 60. You meet traces of it every day when you look at the clock.
wichtigste: The Babylonian number system had the base 60.
Babylonia lay between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris.
Numbers were written in cuneiform on clay tablets.
Two basic signs were enough for the numbers from 1 to 59: a wedge for 1 and a corner hook for 10.
It was a place value system: the position of a sign decided its value.
The 60 minutes of an hour and the 360 degrees of a circle go back to the Babylonians.
