abschnitte.text: Babylonia lay in **Mesopotamia**, the “land between the rivers” **Euphrates** and Tigris, in the area of today's Iraq. The capital Babylon was one of the largest cities of the ancient world. The Sumerians, who lived in this region before the Babylonians, already calculated with 60. Babylonian mathematics was at its height around 4000 years ago.

For the digits from 1 to 59 the Babylonians needed only two basic signs. An upright **wedge** stood for 1, a **corner hook** for 10. For 23, for example, you wrote two corner hooks and three wedges. These signs were pressed into soft clay with a sharpened reed.

The Babylonians had a **place value system** like ours, only with the base 60 instead of 10. A 1 in the sixties place and a 1 in the ones place made 60 + 1 = 61. The next place was worth 60 · 60 = 3600. For a long time there was no sign for zero, so people often had to guess from the context which value was meant. Only later was a special sign used to fill gaps.

The Babylonians wrote on **clay tablets**, which dried in the sun or were fired. That is why thousands of them have survived to this day. People have found calculation tables, exercises by trainee scribes and calculations of fields. The famous tablet **Plimpton 322** contains a list of numbers connected with right-angled triangles.

The number 60 can be divided by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30 and 60, which makes calculating with fractions convenient. That is why an hour has 60 minutes and a minute 60 seconds. Dividing the circle into 360 degrees is also traced back to Babylonian astronomers. They observed the sky very closely and predicted the movements of the Moon and the planets.

begriffe.erklaerung: An ancient script of wedge-shaped signs pressed into soft clay.
A number system with the base 60.
A number system in which the value of a digit depends on its position.
The land between the Euphrates and Tigris, home of one of the oldest civilisations.

gewusst: A Babylonian clay tablet shows a value for the square root of 2 that is accurate to about six decimal places.
The Babylonians knew Pythagoras' theorem more than a thousand years before Pythagoras lived.
When you say “It is 3 hours 45 minutes and 30 seconds”, you are using a piece of Babylonian mathematics.

teile.einleitung: Wool is the soft, crinkly hair of animals, above all sheep. For thousands of years people have spun it into yarn and made warm clothes from it. Wool is a natural fibre made of protein and has amazing properties.
wichtigste: Most wool comes from sheep.
Alpacas, llamas, goats and rabbits also provide wool.
To turn wool into yarn, it is spun.
With knitting needles you can knit wool yarn into jumpers, for example.
A woollen jumper keeps you warm because it traps a lot of air.
If you wash wool too hot, it can felt and shrink.
Felt is a thick fabric made of tightly pressed wool.

abschnitte.text: Most wool comes from **sheep**, which are usually shorn once a year. A good wool sheep such as the **Merino sheep** produces several kilograms of wool a year. Very fine wool also comes from the alpaca from South America. Cashmere and mohair come from goats, and especially fluffy angora wool from the angora rabbit.

Wool is made of a protein called **keratin**, which our hair and fingernails are made of too. The surface of a wool fibre is covered with tiny **scales**, rather like roof tiles. Fresh sheep's wool is coated with a grease called **lanolin** or wool wax. This grease is washed out and used for ointments and creams.

After **shearing**, the wool is washed to remove dirt and grease. Then it is combed so that the fibres lie in one direction. In **spinning**, the fibres are twisted into a long thread, in the past with a spindle or spinning wheel, today mostly by machines. The yarn can then be woven, crocheted or knitted with knitting needles.

Wool keeps you so warm because the crinkly fibres trap a lot of **air**, and air conducts heat poorly. Wool can take up a lot of moisture without feeling wet. It does not pick up smells easily and so does not need washing so often. It also burns poorly and often goes out by itself.

When wool is treated with warm water, soap and rubbing, the scales of the fibres hook into each other. This makes **felt**, a thick, firm fabric used for hats, slippers or bags. Exactly this happens when you wash a woollen jumper too hot: it felts and shrinks. That is why wool is washed cold or on the **wool cycle**.

A few hundred thousand sheep live in Switzerland, for example the **Valais Blacknose sheep**. Their wool is often rather coarse and is used for carpets, blankets or as insulation in houses. Fine wool for clothes usually comes from countries such as **Australia** and New Zealand. Besides natural wool, there are now many synthetic fibres such as polyester, which are made from crude oil.

begriffe.erklaerung: Cutting the wool off a sheep.
Twisting fibres into a long thread.
A protein that wool, hair and nails are made of.
A thick fabric made of tightly pressed wool.
The grease in sheep's wool that is used for creams.

gewusst: A sheep does not stop growing wool by itself, so it has to be shorn.
Australia is one of the countries that produce the most wool.
Felt is one of humanity's oldest fabrics and was already made thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: The kilogram is the unit of mass, that is of how heavy something is. A bag of flour, for example, weighs about one kilogram. The kilogram is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units and is used almost worldwide.
wichtigste: The abbreviation for kilogram is kg.
A kilogram has 1000 grams.
Half a kilogram is 500 grams, a quarter of a kilogram 250 grams.
A bag of flour or a litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram.
Light things such as a bar of chocolate are better measured in grams.
1000 kilograms make a tonne.
Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined by a constant of nature.

abschnitte.text: The **kilogram** is the unit used to give the **mass** of an object. In everyday life we usually call it “weight”. The prefix “kilo” means thousand, so a kilogram has 1000 grams. The kilogram is one of the seven base units of the **International System of Units**, SI for short.

A bag of flour, a bag of sugar or a litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram. Half a kilogram is 500 grams, about a packet of pasta. A quarter of a kilogram is 250 grams, which is often how much a block of butter weighs. A bar of chocolate usually weighs 100 grams, so it is better measured in **grams**.

To convert kilograms into grams, you multiply by 1000. So 2 kg are exactly 2000 g. The other way round, you divide by 1000, and 3000 g are 3 kg. For very heavy things such as cars or lorries, the **tonne** is used, which has 1000 kg.

The kilogram was introduced in France at the end of the 18th century. At first it was defined as the mass of one litre of water. From 1889 a cylinder of platinum and iridium was the standard, the **international prototype kilogram**, which is kept in Sèvres near Paris. Because its mass changed very slightly compared with copies, the kilogram has been defined since 20 May 2019 using the **Planck constant**, an unchanging constant of nature.

In Switzerland the metric system with the kilogram and the metre has applied since the 19th century. Precise measurements are the job of the **Federal Institute of Metrology**, METAS for short, in Wabern near Bern. It checks, for example, whether scales in shops measure correctly. That is why the price per kilogram is often shown on the price label in shops, so that you can compare.

You can add weights just like other numbers. A bag weighing 2 kg and one weighing 3 kg weigh 5 kg together. It is important to add only the same units, so kilograms with kilograms. If you have a mixture of grams and kilograms, you first convert everything into the same unit.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter an object has, measured in kilograms.
A smaller unit; 1000 grams are one kilogram.
A large unit for heavy things; 1 tonne is 1000 kilograms.
A device used to measure mass.
A metal cylinder that used to be the standard for the kilogram.

gewusst: The international prototype kilogram is a small cylinder, only about as high and wide as a matchbox is long.
The kilogram was the last base unit still defined by a real object.
On the Moon a kilogram of flour would have the same mass but would press down only about a sixth as hard.

teile.einleitung: In geometry an edge is the line where two faces of a solid meet. A cube, for example, has 12 edges. Edges connect the vertices of a solid and give it its shape.
wichtigste: An edge is the line where two faces of a solid meet.
Each edge connects two vertices.
A cube has 12 edges of equal length.
A cuboid also has 12 edges, but they are often of different lengths.
A sphere has no edges.
From the length of the edges you can calculate the surface area and volume of a cube.
A skeleton model shows a solid only with its edges, like a frame.

abschnitte.text: A **solid** such as a cube or a box is made of faces, edges and vertices. The **edge** is the straight line where two faces meet. Each edge begins at one vertex and ends at another. If you run your finger over a cube, you feel the edges as sharp lines.

A **cube** has 12 edges, all the same length. A **cuboid**, that is a box, also has 12 edges, of which 4 are always the same length. A pyramid with a square base has 8 edges: 4 on the base and 4 leading to the tip. A tetrahedron, a pyramid made of four triangles, has 6 edges.

For a cube a single edge length is enough to calculate everything. If the edge is 3 centimetres, then each face is 3 times 3, that is 9 square centimetres. The **volume** is 3 times 3 times 3, that is 27 cubic centimetres. All the edges together are 12 times 3, that is 36 centimetres long; this is called the **total edge length**.

If you build a solid only from sticks and balls of modelling clay, you get a **skeleton model**. The sticks are the edges, the balls the vertices. This lets you see clearly how a solid is built and how many edges it has. In maths lessons in Switzerland such models are often built with cocktail sticks or drinking straws.

The Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** found that for many solids, vertices minus edges plus faces gives 2. For a cube that means 8 minus 12 plus 6 equals 2. This rule is called **Euler's polyhedron formula**. With it you can work out the number of edges if you know the vertices and faces.

begriffe.erklaerung: A three-dimensional shape that has length, width and height.
A flat side of a solid, for example a square on a cube.
A model that shows only the edges of a solid, like a frame.
A solid with six rectangular faces, like a shoebox.

gewusst: A cube and an octahedron both have exactly 12 edges.
A cylinder has two curved edges but not a single vertex.
The edges of furniture are often rounded so that people do not hurt themselves.

teile.einleitung: Geometric shapes are figures such as circles, triangles, squares or hexagons. They are all around us, on road signs, in buildings and even in nature. If you know the shapes, you can tell them apart by their corners and sides.
wichtigste: A triangle has 3 corners and 3 sides.
A rectangle has 4 sides and 4 right angles.
A square has 4 sides of equal length and 4 right angles.
A circle has no corners.
A hexagon has 6 sides, an octagon 8 sides.
The faces of a cube are squares.
The stop sign on the road is an octagon.

abschnitte.text: The **triangle** is the simplest shape with straight sides: it has 3 corners and 3 sides. There are acute, right-angled and obtuse triangles. Triangles are very stable, so they are found in bridges, roof frames and electricity pylons. Many warning signs on Swiss roads are red triangles.

A **rectangle** has 4 sides and 4 right angles, and opposite sides are the same length. A **square** is a special rectangle in which all 4 sides are the same length. Doors, books and blackboards are usually rectangular. The squares of a chessboard and the faces of a cube are squares.

The **circle** has neither corners nor straight sides. Every point on its edge is the same distance from the centre; this distance is called the **radius**. Wheels, coins and plates are round like a circle. A circle rolls easily, which is why the wheel is so important.

Shapes with many straight sides are called **polygons**. A pentagon has 5 sides, a hexagon 6 and an octagon 8 sides. The stop sign on the road is a red octagon so that you recognise it immediately. Bees build their honeycombs from hexagons, because these fit together without gaps.

Flat shapes are also called **plane figures**; they have only length and width. Three-dimensional shapes are called **solids**, for example the cube, sphere, cylinder and pyramid. A cube has 6 square faces, 8 corners and 12 edges. A sphere is evenly round all over, like a ball.

If you keep your eyes open, you will find shapes everywhere: windows are rectangles, clocks are circles, snowflakes have six points. The Swiss flag is even square, which is very rare in the world. With building blocks, tangrams or Lego bricks you can put shapes together. Artists use geometric shapes in their pictures too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A point where two sides meet.
A straight line on the edge of a shape.
An angle like the corner of a sheet of paper.
A shape with many straight sides and corners.

gewusst: Only Switzerland and the Vatican have a square national flag.
A classic football is made of pentagons and hexagons.
A triangle can have at most one right angle.

teile.einleitung: Speed tells you how fast something is moving, that is what distance is covered in a certain time. Whether snail, bicycle, train or light: everything that moves has a speed. With a simple formula you can work out distances, times and speeds.
wichtigste: Speed is distance divided by time, in short v = s : t.
In everyday life it is usually measured in kilometres per hour, km/h for short.
In physics people use metres per second, m/s for short.
1 m/s equals 3.6 km/h, so 36 km/h is exactly 10 m/s.
The average speed is the whole distance divided by the whole time.
On Swiss motorways the general speed limit is 120 km/h.
At almost 300,000 km per second, light is the fastest thing there is.

abschnitte.text: **Speed** tells you what distance an object covers in a certain time. It is calculated with v = s : t, where s is the distance and t the time. A cyclist who rides 36 km in 2 hours has an **average speed** of 18 km/h. On the way she sometimes rides faster and sometimes slower, but on average it is 18 km/h.

The most important units are **km/h** and **m/s**. A kilometre has 1000 metres and an hour 3600 seconds, so 1 m/s equals 3.6 km/h. To convert from km/h into m/s, you divide by 3.6, so 36 km/h is exactly 10 m/s. The other way round, you multiply by 3.6, and 25 m/s becomes 90 km/h.

You can also rearrange the formula: distance is speed times time, and time is distance divided by speed. A train travelling at 120 km/h covers 90 km in 45 minutes, that is three quarters of an hour. A hiker walking at 4.5 km/h needs exactly 4 hours for 18 km. A cyclist riding at 12 km/h needs 5 minutes for one kilometre.

In Switzerland there are fixed **speed limits**. In built-up areas the general limit is 50 km/h, outside them 80 km/h, on expressways 100 km/h and on motorways 120 km/h. Many residential areas have 30 km/h zones so that children are safer. The police check speeds with radar and laser devices.

A garden snail crawls only a few metres an hour, while the cheetah briefly reaches over 90 km/h. **Sound** travels about 340 m per second in air. That is how you can estimate how far away a thunderstorm is: if 3 seconds pass between lightning and thunder, it is about 1 km away. **Light**, at almost 300,000 km per second, is much faster, which is why you see the lightning practically at once.

In physics, velocity is a **vector quantity**, so it also has a direction. If the speed changes, this is called **acceleration**, for example when setting off or braking. The speedometer in a car shows the speed at that moment. According to Albert Einstein, who published his theory of relativity in Bern in 1905, nothing can be faster than light.

begriffe.erklaerung: The way something travels, for example in metres or kilometres.
The whole distance divided by the whole time taken.
The change in speed per unit of time.
A measuring device that shows the speed at that moment.

gewusst: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
The Earth races round the Sun at about 30 km per second without us feeling anything.
Swiss hiking signposts usually show walking times in hours and minutes instead of kilometres.

teile.einleitung: The derivative of a function tells you how fast a value is changing at this very moment. On the graph it is the gradient of the tangent at a point. It is the central tool of differential calculus and is used all the time in physics, engineering and economics.
wichtigste: The derivative f'(x) gives the instantaneous rate of change of a function.
Geometrically it is the gradient of the tangent to the graph.
You get it as the limit of the difference quotient.
The difference quotient (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a) gives the average rate of change between a and b.
If f'(x) > 0 on an interval, then f is strictly increasing there.
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and Isaac Newton developed differential calculus in the 17th century.
Not every function can be differentiated everywhere; the absolute value function, for example, cannot at x = 0.

abschnitte.text: Imagine you are cycling up a hill and the slope keeps changing. The **derivative** tells you for every single point how steep it is exactly there. Mathematically it is the gradient of the **tangent**, the straight line that just touches the graph at that point. It is written f'(x), spoken “f dash of x” or “f prime of x”. Its unit is always the unit of the function value per unit of the variable, so for a temperature curve T(t) it is °C per hour.

abschnitte.titel: From difference quotient to differential quotient
abschnitte.text: The **difference quotient** (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a) is the gradient of the secant through two points and gives the average rate of change. If you let the second point move closer and closer to the first, the secant becomes the tangent. This limit is called the **differential quotient**, or simply the derivative. For f(x) = x² this gives f'(x) = 2x. The tangent at the point with x = 3 therefore has the gradient 6 and the equation y = 6x−9.

Speed is the derivative of the distance travelled with respect to time. A falling stone covers roughly the distance s(t) = 4.9t². Its speed is the derivative v(t) = 9.8t, so after 3 seconds it is 29.4 m/s. If you differentiate the speed once more, you get the **acceleration**. In this way the derivative describes the motion of cars, rockets and planets.

With the derivative you can investigate graphs precisely. If f'(x) is positive, the graph rises; if it is negative, it falls. Where f'(x) = 0 there is often a maximum or minimum, a so-called **extremum**. The **normal** is perpendicular to the tangent; its gradient is minus one divided by the tangent's gradient, so for f(x) = x² at the point x = 1 it is −1/2. If a graph has a sharp corner, like the absolute value function at x = 0, there is no single tangent there and so no derivative.

Differential calculus was developed in the 17th century by two scholars independently of each other. The Englishman **Isaac Newton** called his method the “method of fluxions” and used it for the physics of motion. The German **Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz** introduced the notation dy/dx that is still used today. A dispute lasting years broke out between their followers over who had the idea first. Later, mathematicians such as the Basel brothers Jakob and Johann Bernoulli and Leonhard Euler greatly extended the theory.

begriffe.erklaerung: A straight line that touches a curve at one point.
A straight line that cuts a curve at two points.
How strongly one value changes in relation to another.
The value that a quantity gets closer and closer to.
Describes a function that has a derivative at a point.

gewusst: The speedometer in a car is really showing a derivative all the time, namely the derivative of distance with respect to time.
The notation f'(x) with the dash goes back to the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange.
There are functions whose graph is connected everywhere but which have no derivative at a single point.

tsevy6f.t: Irrationality of the square root of 2

teile.einleitung: The square root of 2 is the number that gives exactly 2 when multiplied by itself. It is about 1.414, but it can never be written as a fraction. The proof of this is one of the most famous and elegant proofs in the whole of mathematics.
wichtigste: The square root of 2 is about 1.414.
It is the length of the diagonal in a square with side length 1.
It is an irrational number, so not a fraction of whole numbers.
The classic proof is a proof by contradiction.
In it, you assume that the square root of 2 is a fully simplified fraction p/q.
In the end p and q would both be even, which contradicts the assumption.
The square root of 2 is algebraic, because it is a solution of x² − 2 = 0.

abschnitte.text: If you draw a square with side length 1 and join two opposite corners, you get the **diagonal**. By Pythagoras' theorem, the square of the diagonal is then 1² + 1² = 2. So the diagonal is exactly the square root of 2 long, about 1.414. With a calculator you can see many digits, for example 1.41421356. But however far you calculate, the digits never stop and never repeat.

The proof is a **proof by contradiction**. You pretend the opposite is true and show that nonsense follows from it. So you assume that the square root of 2 equals p/q with natural numbers p and q. In addition, you assume that the fraction is **fully simplified**, so p and q have no common factor left. You are allowed to do this, because every fraction can be simplified that far.

From root 2 = p/q, squaring gives p² = 2q². So p² is an **even number**, and therefore p itself must be even, because the square of an odd number is odd. So you write p = 2k and substitute: 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k². Now q² is even too, and so is q. Then p and q would both be divisible by 2, and the fraction would not be simplified at all: a **contradiction**.

There is also a proof using **prime factorisation**. In a square number such as p², every prime factor appears an even number of times, because all the factors of p are doubled. So the factor 2 appears an even number of times in p². On the other side is 2q², and there the factor 2 appears an odd number of times: an even number of times from q² and once more extra. But a number cannot have two different factorisations at the same time, so the assumption is false.

The Babylonians already knew the square root of 2 amazingly accurately. The clay tablet **YBC 7289** from the Yale collection, about 3700 years old, shows a square with diagonals and a value that is correct to about six decimal places. But it was only the **Pythagoreans** in ancient Greece who discovered that the number is irrational. The proof with even and odd numbers is found in a similar form in writings from the time of Aristotle and Euclid. Today it is regarded as a model example of how to prove something with certainty in mathematics.

begriffe.erklaerung: You assume the opposite and show that something impossible follows from it.
A fraction whose numerator and denominator have no common factor except 1.
A number that can be divided by 2 without a remainder, such as 4, 10 or 36.
Splitting a number into a product of prime numbers, such as 12 = 2 · 2 · 3.

gewusst: An A4 sheet is about root 2 times as long as it is wide, which is why a halved sheet has the same shape again.
The Babylonian clay tablet YBC 7289 is roughly the size of the palm of a hand.
With the same principle of proof you can also show that the square roots of 3, 5 and 7 are irrational.

teile.einleitung: In division with remainder, you divide a number that does not come out exactly. What can no longer be shared out completely is left over as the remainder. You meet this kind of division all the time, for example when sharing out apples or forming groups.
wichtigste: Division with remainder has two results: the whole-number quotient and the remainder.
17 : 5 gives 3 remainder 2, because 3 times 5 is 15 and 2 more are needed to make 17.
The remainder is always smaller than the number you divide by.
When dividing by 5, only the remainders 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 are possible.
If the remainder is 0, the division comes out exactly, as in 45 : 9 = 5.
You check the result with the check: quotient times divisor plus remainder gives the starting number again.

abschnitte.text: In a division you ask how often one number fits into another. Often it does not fit exactly, and then something is left over. What is left over is called the **remainder**. The whole-number result is called the **quotient**, the number being divided the **dividend** and the number you divide by the **divisor**.

For 23 : 4, you look for the largest number in the four times table that is not bigger than 23. That is 20, because 5 times 4 is 20. From 20 to 23 there are still 3 missing, so the result is 5 remainder 3. In the same way, 30 : 7 = 4 remainder 2, 50 : 6 = 8 remainder 2 and 38 : 8 = 4 remainder 6.

You can easily **check** whether a division with remainder is right. You work out quotient times divisor and add the remainder. For 17 : 5 = 3 remainder 2, you work out 3 times 5 plus 2, which gives 17 again. In addition, the remainder must be smaller than the divisor, otherwise you could have divided once more.

If 19 apples are shared equally among 3 children, each child gets 6 apples and 1 apple is left over. If 26 children form groups of 4, there are 6 full **groups** and 2 children are left over. Division with remainder is in the clock too: 30 hours are 1 day and 6 hours. It also helps when packing eggs into boxes of 6.

In ancient Greece, the mathematician **Euclid** already used division with remainder. With his method, the Euclidean algorithm, you find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. In higher mathematics the remainder is often written with the word **modulo**, for example 17 mod 5 = 2. Computers need this calculation very often, for example to check whether a number is even.

begriffe.erklaerung: The whole-number result of a division, that is how often the divisor fits in completely.
What is left over when dividing, because it is not enough for a whole part.
The number you divide by.
The technical word for the remainder of a division, for example 17 mod 5 = 2.

gewusst: You can tell whether a number is even from its remainder when dividing by 2: even numbers have the remainder 0.
You can work out the day of the week with division with remainder too: in 10 days it will be the same day of the week as in 3 days, because 10 : 7 = 1 remainder 3.
Many check digits, for example in account numbers, are calculated with the help of remainders.

teile.einleitung: Folding means turning over a sheet of paper or a piece of fabric so that a sharp edge forms. What sounds simple is full of mathematics: folding creates shapes, symmetries and divisions. In Japan it even became an art of its own, origami.
wichtigste: The line along which you fold a sheet is called the fold line.
The fold line is also a mirror line.
If you fold a square from corner to corner, you get a triangle.
If you fold a square edge to edge down the middle, you get a rectangle.
If you fold a sheet in half twice, it is divided into 4 equal parts.
Origami is the Japanese art of folding figures from paper.
If you cut into a folded sheet, the holes appear twice when you open it.

abschnitte.text: When folding, you lay one part of a sheet exactly on top of another part. Where the paper bends over, the **fold line** forms. The two halves then lie exactly on top of each other. That is why the fold line is also a **mirror line**: what is on one side lies mirrored on the other.

If you fold a square sheet once exactly from corner to corner, you get a **triangle**. If you fold it edge to edge down the middle, you get a **rectangle**. With every further fold down the middle, the number of equal parts doubles: 2 become 4, then 8, then 16. In this way you can make halves, quarters and eighths with paper without a ruler at all.

If you cut a small hole in a folded sheet away from the fold line, the opened sheet has **two holes**. They are mirror images of each other across the fold line. This is how paper cuttings, garlands and paper snowflakes are made. If you paint wet paint on one half of a sheet and fold it together, you get a **symmetrical picture**, a so-called blot painting.

**Origami** is the Japanese art of folding figures from paper, usually without scissors or glue. The word is made up of the Japanese words for “fold” and “paper”. The best-known figure is the **crane**, which is a symbol of good luck in Japan. According to an old legend, a wish comes true if you fold a thousand cranes.

Engineers use folding patterns to pack large things into small spaces. The Japanese Koryo Miura invented a **fold** that lets maps and solar panels for satellites be opened and closed with one pull. Airbags in cars are also folded according to precise patterns. Folding boxes, paper aeroplanes and fans are everyday examples.

abschnitte.titel: How many times can you fold?
abschnitte.text: For a long time it was said that you could fold a sheet of paper in half at most seven times. The reason: with every fold the thickness **doubles**. After ten folds there would already be 1024 layers on top of each other. In 2002 the American schoolgirl Britney Gallivan managed twelve folds with a very long strip of paper.

begriffe.erklaerung: The line along which a sheet is bent over.
A line in which a figure is reflected so that both sides are the same.
The Japanese art of folding figures from paper.
When both sides of a figure are mirror images of each other.

gewusst: With a square sheet you can make an equilateral triangle by folding cleverly.
If you could fold a sheet of paper 42 times, the stack would be about as thick as the distance to the Moon.
Origami folding patterns help in space travel to pack large solar sails into small rockets.

teile.einleitung: Wax is a substance that is solid and mouldable at room temperature and melts with only a little warmth. Bees build their honeycombs from it, and people use wax to make candles, ski wax and protective coatings for cheese. There are waxes from animals, from plants and from crude oil.
wichtigste: Wax is solid and mouldable at room temperature and melts at a little over 40 degrees.
Honeybees produce beeswax and build their honeycombs from it.
Most candle wax today is made from crude oil and is called paraffin.
Liquid wax turns solid again as it cools.
A layer of wax makes water roll off.
In the middle of a candle there is a thread called the wick.
Wax is also used for ski wax, cheese rinds and cosmetics.

abschnitte.text: Young worker **honeybees** sweat out wax as thin flakes from special glands on their abdomen. From these they build **honeycombs** with their six-sided cells. In the cells they store honey and pollen and raise their young. Beekeepers melt down old combs and so obtain beeswax. It smells pleasantly of honey and is used for candles, ointments and wood care.

Many plants coat their leaves and fruit with a thin **layer of wax**. It protects them from drying out and makes rainwater roll off. That is why apples shine when you rub them, and cabbage leaves look bluish and frosted. Carnauba wax is obtained from the leaves of a Brazilian palm; it is found in car polishes and as a coating on sweets.

Most candle wax today is **paraffin**. It is obtained from crude oil and consists of long chains of carbon and hydrogen atoms. Paraffin is cheap, has no smell and is easy to colour. There are also candles made of **stearin**, which is produced from plant or animal fats. Chemically speaking, true waxes such as beeswax are compounds of long-chain fatty acids and alcohols.

When you light the **wick**, the heat melts the wax below it. The liquid wax rises up the wick, rather like water in a piece of kitchen roll. At the top it turns into vapour, and the wax vapour burns in the flame. So it is really the wax that burns, not the wick. In **candle dipping** you dip a wick into liquid wax again and again until the candle grows thicker layer by layer, a popular custom in Switzerland during Advent.

People rub **ski wax** onto the underside of skis and snowboards so that they glide better and are protected from moisture. Some cheeses such as Edam are coated with wax on the outside so they do not dry out. Wax crayons are made of wax and colour pigments. Lip balm, shoe polish and furniture polish also contain wax. In wax museums you can marvel at life-size wax figures of famous people.

begriffe.erklaerung: A structure built by bees from many six-sided wax cells.
A wax obtained from crude oil.
The thread in a candle that carries the liquid wax to the flame.
A candle material made from plant or animal fats.
Makes water roll off instead of soaking it up.

gewusst: To make one kilogram of beeswax, bees have to eat many times that amount of honey, because making wax takes a lot of energy.
A candle that has just been blown out can sometimes be relit without touching the wick, if you hold a flame to the rising wax vapour.
The ancient Egyptians already used beeswax, for example for writing tablets and figures.

teile.einleitung: An exponential function is a function in which the variable is in the exponent, for example f(x) = 2ˣ. It describes processes in which something is multiplied or reduced by the same factor at equal time intervals. This is how colonies of bacteria grow and how radioactive substances decay.
wichtigste: In an exponential function such as f(x) = 3ˣ, x is in the exponent.
Every graph of f(x) = bˣ with b > 0 passes through the point (0|1).
If b > 1 the function grows; if 0 < b < 1 it is strictly decreasing.
On the left, the graph of f(x) = 2ˣ approaches the x-axis, which is a horizontal asymptote.
Euler's number e is about 2.718.
The function f(x) = eˣ is the same as its own derivative.
Exponential growth becomes very large very quickly.

abschnitte.text: In an **exponential function**, a fixed number b, the **base**, is raised to the power x. With f(x) = 2ˣ the value doubles when x increases by 1: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. Often there is also a starting value in front, for example f(x) = 5 · 2ˣ; then f(3) = 5 · 8 = 40. In contrast, in a power function such as x², the variable is down in the base.

Because b⁰ = 1, every graph of f(x) = bˣ passes through the point **(0|1)**. The function values are always positive. For f(x) = 2ˣ, the graph gets closer and closer to the x-axis for very small x without touching it. Such a line is called an **asymptote**. For 0 < b < 1, for example with 0.5ˣ, the graph falls, and for large x the values approach 0.

A special base is **Euler's number** e, about 2.718. It is named after the Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler**. The function f(x) = eˣ has a unique property: its derivative is eˣ again. That is why it is often simply called “the” exponential function, and it plays a central role in the natural sciences.

Under good conditions, bacteria divide at regular intervals, so their number doubles again and again. This is **exponential growth**. Money with compound interest also grows exponentially, although more slowly. But such growth cannot go on for ever in nature, because at some point food or space runs out.

Exponential functions also describe decreases. Radioactive substances decay in such a way that after a certain time only half is left; this time is called the **half-life**. Hot tea also cools down to room temperature roughly exponentially. With radiocarbon dating, the age of old bones and wood can be calculated in this way.

People often underestimate exponential growth. If you fold a sheet of paper 10 times, it would be 2¹⁰ = 1024 layers thick. After 42 folds it would, in theory, be thicker than the distance from the Earth to the Moon, even though nobody can actually do it. That is why it is important to understand such functions, for example with epidemics or chain letters.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number that is multiplied by itself several times in a power.
The raised number that says how many times to multiply.
A line that a graph gets closer and closer to without reaching it.
The time after which only half of a substance is left.

gewusst: According to an old legend, the inventor of chess asked for one grain of rice on the first square and twice as many on each following square, which would come to far more rice than exists on Earth.
Euler's number e has infinitely many decimal places that never repeat in a pattern.

teile.einleitung: A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between molecules. It forms when a hydrogen atom is bonded to a strongly electronegative atom such as oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine. These little bridges explain why ice floats, why water only boils at 100 °C and how our genetic material holds together.
wichtigste: Hydrogen bonds act between neighbouring molecules, for example between water molecules.
The hydrogen must be bonded to a strongly electronegative atom such as O, N or F.
A hydrogen bond is much weaker than a covalent bond.
In ice, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules further apart, which is why ice floats.
Water is densest at about 4 °C.
Hydrogen bonds between the bases hold the two strands of DNA together.
They cause the high surface tension on which pond skaters can walk.

abschnitte.text: Oxygen, nitrogen and fluorine pull strongly on electrons; they are strongly **electronegative**. If a hydrogen atom is bonded to one of these atoms, the hydrogen becomes slightly positively charged. It is then attracted by a lone pair of electrons on a neighbouring molecule. This attraction is called a **hydrogen bond**. It is much weaker than a real **covalent bond**, but because there are so many of them, their effect is huge.

A water molecule can form hydrogen bonds with up to four neighbours. That is why water only boils at 100 °C, although hydrogen sulphide, which is built in a similar way, is already a gas at about minus 60 °C. Without hydrogen bonds, water on Earth would be a gas. **Ammonia**, NH₃, and hydrogen fluoride also form hydrogen bonds, but methane does not.

When water freezes, its molecules arrange themselves into a regular lattice with many gaps. The hydrogen bonds hold them further apart than in liquid water. That is why ice is lighter than water and floats on top. Liquid water is densest at about **4 °C**. So the water at the bottom of a frozen lake such as the Lac de Joux is about 4 °C, and fish can survive the winter.

At the surface of water, the molecules attract each other strongly and form a kind of thin skin. This **surface tension** is so strong that **pond skaters** can walk on it without sinking. Even a paper clip laid down carefully can float on water. Drops are round because surface tension pulls them together.

**DNA** consists of two strands that look like a twisted rope ladder. Its rungs are base pairs joined by hydrogen bonds. Because these bonds are weak, the cell can easily open the strands to copy them. The shape of **proteins** is also fixed by hydrogen bonds.

begriffe.erklaerung: How strongly an atom pulls the electrons in a bond towards itself.
A weak attraction between a slightly positive hydrogen atom and an atom of a neighbouring molecule.
How much mass there is in a certain volume.
A force that holds the surface of a liquid together like a thin skin.

gewusst: If ice were heavier than water, lakes would freeze from the bottom up and many water creatures would die.
Snowflakes have six arms because hydrogen bonds arrange the ice lattice in a hexagon.
Freezing water expands and can split rocks; this is called frost shattering.

teile.einleitung: Jakob Bernoulli was a Swiss mathematician from Basel and one of the first great researchers of the famous Bernoulli family. He laid important foundations of probability theory and calculus. Many terms in mathematics still bear his name today.
wichtigste: Jakob Bernoulli lived from 1655 to 1705 and taught in Basel.
He was the first to prove the law of large numbers.
His main work, “Ars Conjectandi”, only appeared in 1713, after his death.
In 1683 he came across the number now called e while calculating compound interest.
In 1690 he was the first to use the term “integral” in print.
His younger brother Johann also became an important mathematician.
He wanted a logarithmic spiral on his gravestone.

abschnitte.text: Jakob Bernoulli was born in **Basel** in 1655 into a wealthy merchant family. At his father's wish he first studied theology, but he secretly studied mathematics and astronomy. After travelling through France, the Netherlands and England, he returned to Basel. From 1687 he was professor of mathematics at the **University of Basel** and remained so until his death in 1705.

Jakob Bernoulli is regarded as one of the founders of **probability theory**. He was the first to prove the **law of large numbers**: if you repeat a random experiment very often, the relative frequency gets closer to the probability. So if you toss a coin a thousand times, heads comes up in roughly half the cases. His main work on this, the “Ars Conjectandi”, was only published in 1713 by his nephew Nikolaus Bernoulli.

While calculating **compound interest**, Bernoulli discovered a special number in 1683 that is now called e and is about 2.718. He worked early on with Leibniz's new calculus and in 1690 was the first to use the word “integral” in print. The **Bernoulli numbers** and a curve shaped like a figure eight lying on its side, the lemniscate of Bernoulli, are named after him. A random experiment with only two outcomes, such as hit or miss, is called a **Bernoulli trial** in his honour.

Jakob's younger brother **Johann Bernoulli** also became a famous mathematician and later the teacher of Leonhard Euler. The brothers worked together at first, but later fell into a fierce quarrel and set each other tricky problems. Altogether the Basel Bernoulli family produced many important mathematicians and physicists over several generations. Johann's son Daniel Bernoulli, for example, became known for his research on flowing liquids.

Jakob Bernoulli admired the **logarithmic spiral** because it always looks the same when enlarged. He wanted this curve on his gravestone, together with the Latin motto “Eadem mutata resurgo”, which means roughly “Though changed, I rise again the same”. But the stonemason carved a simple Archimedean spiral, in which the turns are the same distance apart. The gravestone can still be seen today in the cloister of **Basel Minster**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how certain it is that an event happens, between 0 and 1.
With many repetitions, the frequency gets closer to the probability.
A random experiment with exactly two possible outcomes.
A spiral that opens out more and more and looks the same on a small and a large scale.
An important number in mathematics, about 2.718.

gewusst: The Bernoulli family produced so many mathematicians that they are told apart with Roman numerals, which is why he is also called Jakob I Bernoulli.
A snail shell or the shell of a nautilus has roughly the shape of a logarithmic spiral.
The motto on Jakob's gravestone refers to the spiral, which looks the same again after every enlargement.

teile.einleitung: The incircle of a triangle is the largest circle that fits completely inside the triangle. It touches all three sides from the inside. Every triangle has exactly one incircle, and you can construct it with compasses and a set square.
wichtigste: The incircle touches all three sides of a triangle from the inside.
Its centre is the point where the three angle bisectors meet.
The centre of the incircle always lies inside the triangle.
The radius is measured as the perpendicular distance from the centre to a side.
The sides of the triangle are tangents to the incircle.
A quadrilateral with an incircle is called a tangential quadrilateral.
Every square and every rhombus has an incircle.

abschnitte.text: The **incircle** is a circle that lies inside a shape and touches each side at exactly one point. These points are called **points of contact**. The sides only touch the circle; they do not cut it, which is why they are called **tangents**. Every triangle, whatever it looks like, has exactly one incircle.

The centre of the incircle is the same distance from all three sides. Exactly the points on the **angle bisectors** have this property; these are the lines that divide an angle into two equal halves. That is why the three angle bisectors of a triangle meet at the centre of the incircle. This point always lies inside the triangle, even in obtuse-angled triangles.

First you draw two **angle bisectors** with compasses or a set square. Where they cross is the centre M of the incircle. Then from M you drop a **perpendicular** onto one side. The length of this perpendicular is the radius, and you use it to draw the incircle.

Not every quadrilateral has an incircle; a long rectangle, for example, does not. A quadrilateral with an incircle is called a **tangential quadrilateral**. In it, the sums of opposite sides are equal. Every **rhombus** and every square meets this condition, and a square with a side length of 8 cm has an incircle with a radius of 4 cm.

There is a simple relationship between the radius r of the incircle and the area A of a triangle. A = r · s, where s is half the perimeter. In the right-angled triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5, the area is 6 and half the perimeter is 6, so the radius of the incircle is 1. Every regular polygon, such as a hexagon, also has an incircle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line that divides an angle into two equal parts.
A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point.
The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge.
A line from a point that meets a straight line at a right angle.
A circle that passes through all the corners of a shape.

gewusst: The centre of the circumcircle can lie outside a triangle, but the centre of the incircle never does.
In an equilateral triangle, the centre of the incircle and the centre of the circumcircle are at the same point.
The incircle is the largest circle you can cut out of a triangular piece of cardboard.

teile.einleitung: In geometry a vertex, or corner, is a point where lines or edges meet. A triangle has three vertices, a cube eight. Vertices help us describe, count and tell shapes apart.
wichtigste: A vertex is a point where sides or edges meet.
At each vertex of a cube, three edges meet.
A cube has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces.
Polygons such as triangles and quadrilaterals are named after the number of their corners.
A circle and a sphere have no corners.
In mathematics, vertices are usually labelled with capital letters such as A, B and C.
Euler's formula links the number of vertices, edges and faces of a solid.

abschnitte.text: A **corner** is a point where two sides of a flat shape or several edges of a solid meet. In technical language it is also called a **vertex**. A vertex itself has no length and no area; it is just a point. At every corner of a flat shape there is an **angle**.

Flat shapes with straight sides are called **polygons**. They are named after the number of their corners: triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon and so on. A polygon always has as many corners as sides. Corners are usually labelled with capital letters; a triangle, for example, is then called ABC.

Solids such as cubes, cuboids and pyramids have vertices too. A **cube** has 8 vertices, at each of which 3 edges and 3 faces meet. A pyramid with a square base has 5 vertices, counting the tip. Spheres, cylinders and cones have no real vertices, even though the cone has a point.

The Swiss mathematician **Leonhard Euler** from Basel discovered an amazing rule in the 18th century. For many solids, vertices minus edges plus faces always gives 2. For a cube that is 8 minus 12 plus 6, which is 2. This rule is called **Euler's polyhedron formula** and also works for pyramids and many other solids.

We meet corners everywhere: on tables, books, rooms and houses. Because sharp corners can be dangerous, furniture for children is often made with **rounded** corners. In football there is the corner kick, which is taken from the corner of the pitch. And in traffic, a street corner is a place where you need to take special care.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for a corner in geometry.
A flat shape with straight sides, for example a triangle or a hexagon.
A line where two faces of a solid meet.
The opening between two lines that meet at a point.

gewusst: A cube has exactly as many vertices as an octahedron has faces, namely 8.
The formula vertices minus edges plus faces equals 2 comes from the Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler.
A circle has not a single corner, although you can imagine it as a polygon with infinitely many corners.

teile.einleitung: A cone is a geometric solid with a round base and a single tip. An ice-cream cone, a party hat or a traffic cone on the road have roughly this shape. The cone is closely related to the circle and the cylinder.
wichtigste: A cone has a circular base and a tip.
An ice-cream cone is roughly the shape of a cone.
A cone has exactly 1 tip and 1 round edge.
Its side surface is called the curved surface; it is curved.
A cone holds a third as much as a cylinder with the same base and height.
If you cut a cone, you get circles, ellipses, parabolas or hyperbolas.

abschnitte.text: A **cone** consists of a circular **base** and a curved surface that narrows to a point at the top. The highest point is called the **tip** or apex. If the tip is exactly above the centre of the circle, it is called a right circular cone. The distance from the tip to the base is the height. An ice-cream cone is a cone standing on its head.

A cone has two surfaces: the flat base and the curved **surface**. It has one edge, namely the round rim of the base. It also has exactly one tip. If you stand it on its base, it stands firmly. If you lay it on its side, it rolls round in a circle about its tip.

If you cut open the curved surface of a cone, you get a piece of a circle that looks like a slice of cake. Together with the round base it forms the **net** of the cone. The **volume** is worked out like this: base area times height, and a third of that. So a cone holds exactly a third as much as a cylinder with the same base and the same height. You can try this out by filling the cone with sand three times and pouring it into the cylinder.

If you cut a cone with a flat surface, different curves appear: the **conic sections**. A cut parallel to the base gives a circle, a sloping cut an ellipse. Other cuts give a parabola or a hyperbola. The Greek mathematician Apollonius of Perga studied these curves closely more than 2000 years ago. Today we know that planets travel round the Sun on ellipses.

You find cone shapes in many places. The orange **traffic cones** at roadworks are cone-shaped so that they stand firmly and can be stacked. Many volcanoes, such as Mount Fuji in Japan, have the shape of a cone. Funnels, church spires and the hats at birthday parties are cones too. The beam of a torch also spreads out in the shape of a cone.

begriffe.erklaerung: The flat, round surface on which a cone stands.
The highest point of a cone.
The curved side surface of the cone.
A curve formed when a cone is cut by a plane.

gewusst: A cone with an angular instead of a round base is called a pyramid.
The light-sensitive cells in the eye with which we see colours are called cones because of their shape.

teile.einleitung: When expanding and simplifying, you change how a fraction looks, but not how big it is. 2/3, 4/6 and 12/18 all stand for exactly the same share. You need these two techniques almost everywhere when calculating with fractions.
wichtigste: When expanding, you multiply the numerator and denominator by the same number.
When simplifying, you divide the numerator and denominator by the same number.
The value of the fraction always stays the same.
3/5 expanded by 4 gives 12/20.
12/18 fully simplified gives 2/3.
A fraction is fully simplified when the numerator and denominator have no common factor except 1.
The quickest way to simplify is with the highest common factor.

abschnitte.text: If you divide a bar of chocolate into 3 pieces and eat 2, you have eaten 2/3. If you divide it into 6 pieces and eat 4, you have eaten exactly the same amount, namely 4/6. The fractions look different but have the same **value**. Such fractions are called **equivalent**.

When **expanding**, you multiply the numerator and denominator by the same number. 3/5 expanded by 4 gives 12/20. Expanding 2/7 by 3 gives the fraction 6/21. You expand mainly to give fractions a common denominator, for example before adding. If a denominator is missing, as in 5/6 = 35/?, you can see that the fraction was expanded by 7, so the denominator is 42.

When **simplifying**, you divide the numerator and denominator by the same number. 45/60 can be simplified by 15 to give 3/4. 30/42 becomes 5/7 when simplified by 6. Simplified fractions are clearer and easier to compare.

A fraction is **fully simplified** when the numerator and denominator have no common factor left except 1. 8/15 is such a fraction, because 8 = 2 · 2 · 2 and 15 = 3 · 5. You get there fastest by simplifying with the **highest common factor**; for 12/18 it is 6. But you can also simplify in several small steps, for example first by 2 and then by 3.

**Divisibility rules** help when simplifying. Even numbers can be divided by 2, and a number can be divided by 3 if its digit sum can be divided by 3. If a number ends in 0 or 5, it can be divided by 5. With these rules you can often spot common factors at a glance.

begriffe.erklaerung: Multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number.
Dividing the numerator and denominator by the same number.
The largest number by which two numbers can be divided without a remainder.
Fractions that look different but have the same value.

gewusst: Every fraction has infinitely many equivalent fractions, because you can expand by any number at all.
You may neither expand nor simplify by 0, because you cannot divide by 0.

teile.einleitung: The highest common factor, HCF for short, is the largest number by which two or more numbers can be divided without a remainder. You need it, for example, to simplify fractions or to divide things into the largest possible equal pieces. More than 2000 years ago the Greek mathematician Euclid already knew a clever method for finding it.
wichtigste: The HCF is the largest number that divides two numbers without a remainder.
The HCF of 24 and 36 is 12.
The HCF of 45 and 75 is 15.
The HCF of 84 and 126 is 42.
If two numbers have an HCF of 1, they are called coprime, like 17 and 23.
With the HCF you can simplify fractions completely.
With Euclid's method you can find the HCF of large numbers too.

abschnitte.text: A **factor** of a number is a number by which it can be divided without a remainder. The factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24; the factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36. The numbers that appear in both lists are called **common factors**. The largest of them is 12, so the HCF of 24 and 36 is 12. This is written HCF(24, 36) = 12.

Every number can be split into **prime factors**, that is prime numbers that multiply to give the number. 84 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 7, and 126 is 2 times 3 times 3 times 7. Now you take all the factors that appear in both: 2, 3 and 7. Multiplied, that gives 42, which is the HCF of 84 and 126. This method is clear when the numbers are not too big.

Around 300 BC the Greek mathematician **Euclid** described a method that is now called the **Euclidean algorithm**. You divide the larger number by the smaller one and look only at the remainder. Then you divide the smaller number by this remainder and repeat until the remainder is zero. The last divisor is the HCF. With 75 and 45, the remainder is first 30, then 15, then 0, so the HCF is 15.

Two ribbons are 48 and 72 centimetres long and are to be cut without any left over into the longest possible pieces of equal length. The HCF of 48 and 72 is 24, so each piece will be 24 centimetres long. The HCF also helps with sharing out: from 24 apples and 36 pears you can make at most 12 identical fruit baskets. When laying tiles, the HCF tells you the largest square tile that fills a room without cutting. Gearwheels and rhythms in music are also connected with factors.

To simplify a **fraction**, you divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number. If you divide by the HCF, the fraction is fully simplified in one step. So with the HCF 12, twenty-four thirty-sixths become two thirds. If the numerator and denominator are **coprime**, the fraction cannot be simplified any further. This is the case, for example, with seventeen twenty-thirds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number by which another number can be divided without a remainder.
A number greater than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and itself.
Describes two numbers whose only common factor is 1.
A precise step-by-step set of instructions for solving a task.

gewusst: The Euclidean algorithm is one of the oldest known methods of calculation in the world.
Two different prime numbers are always coprime.
If you multiply the HCF and the lowest common multiple of two numbers, you get exactly the product of the two numbers.

teile.einleitung: Large numbers are numbers such as a million, a billion or far more. We need them, for example, to give the population of countries, distances in space or sums of money. So that they are easy to read, there are fixed names and rules for writing them.
wichtigste: After a thousand come the million, the billion, the trillion and the quadrillion.
A million has 6 zeros, a billion has 9 zeros.
Ten hundred thousands together make a million.
A thousand thousands also make a million.
Straight after 999,999 comes the number 1,000,000.
Half a billion is 500 million.
Large numbers are written in groups of three so that they are easier to read.

abschnitte.text: After a thousand comes the **million**, with 6 zeros. A thousand million make a **billion**, with 9 zeros. A thousand billion make a **trillion**, with 12 zeros, and after that come the quadrillion, the quintillion and so on. Careful: in German a billion is called “Milliarde”, and the German word “Billion” means a trillion; this often leads to confusion.

Large numbers are divided into **groups of three** from the right, for example 2,300,000. In Switzerland an apostrophe is often used for this, so 2'300'000. That way you can see at a glance how many millions and thousands there are. In words, 4,500,000 is written as “four million five hundred thousand”.

In the **place value table** every digit has its place: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and so on. Each place is worth ten times as much as the place to its right. So ten hundred thousands make a million, and so do a thousand thousands. With **powers of ten** this can be written briefly: a million is 10 to the power of 6.

About 9 million people live in Switzerland (as of 2025). On the whole Earth there are about 8.2 billion people (as of 2025). In one year light travels about 9.5 trillion kilometres; this distance is called a **light year**. Such numbers are so large that you can hardly imagine them any more.

If you count one number per second, you need about eleven and a half days without a break to reach a million. For a billion you would need more than 30 years. An especially famous number is the **googol**, a 1 with 100 zeros. Even so, there is no largest number, because you can always add 1.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thousand times a thousand, a 1 with 6 zeros.
A thousand million, a 1 with 9 zeros.
A thousand billion, a 1 with 12 zeros.
The value a digit gets from its position in the number.
A short way of writing numbers such as 10, 100 or 1000, for example 10 to the power of 3.

gewusst: The name of the search engine Google was taken from the number googol.
An English “billion” is only a “Milliarde” in German.
Numbers never stop; you can always make an even bigger one.

teile.einleitung: Units of capacity are units for the volume of liquids and other substances that are poured into containers. The best-known unit of capacity is the litre, along with the decilitre, centilitre, millilitre and hectolitre. We need them for cooking, shopping and wherever liquids are measured out.
wichtigste: Units of capacity tell you how much fits into a container.
The basic unit of capacity is the litre (l).
1 litre has 10 decilitres, 100 centilitres and 1000 millilitres.
A hectolitre has 100 litres.
2.5 litres are 25 decilitres.
Four bottles of 7.5 dl each contain 3 litres altogether.
1 litre is the same size as 1 dm³, and 1 millilitre is the same size as 1 cm³.

abschnitte.text: **Units of capacity** measure the contents of hollow containers such as bottles, cups, buckets or barrels. So they tell you how much liquid fits in. In the past, grain or salt, which was also poured into containers, was measured in this way. Today units of capacity are used mainly for drinks, milk, fuel and ingredients in cooking. The most important unit is the **litre**.

From the litre there are smaller and larger units. The **decilitre** (dl) is a tenth of a litre, the **centilitre** (cl) a hundredth and the **millilitre** (ml) a thousandth of a litre. The **hectolitre** (hl) is a hundred times as big as a litre. You also know the prefixes deci, centi, milli and hecto from units of length such as the decimetre and centimetre. They mean tenth, hundredth, thousandth and hundredfold.

Between litres and decilitres the conversion factor is 10, so 2.5 litres are exactly 25 dl. A litre has 100 cl and 1000 ml. If you want to add different amounts together, you first convert everything into the same unit. Four bottles of 7.5 dl each make 30 dl, and that is 3 litres. Larger amounts such as 350 litres can also be written as 3.5 hectolitres.

Units of capacity are closely linked to **units of volume**, which are needed for solids such as cubes and cuboids. A litre is exactly as big as a cubic decimetre, that is a cube with an edge length of 10 cm. A millilitre equals a cubic centimetre, a little cube with a side length of 1 cm. 1000 litres make a cubic metre. This lets you work out how much water fits into an aquarium or a swimming pool.

In Swiss restaurants drinks are often ordered in decilitres, for example 3 dl of a soft drink. On drinks bottles the contents are often given in litres, on small bottles also in centilitres, for example 33 cl. Medicines for children are measured out in millilitres with a small cup or a syringe. Winegrowers, breweries and dairies calculate in **hectolitres**. A large wooden barrel for wine can hold several thousand litres.

Before the metric system was introduced, every region had its own units of capacity. In Switzerland, for example, the Mass and the Saum were used for wine. These measures were different sizes from place to place, which led to disputes in trade. That is why the litre, which is the same everywhere, was introduced in the 19th century. In Britain and the USA other measures such as the **gallon** and the pint are still partly used today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure for the contents of a container.
A tenth of a litre, shortened to dl.
A hundredth of a litre, shortened to cl.
A hundred litres, shortened to hl.

gewusst: An American gallon holds just under 3.8 litres, a British gallon about 4.5 litres.
A drop of water is roughly a twentieth of a millilitre, so a litre takes about 20,000 drops.
